teile.einleitung: Cumulating (in German “kumulieren”) is a word from electoral law and means writing a name twice on the ballot paper. This gives your favourite candidate two votes at once. In Switzerland this is allowed in many elections, for example in the National Council elections.
wichtigste: Cumulating means writing a name twice on the ballot paper.
The cumulated person thus receives two votes instead of just one.
In the National Council elections you may write a name at most twice.
Cumulating is only common in proportional elections with lists.
Parties sometimes put names on their list twice already; this is called pre-cumulating.
The word comes from the Latin “cumulare”, which means to pile up.
Together with splitting your vote between lists (panachage), cumulating gives voters a lot of freedom.

abschnitte.text: When **cumulating**, you write the name of a person twice on the ballot paper. This shows that you would particularly like to see this person in parliament. He or she then receives two **candidate votes** from this voter. In the end, who is elected depends on who has the most votes within their list.

In the **National Council elections** a name may appear on the ballot paper at most twice. If someone writes a name down three times, the third entry is struck out. In total you may only write down as many names as the canton has seats. The canton of Zurich, for example, has had exactly 36 seats since the 2023 election, so its ballot paper has 36 lines.

Some parties print the names of their candidates on the list twice already. This is called **pre-cumulating**. That way these people automatically receive double votes if someone hands in the list unchanged. Parties often do this when they only have a few candidates, so that the list is still full.

Cumulating goes together with **panachage**. With panachage you write names from other lists on your ballot paper. You can also cross out names you do not want to vote for. These options only exist in **proportional elections**, in which seats are distributed according to the strength of the parties.

Through cumulating, voters can decide for themselves which people from a party are elected. So they do not just vote for a party but also for very specific people. This gives citizens more influence. In some other countries this is not possible; there the party alone decides the order of its list.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sheet on which you write the names in an election.
A person who stands for election.
A ballot paper with the names of a party's candidates.
An election in which seats are distributed according to the parties' share of the vote.

gewusst: In some German federal states you may also cumulate in local elections, there sometimes even up to three votes per person.
Anyone who writes a name three times on the ballot paper does not make it invalid; the third entry simply does not count.

teile.einleitung: Someone who moves to a new municipality often does not know anyone there yet. That is why many Swiss municipalities invite their new residents to a welcome event (Neuzuzügeranlass). There they are welcomed and introduced to the village or town.
wichtigste: At the **welcome event** the municipality greets its new residents.
Those invited are people who have **recently moved to the municipality**, often with their family.
Often the **mayor** gives a short speech.
**Clubs and associations** also introduce themselves.
Some municipalities organise a **walk around the village**.
At the end there is often an **apéro**.

abschnitte.text: After a move, many things are new: the streets, the school, the neighbours. So that new people quickly feel at home, many municipalities invite them to a **welcome event**. Everyone who has moved there recently is invited. They are often allowed to bring their **family**. The aim is simple: new people should feel **welcome**.

The event usually begins with a short speech by the **mayor**. In this way the newcomers get to know the **authorities**. The municipality explains what there is in the place and how life there works. You find out, for example, about the **municipal assembly**, waste disposal or the schools. This helps new people find their way around better.

Often the village **clubs** introduce themselves too, for example the gymnastics club, the brass band or the fire brigade. This way newcomers quickly find a suitable hobby and new acquaintances. Some municipalities take their guests on a **walk around the village**. They show important places such as the **municipal building**, the school or the library.

After the speeches there is often an **apéro** with something to drink and small snacks. Now people can chat with each other. The newcomers get to know other new residents, members of the authorities and club members. Many first contacts in the new place are made right here.

gewusst: In Switzerland the apéro is a fixed tradition at many municipal events.
Anyone who moves must register with the residents' registration office of the new municipality, so the municipality also knows whom it can invite.

teile.einleitung: Switzerland has four national languages: German, French, Italian and Romansh. That is why the country also has four names: Schweiz, Suisse, Svizzera and Svizra.
wichtigste: The four national languages are German, French, Italian and Romansh.
Around 6 in 10 people have German as their main language.
Switzerland is called Suisse, Svizzera and Svizra.
The French-speaking part is called Romandy.
In German-speaking Switzerland people speak Swiss German in everyday life.
“Allegra” is a Romansh greeting.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Constitution** names four **national languages**: German, French, Italian and Romansh. German is the most common: around **6 in 10** people in Switzerland have German as their main language. It is followed by French, Italian and Romansh, which only a small minority speaks. Many people also speak other languages, for example English, Portuguese or Albanian.

**German-speaking Switzerland** lies in the north, east and centre of the country. The French-speaking west is called **Romandy** or Western Switzerland. Italian is spoken mainly in **Ticino** and in some valleys of the Grisons. **Romansh** is spoken in parts of the **Grisons**, for example in the Engadine. Some cantons such as Fribourg, Valais and Bern are bilingual, and the Grisons is even trilingual.

In everyday life, people in German-speaking Switzerland mostly speak **dialect**, that is **Swiss German**. There are many different dialects, for example Bernese German or Basel German. At school people write **High German**, also called Standard German. Newspapers and books are also mostly written in Standard German.

In French Switzerland is called **Suisse**, in Italian **Svizzera** and in Romansh **Svizra**. In Italian you say hello with **“Buongiorno”** and goodbye with **“Arrivederci”**. In French you say “Bonjour” and “Au revoir”. A typical Romansh greeting is **“Allegra”**, which you hear in the Engadine, for example.

gewusst: Coins and stamps often say “Helvetia”, the Latin name of Switzerland, so that no national language is favoured.
Romansh has been a national language of Switzerland since a popular vote in 1938.

teile.einleitung: A Parliamentary Investigation Committee, PUK for short, is the strongest control tool of the Swiss parliament. It is only set up for events of great importance and has special rights.
wichtigste: The PUK is based on parliamentary oversight under Article 169 of the Federal Constitution.
It is set up by a simple federal decree of both councils.
A PUK may formally question witnesses and see all files.
The PUK of 1989 uncovered the secret files scandal (Fichenaffäre).
The PUK on the Military Department in 1990 revealed the secret organisations P-26 and P-27.
Isabelle Chassot chaired the PUK on Credit Suisse; the report appeared in December 2024.

abschnitte.text: According to **Article 169** of the Federal Constitution, the Federal Assembly has **oversight** of the Federal Council, the administration and the courts. In the case of particularly serious events it can set up a PUK. The rules are in the **Parliament Act**. Both councils must agree, by means of a **simple federal decree**. This sets out the mandate and the budget.

A PUK has more rights than the standing committees. It can **formally examine witnesses**, that is question them officially. It may see all **files** and appoint **investigators**. **Official secrecy** cannot be used against it. Both councils provide the same number of members. The president and vice-president come from **different councils**.

The origin is considered to be the **Mirage affair** of 1964. The costs of new Mirage fighter jets rose massively. The Federal Council needed an additional credit of almost 580 million francs. An investigation under **Kurt Furgler** led to only 57 aircraft being bought.

In 1989 a PUK under **Moritz Leuenberger** investigated the Justice Department (FDJP) after the resignation of Federal Councillor Elisabeth Kopp. This brought the **secret files scandal** to light: the federal police had kept watch on hundreds of thousands of people. In 1990 the **PUK on the Military Department** investigated the intelligence services and the secret groups **P-26** and **P-27**. They worked without sufficient legal basis or control. In 1995 a PUK dealt with the **Federal Pension Fund**.

After the collapse of the major bank **Credit Suisse**, parliament set up a PUK again. The chair was Council of States member **Isabelle Chassot** from Fribourg, and the vice-chair Franziska Ryser. The report appeared on **20 December 2024**. A PUK does not always come about: in 2010 the National Council wanted a PUK on the financial crisis and the rescue of UBS, but the Council of States said no.

gewusst: There have only been a few PUKs in the history of the federal state, which is why each one is a big event.
The secret files scandal caused big protests; many people demanded to see their file.

teile.einleitung: When you draw lots, chance decides. For example, you pull a slip of paper out of a hat or toss a coin. This is fair because everyone has the same chance.
wichtigste: When drawing lots, chance decides.
You can draw lots with a coin or with slips of paper in a hat.
Pulling out a slip without looking is called drawing lots.
When drawing lots, everyone has the same chance.
In a tie, lots can decide.
In National Council elections, too, lots can decide when the votes are equal.

abschnitte.text: When you **draw lots**, **chance** decides what counts. For example, you write two names on slips of paper and put them in a hat. A child pulls out a slip **without looking**. This is called **drawing lots**. The name on the slip that is drawn wins. Nobody can know beforehand what the result will be.

A **coin** can also be used to draw lots. A coin has **two sides**: heads and tails. That is why it is a good choice when you have to choose between two suggestions. Before the toss you agree which side stands for which suggestion. Then you toss the coin and see which side lands face up. In football, for example, this is how the choice of ends is decided before the match.

When drawing lots, **each side has the same chance**. Nobody is favoured, and nobody can influence the result. That is why lots are often used when there is a **tie**. If, for example, two candidates have the same number of votes, lots can decide. That way there is still a result and everyone can accept it.

Drawing lots also exists in politics. If two people have exactly the same number of votes in the **National Council elections** but there is only one seat, **lots** decide. This is laid down in the **Federal Act on Political Rights**. It happens very rarely. But in **2011** in **Ticino**, lots really did have to decide between two people.

gewusst: In ancient Athens many offices were not elected but allocated among the citizens by lot.
The word “lottery” is related to the word lot.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland most judges belong to a party. Many regularly pay their party part of their income. This levy is called a mandate tax or mandate levy.
wichtigste: With the mandate levy, judges give part of their income to their party.
The parties describe the contributions as voluntary, but in practice they are expected.
The party nominates candidates, who therefore do not have to run their own election campaign.
GRECO of the Council of Europe criticises the mandate levy.
Critics see the independence of the judiciary at risk.
For the year 2023 the Swiss Federal Audit Office published the contributions of federal judges for the first time.

abschnitte.text: The judges of the **Federal Supreme Court** are elected by the **Federal Assembly**. In practice the **parties** nominate the candidates. The seats are distributed roughly according to the strength of the parties. This has an advantage for the candidates: they do not have to run **their own election campaign**, because the party secures them the necessary votes in parliament. In return the party expects regular money from the elected judges.

The **mandate levy** is not a state tax. It is a payment that elected office-holders make to their own party. There is **no legal obligation** to pay it. The parties therefore stress that the contributions are **voluntary**. In fact, however, elected judges are expected to pay. According to SRF, in 2020 judges from the Greens paid around **15,000 francs** a year, and those from the SP about 13,000 francs. For many parties this is an important **source of income**.

**GRECO**, the Group of States against Corruption of the **Council of Europe**, criticises the close ties between judges and parties. It calls for federal judges to stop paying a mandate levy. Critics fear that judges remain financially and politically **dependent** on their party. But judges should only be bound by the **law**. The mandate levy could thus weaken the **independence of the judiciary**. Internationally, this practice is very unusual.

For a long time it was unclear exactly how much money was involved. Under the new **transparency rules** on political financing, parties must report contributions from office-holders every year. The **Swiss Federal Audit Office** published the contributions of federal judges for the year **2023** for the first time. So today anyone can look up how much the judges pay their parties. Supporters of the current system say that party membership makes the political views of judges openly visible.

gewusst: In 2021 the voters clearly rejected the Justice Initiative. It wanted federal judges to be chosen by lot from a pool of experts.
Many cantonal judges and other elected office-holders also pay their party a mandate levy.

teile.einleitung: A postulate is a parliamentary proposal. With it, parliament instructs the Federal Council to examine a question and write a report on it.
wichtigste: A postulate asks the Federal Council for a report examining a question.
It can be submitted by council members, parliamentary groups or committees.
The approval of the council in which it was submitted is enough.
The Federal Council first proposes acceptance or rejection.
A postulate is fulfilled with a postulate report.
The word comes from the Latin “postulare”, to demand.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin **“postulare”**, which means to demand or request. With a **postulate**, parliament asks the Federal Council to **examine** something. It is to find out, for example, whether a new law or a measure is necessary. It writes a **report** on this. So a postulate is weaker than a motion, which obliges the Federal Council to draw up a proposal.

Postulates are **proposals** from parliament. They can be submitted by individual **council members**, **parliamentary groups** or **committees**. Besides the postulate there are other proposals: with the **motion** parliament gives a binding instruction, and with the **interpellation** and the **question** it asks the Federal Council questions. Many cantonal and municipal parliaments also have the postulate.

For each new postulate the Federal Council gives a recommendation: it proposes **acceptance or rejection**. The council must then decide. Unlike with a motion, the approval of the council in which the postulate was submitted is enough. The other council does not have to vote on it.

Once a postulate has been accepted, the Federal Council fulfils it with a **postulate report**. This states what it has examined and what it proposes. Such reports can later be the basis for new laws. Once the Federal Council has fulfilled the postulate, parliament can **write it off**, that is declare it dealt with.

gewusst: A postulate only needs the approval of a single council.
A postulate report can be the first step towards a new law.

teile.einleitung: Freedom of residence (freedom of establishment) is a fundamental right in the Federal Constitution. It allows all Swiss citizens to live anywhere in the country. However, this right did not always apply equally to everyone.
wichtigste: Freedom of residence is set out in **Article 24** of the Federal Constitution.
Swiss citizens may settle **anywhere** in Switzerland.
Art. 24 para. 2 allows people to **leave** Switzerland and **re-enter** it.
In 1848 freedom of residence only applied to **Christian Swiss**; since **1866** it has also applied to Jewish Swiss.
For people from the EU the **Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons** applies.
After a move you must **register with the new municipality**.

abschnitte.text: According to **Art. 24** of the Federal Constitution, Swiss citizens may settle anywhere in the country. No municipality may forbid anyone to move there, not even because of **poverty**. In the past municipalities could turn away poor people; today this is ruled out. **Paragraph 2** also guarantees the right to leave Switzerland or to enter Switzerland. Settling is free, but you must register within a set time with the **residents' registration office** of the new municipality.

The Federal Constitution of **1848** introduced freedom of residence, but only for **Christian Swiss**. Jewish Swiss were excluded from it. Only with a **partial revision** in **1866** were freedom of residence and equality before the law extended to them. Of nine proposals, this was the only one that was accepted. The constitution of **1874** laid down that residents could also vote and elect in their new place after three months. At that time this only applied to men.

**Art. 39 para. 2** states that you exercise your political rights at your **place of residence**. Anyone who moves then votes in the new municipality. According to **para. 4**, the cantons may set a waiting period before newcomers may have a say in cantonal and municipal matters. This period is at most **three months**.

Art. 24 only applies to Swiss citizens. For people from the **European Union**, the **Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons** regulates living and working in Switzerland. It has applied since **2002**. EU citizens may live and work in Switzerland under certain conditions, for example if they have a job here.

gewusst: In the constitutional revision of 1866, of nine proposals only the one on equal rights for Jewish Swiss was accepted.
In the past municipalities could turn away poor people; today the Federal Constitution forbids this.

teile.einleitung: The Parliamentary Services are the staff of the Swiss parliament. They support the National Council and the Council of States in their work, so that sessions and committee meetings run smoothly.
wichtigste: The Parliamentary Services are anchored in Article 155 of the Federal Constitution.
They are led by the Secretary General of the Federal Assembly.
The Secretary General is also Secretary of the National Council.
In 2017 around 310 people worked for the Parliamentary Services.
In the past the Federal Chancellery also did work for parliament.
In French they are called “Services du Parlement”.

abschnitte.titel: Staff of its own for parliament
abschnitte.text: According to **Article 155** of the Federal Constitution, the Federal Assembly has **Parliamentary Services**. In the past the **Federal Chancellery** served both the Federal Council and parliament. With the Federal Constitution of 1999, the Parliamentary Services became fully independent. Today the Federal Chancellery is the staff of the Federal Council. In French the Parliamentary Services are called “Services du Parlement”, in Italian “Servizi del Parlamento”.

At the top is the **Secretary General of the Federal Assembly**. This person is also **Secretary of the National Council**. The deputy is Secretary of the Council of States. In 2017 around **310 people** worked for the Parliamentary Services in about 217 full-time positions. Many of them work part-time.

The Parliamentary Services plan the **sessions** and **committee meetings**. They do the secretarial work and write reports, **minutes** and translations. The minutes of the committees are not public. They also look after **foreign delegations**, plan trips by council members and inform the public about parliament. Putting laws into force, on the other hand, is not one of their tasks; that is a matter for the Federal Council.

gewusst: The Federal Assembly can also call on offices of the federal administration for its work.
Because Switzerland has a militia parliament, council members particularly depend on the support of the Parliamentary Services.

teile.einleitung: The large dome is the landmark of the Federal Palace in Bern. On the outside it is green; on the inside a coloured glass dome shines with the Swiss coat of arms and the coats of arms of all the cantons.
wichtigste: The outside of the dome is covered with copper.
The green colour comes from the patina on the copper.
Inside there is a dome made of coloured glass.
In the middle is the Swiss coat of arms, around it are the cantonal coats of arms.
The dome bears the words “Unus pro omnibus, omnes pro uno”.
The coat of arms of the canton of Jura was only added in 1981.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Palace** in Bern is the seat of parliament and government. The outside of its dome is covered with **copper sheeting**. Copper reacts with air and rain and over time forms a turquoise-green layer. This layer is called **patina**. It forms by itself and protects the metal.

Beneath the outer dome is an **inner dome made of coloured glass**. This lets light into the **Dome Hall**. In the middle you can see the **Swiss coat of arms** as a mosaic, surrounded by oak leaves and held by two female figures. All around it the **coats of arms of the cantons** are painted on glass. They stand for the cantons that together form Switzerland.

The dome bears the Latin motto **“Unus pro omnibus, omnes pro uno”**. This means **“One for all, all for one”**. The motto expresses that the cantons stick together. It is regarded as the unofficial motto of Switzerland.

abschnitte.titel: The coat of arms of Jura
abschnitte.text: When the Federal Palace was built, the **canton of Jura** did not yet exist. It was only created in 1979 as the youngest canton of Switzerland. Its coat of arms was added to the glass dome in **1981**. Since then all the cantons have been represented in the dome.

There are several figures in the Dome Hall. By the stairs of the entrance hall stand **two bears**; the bear is the heraldic animal of Bern. On the staircase in the Dome Hall there are four bronze figures of **mercenary soldiers (Landsknechte)**. Each one stands for one of the **four national languages** of Switzerland.

gewusst: The Federal Palace was opened in 1902; the architect was Hans Wilhelm Auer.
You can visit the Federal Palace on free guided tours.

teile.einleitung: Legislative planning is the Federal Council's roadmap for four years. It sets out which goals the government wants to achieve in a legislative period and how it intends to pay for them.
wichtigste: A legislative period at federal level lasts four years.
At the start of each legislative period the Federal Council presents parliament with its dispatch on legislative planning.
The 2023 to 2027 legislative planning has four guidelines and 25 goals.
One guideline concerns protecting the climate and natural resources.
The annual goals make the planning concrete for each year.
In its management report the Federal Council shows what it has achieved.
The legislative financial plan adds the financial side to the planning.

abschnitte.text: A **legislative period** is the term of office of parliament and government. At federal level it lasts **four years**. After the elections the National Council is completely re-elected, and the Federal Assembly elects the Federal Council anew. At the start of each legislative period the **Federal Council** writes a **dispatch on legislative planning**. In it, it sets out its political guidelines and goals for the next four years.

The goals are arranged under **guidelines**. A guideline is a big topic under which there are several goals. In the **2023 to 2027** legislative planning there are **four guidelines** and **25 goals**. One guideline concerns, for example, prosperity and digitalisation, another the **protection of the climate and natural resources**. Each goal comes with concrete **measures**. In the 2019 to 2023 legislative period there were still three guidelines.

The Federal Council proposes the legislative planning, but **parliament** debates it. The National Council and the Council of States can change goals, delete them or add new ones. At the end they adopt the plan. In this way government and parliament decide together where politics should go in the coming years.

Good plans need money. That is why legislative planning includes a **legislative financial plan**. It shows how the planned projects are to be financed. So that the planning is not just on paper, the Federal Council sets **annual goals** every year. They are derived from the legislative planning and describe the steps for a single year.

abschnitte.titel: Accounting for it in the management report
abschnitte.text: At the end of each year the Federal Council takes stock. In the **management report** it compares its goals with the results. The report goes to parliament. There it is examined by the **Control Committees**. They check whether the government and the administration have done good work. This makes visible what has been achieved and what has not.

gewusst: Legislative planning is a cycle: plan, carry out and then account for it in the management report.
Many cantons and municipalities also draw up their own government programme for their term of office.

teile.einleitung: With a parliamentary initiative, parliament itself proposes a new law or a change. Unlike with many other proposals, the draft here is written not by the Federal Council but by a committee of parliament.
wichtigste: It can be submitted by individual members, parliamentary groups and committees.
A parliamentary initiative is not the same as a popular initiative.
First there is a preliminary examination by the responsible committee.
If one committee gives it the go-ahead, the committee of the other council must agree.
After that the committee normally has two years to draw up a draft.
The Federal Council may only give an opinion on the draft.

abschnitte.text: Usually the **Federal Council** drafts new laws and parliament debates them. With the **parliamentary initiative** it can be done differently. Here the proposal comes from parliament itself. It can be submitted by individual **members**, **parliamentary groups** and **committees**. If a committee submits it, it is called a **committee initiative**. Do not confuse them: a popular initiative comes from the people and needs signatures.

The first phase is called the **preliminary examination**. The responsible committee clarifies whether a law is really needed. Then it decides whether to **give the initiative the go-ahead**. For it to continue, the corresponding **committee of the other council** must also agree. Only then may work on the draft begin.

After the decision, the committee normally has **two years** to draw up a proposal. Its preliminary draft also goes into the **consultation procedure**. In this way cantons, parties and associations can give their opinion on it. The Federal Council does not help to write it, but may give an **opinion**. After that the two councils debate the proposal like any other law.

The parliamentary initiative is regarded as the **strongest proposal** in parliament. With a motion, for example, the Federal Council must take action and write the draft. With a parliamentary initiative, parliament writes the draft itself. So it does not depend on the government. The rules for this are in the **Parliament Act**.

gewusst: Cantons can also make a proposal to the federal parliament; this is then called a cantonal initiative.
Many important changes in the law in recent decades go back to parliamentary initiatives.

teile.einleitung: The principle of transparency (Öffentlichkeitsprinzip) means that in principle everyone may see official documents of the federal administration. You do not have to give a reason for this. It has applied since 2006 and makes the work of the state more transparent.
wichtigste: Under the principle of transparency, every person may in principle see official documents.
No reason needs to be given.
The law is called the Freedom of Information Act and is abbreviated BGÖ.
It has applied in the federal administration since 1 July 2006.
Before that, the principle of secrecy applied.
If a request is refused, you can turn to the Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner.

abschnitte.text: Under the **principle of transparency**, everyone in principle has access to **official documents** of the federal administration. These can be reports, contracts or letters. Anyone who asks to see them does **not have to give a reason** or prove any special interest. On the contrary: the administration must give reasons if it refuses access. Only in **exceptional cases** set out in law do documents stay secret, for example to protect security or personal data.

In the past the **principle of secrecy** applied in the federal administration. Documents were secret in principle unless they were expressly released. The **Freedom of Information Act**, **BGÖ** for short, of 17 December 2004 reversed this. It came into force on **1 July 2006**. Many cantons now have their own laws with a similar principle for their administration.

If the administration rejects a request, you can turn to the **Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner**, **FDPIC** for short. He or she carries out a **mediation procedure** and makes a recommendation. After that you can also go to court. Since a change in the law passed by parliament in 2022, access has in principle been **free of charge**. A fee can only be charged for particularly time-consuming requests.

The principle of transparency creates **openness**. The population can better understand what the administration is doing. It is particularly important for **journalists**. They can request documents for their research and so check the work of the authorities. Sometimes they uncover mistakes or abuses in the process.

gewusst: Anyone may make a request for access, even without a Swiss passport.
A request can be completely informal, for example by email.

teile.einleitung: In a mandatory referendum, a proposal automatically goes to the people. Nobody has to collect signatures for it. This applies above all to every change to the Federal Constitution.
wichtigste: Every change to the Federal Constitution must be put to a vote.
Usually a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons are needed.
The mandatory constitutional referendum has existed since the first Federal Constitution of 1848.
Joining supranational communities is also subject to the mandatory referendum (Article 140 of the Federal Constitution).
In 1992 the people and the cantons rejected joining the EEA, and in 1986 joining the UN.
Today's Federal Constitution was accepted on 18 April 1999.

abschnitte.titel: What must go to the people
abschnitte.text: The rules are in **Article 140** of the Federal Constitution. All **changes to the Federal Constitution** are subject to the mandatory referendum. So is joining organisations for **collective security** and **supranational communities**. Certain federal laws declared urgent that have no basis in the constitution are also included. No signatures are needed for this.

abschnitte.titel: Majority of the people and of the cantons
abschnitte.text: A proposal in a mandatory referendum usually needs a **double majority**. The **majority of the people** means that more than half of the voters say yes. The **majority of the cantons** means that most of the cantons agree. There are 23 cantonal votes because six cantons have only **half a cantonal vote** each. Two halves together make a whole, so for example 11 whole votes and 2 halves, that is 12 out of 23, are enough.

There is an exception for a **total revision**, that is a completely new constitution. If a popular initiative calls for a total revision, at first only the people decide on the **preliminary question** of whether it should take place at all. Here the majority of the cantons does not count. The people and the cantons then vote on the new constitution itself. The Federal Constitution in force today was accepted on **18 April 1999** and came into force on 1 January 2000.

On 16 March 1986 around three quarters of voters and all the cantons rejected **joining the UN**. Only in 2002 did Switzerland say yes to the UN, through a popular initiative. On **6 December 1992** Switzerland voted on joining the **European Economic Area** (EEA). The people narrowly rejected it, the cantons clearly.

The very first Federal Constitution of **1848** required the people and the cantons to approve changes to the constitution. This makes the mandatory referendum the **oldest popular right** in the federal state. Later the optional referendum and the popular initiative were added. There are also mandatory referendums in the cantons.

gewusst: Because every change to the constitution must go to the people, Switzerland votes more often than almost any other country.
In 1986 all the cantons rejected joining the UN; in 2002 it was accepted after all.

teile.einleitung: Night-time quiet hours are the time at night when everyone should be quiet. They protect people's sleep. In Switzerland they are laid down in the rules of the municipalities and in house rules.
wichtigste: During **night-time quiet hours** everyone should be quiet so that people can sleep.
In many Swiss municipalities quiet hours begin at **10 pm**.
The exact time can be slightly different depending on the municipality and the house rules.
Many house rules also have a **midday quiet period**.
On **Sundays** special quiet often applies in Switzerland.
Loud music, vacuuming or slamming doors are disturbing at night.

abschnitte.text: People need **peaceful sleep** to stay healthy. In a **block of flats** many people live close together. What is loud in one flat can often be heard next door too. That is why there are fixed times when everyone shows consideration. Night-time quiet hours protect everyone from noise at night.

In many Swiss municipalities and house rules, quiet hours begin at **10 pm**. They last until the morning. The **municipalities** set the exact times in their regulations, and the **house rules** can contain further rules. That is why it is worth knowing the rules where you live.

At night you turn **loud music** down or off. Noisy jobs such as **vacuuming** or drilling are better done during the day. Late in the evening you close doors **quietly**, because slamming doors can be heard throughout the building. You also speak quietly in the stairwell at night. That way you do not disturb anyone's sleep.

Besides night-time quiet hours, many Swiss house rules also have a **midday quiet period**. Then you should also be quiet, for example for small children or people who work shifts. **Sunday** is a day of rest in Switzerland. Noisy jobs such as **mowing the lawn** are forbidden on Sundays in many municipalities. Special quiet often applies on public holidays too.

gewusst: In many Swiss municipalities mowing the lawn on a Sunday is forbidden.
The rules on night-time quiet can differ from municipality to municipality.

t18nbrm0.t: Members of the Council of States

teile.einleitung: The Council of States is the chamber of the cantons in the Swiss parliament. Here it does not matter how many people live in a canton: small and large cantons have the same number of seats. In total, the Council of States has 46 members.
wichtigste: The Council of States has **46 members**.
Most cantons have **two seats**, no matter how big they are.
**Six cantons** have only one seat: the former half-cantons.
They are Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
Uri and Zurich each have two seats in the Council of States.
**Jura** is the youngest canton and has had two seats since 1979.

abschnitte.text: In the National Council large cantons have many seats. In the **Council of States** it is different: here each canton represents its interests with the same number of votes. So **Uri** and **Zurich** each have two seats, even though many more people live in Zurich. **Bern** and **Glarus** also have two each. This protects the small cantons from being outvoted by the large ones.

Six cantons have only one seat. They are the former **half-cantons**: Obwalden and Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft, and Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden. Two of each used to belong together. So Obwalden and Nidwalden together have two seats. Since the Federal Constitution of 1999 they are officially no longer called half-cantons, but they still have only one seat.

Switzerland has 26 cantons. **20 cantons** have two seats each, which makes 40. Then there are the **6 cantons** with one seat each. 40 plus 6 makes **46 seats**. Together with the 200 members of the National Council they form the **Federal Assembly**.

Each canton decides for itself how the members of the Council of States are elected. Almost everywhere the people elect them on the same day as the National Council. Usually the **majority system** applies: whoever gets the most votes is elected. The canton of **Jura**, which has only existed since 1979, is the youngest canton in the Council of States. Since then it has also had two seats.

gewusst: In the Council of States, a canton with a few tens of thousands of inhabitants has as much weight as Zurich.
Since the founding of the canton of Jura in 1979, the Council of States has had 46 seats.

teile.einleitung: The National Council is the more important of the two chambers of the Austrian parliament. It has 183 members and meets in the Parliament Building on Vienna's Ringstrasse. The name is the same as in Switzerland, but some of the rules are different.
wichtigste: Since 1971 the Austrian National Council has had **183 members**.
Since 2007 a legislative period has lasted **five years**.
Since 2007 you have been able to vote in Austria **from the age of 16**.
To win seats, a party needs **4 per cent** of the votes or a basic seat.
The National Council and the Federal Council together form the **Federal Assembly**.
In May 2019 the National Council removed a government by a **vote of no confidence** for the first time in the Second Republic.

abschnitte.text: The Austrian parliament consists of the **National Council** and the **Federal Council**. The National Council is the more important chamber, because it is directly elected by the people. Since 1971 it has had **183 members**. When it meets together with the Federal Council, it forms the **Federal Assembly**. The newly elected Federal President takes his **oath of office** before it.

With the electoral reform of 2007, the **legislative period** was extended from four to five years. Early dissolution remains possible. In the same year Austria lowered the **voting age to 16**. It was thus the first EU country with a voting age of 16 at national level. A party needs at least **4 per cent** of the valid votes nationwide or a **basic seat** in a regional constituency.

After the **Ibiza affair**, the National Council passed a vote of no confidence in Sebastian Kurz's government on 27 May 2019. This was the first time in the **Second Republic**. Afterwards a caretaker government under **Brigitte Bierlein** ran the country. In the election of 29 September 2024 the **FPÖ** became the strongest party for the first time, with around 29 per cent. However, the government was then formed by the ÖVP, SPÖ and NEOS.

The National Council meets in the **Parliament Building** on Vienna's Ringstrasse. The architect **Theophil Hansen** designed it in the style of ancient Greece. It was completed in 1883. After a major **renovation** the building reopened in 2023. It is one of the best-known buildings in Vienna.

gewusst: In 2007 Austria was the first EU country where you could vote in national elections at the age of 16.
The 4 per cent threshold is lower than in Germany, where it is 5 per cent.

teile.einleitung: A parliament is an assembly of elected representatives of the people who pass laws. The parliament of Switzerland is called the Federal Assembly and consists of the National Council and the Council of States. It meets in the Federal Palace in Bern.
wichtigste: The Swiss federal parliament is called the Federal Assembly.
It consists of the National Council with 200 seats and the Council of States with 46.
When both councils meet together, the United Federal Assembly has 246 members.
Parliament holds four ordinary sessions every year.
A new federal law needs the approval of both councils.
Because most members also have a job, it is called a militia parliament.
Members from the same or similar parties form a parliamentary group.

abschnitte.text: A **parliament** is the law-making power in a state, the **legislature**. Its members are elected by the people and represent their interests. Parliament makes laws, decides on the state's money and keeps a check on the government. The word comes from the French “parler”, which means to speak.

The Swiss **Federal Assembly** has two chambers. The National Council with 200 members represents the people. The **Council of States** with 46 members represents the cantons; each canton has two seats and the six former half-cantons one each. Both councils have exactly the same say; this is called a bicameral system with equal chambers.

Parliament meets four times a year for a three-week **session**: in spring, summer, autumn and winter. If necessary there are additional special sessions. Between sessions, committees prepare the items of business. The members join together in parliamentary groups; a group needs at least five members from one council.

A new federal law is first debated in one council and then in the other. If the councils do not agree, the text is sent back and forth; this is called the **procedure for resolving differences**. If that does not help, a conciliation conference made up of both councils looks for a solution. Only when both councils have agreed is the law passed; after that the people can still call a referendum.

For certain tasks both councils meet together as the **United Federal Assembly** with 246 members. It elects the seven members of the Federal Council, the Federal Chancellor and the federal judges. In time of war it also elects the General of the army. Cantons and many larger municipalities also have their own parliaments, for example the Grand Council, the cantonal council or the municipal council.

begriffe.erklaerung: The law-making power in the state.
A sitting period of parliament lasting several weeks.
A group of council members with similar political views.
The back and forth between the councils until they agree.

gewusst: The Federal Palace in Bern, where parliament meets, was opened in 1902.
In Switzerland the people can still stop a law passed by parliament with a referendum.

teile.einleitung: Bullying means that someone is deliberately picked on, laughed at or left out again and again. This can happen at school, in a club or on the internet. Anyone who sees bullying can help, and that is important.
wichtigste: Bullying is when someone is picked on **deliberately, again and again**.
Laughing at someone and **leaving them out** can also be bullying, not just hitting.
A bullied child is **never to blame**.
Anyone who reports bullying to a teacher is **not telling tales but helping**.
**Bystanders** can stop bullying too.
If you get nasty messages in a chat, take a **screenshot** and show it to adults.

abschnitte.text: We speak of **bullying** when a child is picked on again and again over a longer period. This can happen with words, for example by laughing at, insulting or spreading rumours. It can also mean deliberately never letting someone join in. Sometimes someone is pushed or their things are hidden. A one-off argument is not bullying.

Bullied children often feel **sad and lonely**. Some are afraid to go to school or get tummy aches. What matters is: a bullied child is **never to blame**. The responsibility lies with the children who do the bullying. Anyone who stands by a bullied child shows them that they are not alone and gives them courage.

There are often many **bystanders** when bullying happens. They have great power: if they stop laughing along, bullying becomes less fun. Anyone who sees bullying gets **help from adults**, for example from the teacher or parents. This is **not telling tales**. Someone who tells tales wants to harm someone. Someone who reports bullying wants to protect someone.

When someone is picked on in a chat or on social media, this is called **cyberbullying**. If you receive nasty messages, it is best not to reply. Take a **screenshot** as evidence and show it to an adult you trust. In Switzerland you can also contact the **Pro Juventute** helpline on **147**. They will listen to you and help.

gewusst: Pro Juventute's number 147 is free for children and young people in Switzerland.
Bullying often stops when several bystanders take the side of the child being picked on together.

teile.einleitung: Normally laws in Switzerland are made in parliament, often with the people having a say. But in serious crises things sometimes have to happen very quickly. For this, the Federal Constitution gives the Federal Council emergency ordinance powers, that is the right to issue temporary emergency ordinances.
wichtigste: The basis for emergency ordinances on security is **Art. 185 para. 3 of the Federal Constitution**.
For foreign policy, **Art. 184 para. 3 of the Federal Constitution** applies.
Emergency ordinances must always be **temporary**.
Without a draft law submitted to parliament, an emergency ordinance lapses after **six months**.
A replacement ordinance of the Federal Assembly applies for at most **three years**.
Emergency law was used, for example, during the **Covid-19 pandemic** in 2020 and in the **takeover of Credit Suisse** in 2023.

abschnitte.text: According to **Art. 185 para. 3 of the Federal Constitution**, the Federal Council may issue ordinances and rulings if a **serious disturbance** of public order or of internal or external security has occurred or is directly threatening. Mere political urgency is not enough. **Art. 184 para. 3** gives it a similar right to protect the country's interests in its **foreign relations**. Such ordinances are based directly on the constitution.

The constitution expressly requires emergency ordinances to be **temporary**. Emergency law should not become a permanent state of affairs. Since a change in the law in **2011**, the **Government and Administration Organisation Act** (RVOG) has regulated the time limits more precisely. If the Federal Council does not submit a draft law within **six months**, the ordinance ceases to apply. An ordinance of the Federal Assembly that replaces it also applies for at most **three years**.

During the **Covid-19 pandemic**, the Federal Council declared an “extraordinary situation” on **16 March 2020**. Until 19 June 2020 it issued numerous emergency ordinances. In **March 2023** it used an emergency ordinance to make possible the takeover of **Credit Suisse** by **UBS**. In this way guarantees and liquidity assistance could be provided quickly. Parliament could only debate it afterwards.

In the **Second World War**, parliament gave the Federal Council very far-reaching powers with the **Full Powers Decree** of August 1939. This is known as the **full powers regime**. At that time the Federal Council was allowed to govern largely without parliament. Today the constitution pays more attention to control. If the Federal Council calls up more than **4,000 members of the armed forces** for active service, or if the deployment is expected to last longer than three weeks, the Federal Assembly must be convened immediately under **Art. 185 para. 4**.

gewusst: During the 2020 pandemic, the Federal Council governed for around three months in the “extraordinary situation”.
The full powers regime of the Second World War stood outside the normal constitutional order.

teile.einleitung: The rule of applicable law (in German “Massgeblichkeitsgebot”) is an important rule of the Federal Constitution. It is in Article 190 and says that the courts must apply federal laws and international law, even if a federal law contradicts the constitution.
wichtigste: The rule of applicable law is set out in Article 190 of the Federal Constitution.
The article bears the heading “Applicable law”.
Federal laws and international law are binding on the Federal Supreme Court and all authorities that apply the law.
Even a federal law that contradicts the constitution must be applied.
The Federal Supreme Court can, however, examine cantonal laws for their constitutionality.
The court may find that the constitution has been breached, but must still apply the law.

abschnitte.text: Article 190 of the **Federal Constitution** bears the heading **“Applicable law”**. It says, in essence: **federal laws** and **international law** are binding on the Federal Supreme Court and the other authorities that apply the law. Binding means that they must apply these rules. This rule is called the **rule of applicable law** or **duty to apply**. It applies not only to the Federal Supreme Court but also to administrative authorities and cantonal courts.

In many countries a constitutional court can strike down a law if it breaches the constitution. In Switzerland this is not possible for **federal laws**. There is no **constitutional review** of federal laws here. Even an **unconstitutional** federal law remains applicable. One reason for this: federal laws are passed by parliament, and the people can vote on them with a **referendum**. That is why they should have the last word, not the judges.

Article 190 is a **duty to apply**, not a **ban on examination**. So the Federal Supreme Court may investigate whether a federal law is compatible with the constitution. It can also **find** that there is a breach. But it must still apply the law. With such a finding, however, the court can prompt the legislator to correct the law.

Article 190 only protects federal laws and international law. With **cantonal laws** it is different. The Federal Supreme Court can examine whether a cantonal act is compatible with the Federal Constitution. If it breaches it, the court can **strike it down** or **not apply** it in an individual case. In this way the Federal Supreme Court ensures that the cantons respect fundamental rights and federal law.

It becomes difficult when a federal law and an international treaty contradict each other. In the **Schubert** case in **1973**, the Federal Supreme Court decided that the legislator can **deliberately** depart from older international law. Then the more recent federal law takes precedence. This is called the **Schubert practice**. The Federal Supreme Court later restricted this practice where **human rights** are concerned.

gewusst: In Switzerland, for federal laws, it is not a court but ultimately parliament and the people who have the last word.
There have been several attempts in parliament to introduce constitutional review for federal laws, but they were rejected.

teile.einleitung: The Children's Rights Ombudsman Switzerland (Ombudsstelle Kinderrechte Schweiz) is a place children and young people can turn to. It helps when young people feel that their rights are not being respected.
wichtigste: An ombudsman's office is an independent body that gives advice and mediates neutrally.
The Children's Rights Ombudsman Switzerland began its work in 2021.
It is aimed mainly at children and young people.
It helps especially in difficult proceedings with authorities, for example in divorces or decisions by the child protection authority.
It is easy to reach: you can contact it simply and without hurdles.
The word ombudsman comes from Swedish.

abschnitte.text: An **ombudsman's office** is an **independent** place to turn to. It listens, gives advice and mediates between those affected and authorities or institutions. Independent means: it does not work for any authority or party and does not take sides. Only in this way can it mediate fairly. The word **ombudsman** comes from Swedish and means something like commissioner or representative. In Sweden this office has existed since the 19th century.

The **Children's Rights Ombudsman Switzerland** has existed since **2021**. It is supported by foundations and cantons. It mainly advises children and young people and explains everything in a way children can understand. It helps, for example, when parents **divorce**, when children are **placed outside their family** or with decisions by the **child protection authority**. The office is **easy to reach**: children can get in touch without complicated forms and without a lawyer.

Children have rights of their own. They are set out in the **UN Convention on the Rights of the Child**, which also applies to Switzerland. An important right is the **right to be heard**: children should be allowed to give their opinion in proceedings that affect them. The ombudsman's office helps them to put their point of view across clearly. In this way decisions about children are not made without them.

gewusst: In Switzerland there are also ombudsman's offices for other areas, for example for banks or insurance.
Switzerland ratified the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child in 1997.

teile.einleitung: The militia system means that many people in Switzerland hold a public office alongside their actual job. So parliament includes farmers, teachers, doctors and craftsmen. The militia system shapes Swiss politics, the army and many municipalities.
wichtigste: In the militia system many politicians hold their office alongside another job.
The federal parliament is therefore regarded as a militia parliament.
Parliament meets four times a year for a three-week session.
The Swiss Army is also organised on the militia principle.
In many municipalities councillors, firefighters and school boards work part-time.
The word militia comes from the Latin “militia”, which means military service.
Many municipalities today find it hard to find enough people for their offices.

abschnitte.text: In the **militia system**, public tasks are not only carried out by professionals but by citizens alongside their work. The idea is that everyone contributes to the common good. Someone who holds a **militia office** brings experience from their own working life. In this way politics stays close to people's everyday lives.

The 246 members of the Federal Assembly meet four times a year for a three-week **session** in Bern. In between they have committee meetings and often work in their own jobs. That is why it is called a **militia parliament**. In reality, however, the office takes a lot of time today; many members of parliament spend more than half their working time on politics.

The militia system is particularly important in Switzerland's roughly 2,100 municipalities. Many municipal councillors, members of school boards or of the polling station staff hold their office alongside their job. Most fire brigades also consist of **militia firefighters**. Without this commitment, many small municipalities could not carry out their tasks.

The **Swiss Army** is also a militia army. The soldiers are not professional soldiers but do their service in recruit school and refresher courses. Afterwards they return to their everyday lives. Only a small part of the army consists of professional military personnel.

One advantage is that the militia system is cheaper and many different professions are represented in politics. Critics say that militia politicians sometimes have too little time to get to grips with difficult topics. In addition, many people find it hard to juggle work, family and office. That is why municipalities are looking for new solutions, for example better pay or more flexible working hours.

begriffe.erklaerung: A public office that you hold alongside your job.
A sitting period of parliament lasting several weeks.
In addition to your main work.
The well-being of all people in a community.

gewusst: The members of the Federal Council are not militia politicians; they hold their office full-time.
According to estimates, tens of thousands of people in Switzerland are involved in a militia office in their municipality.

teile.einleitung: Panachage (in German “panaschieren”) means writing names from different lists on the same ballot paper in an election. This lets you vote for candidates from several parties. In Switzerland this is allowed in proportional elections such as the National Council elections.
wichtigste: Panachage means writing names from different lists on the same ballot paper.
To do this, you can cross out names on a list and write in others.
The word comes from the French “panacher”, which means to mix.
Panachage is allowed in proportional elections such as the National Council election.
A vote for a person added by panachage also counts for their party.
Empty lines count as party votes for the list whose name is at the top of the ballot paper.
Together with cumulating, panachage gives voters a lot of freedom.

abschnitte.text: With **panachage** you mix names from different party lists. For example, you take one party's list, cross out a name and write in its place the name of a person from another list. In this way you can vote for people you particularly like, even if they are not in your favourite party. The French word “panacher” means to mix.

You can take a pre-printed **list** and cross out names on it and add others. But you can also take a blank ballot paper and write in all the names yourself. In total you may not write down more names than the canton has seats. It is important to write the names clearly.

Every vote for a person counts as a **candidate vote** for that person and as a **party vote** for their party. So anyone who adds a person from another list also helps that person's party. Empty lines on the ballot paper go to the party whose name is at the top of the ballot paper. If a blank ballot paper has no party name, empty lines count for nobody.

Panachage is often mentioned together with **cumulating**. When cumulating, you write a name twice on the ballot paper. Together, both give voters the chance to fill in their ballot paper entirely as they wish. Such freedoms are common in Switzerland and in some German federal states, but not in many other countries.

Someone who gets many votes from other lists is regarded as popular across party lines. After the elections the cantons publish how many **votes from other lists** someone has received. Some candidates move up their list as a result and are elected. In this way voters can directly influence which people get into parliament.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ballot paper with the names of one party.
A vote that helps a party in the distribution of seats.
A vote for a particular person.
Writing a name twice on the ballot paper.

gewusst: In proportional elections a party sometimes even wins an extra seat through votes from other lists.
Anyone who writes the name of someone from another party on their ballot paper takes a party vote away from their own party.

teile.einleitung: After its meetings, the Federal Council informs the public at a press conference. There members of the Federal Council and the Federal Council spokesperson explain what the government has decided.
wichtigste: The Federal Council usually meets once a week.
The press conferences usually take place in the Federal Palace Media Centre in Bern.
They are led by the Federal Council spokesperson, who is also Vice-Chancellor.
The responsible members of the Federal Council present their items of business.
Under the principle of collegiality, they also defend decisions they themselves opposed.
Press releases are also published.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Council** normally meets **once a week** in the Federal Palace in Bern for its meeting. There it makes many decisions. Afterwards the most important of them are announced publicly. This is what the **press conference** is for. It usually takes place in the **Federal Palace Media Centre** and is also broadcast on the internet. So anyone can watch.

The responsible members of the Federal Council present their items of business themselves and answer questions from journalists. The conference is led by the **Federal Council spokesperson**. He is also **Vice-Chancellor** in the Federal Chancellery. He also gives information about other decisions. Besides the conference, the Federal Council publishes its important decisions on the day of the meeting as **press releases**. So everyone can find out directly.

The Federal Council decides as a **collegial body**, that is as a group of seven members with equal rights. Under the **principle of collegiality**, all of them defend the decisions together in public. This also applies when a member was outvoted internally. That is why a federal councillor sometimes presents a decision at the press conference that he or she personally opposed. Differing opinions usually remain **confidential**.

gewusst: You can follow the Federal Council's press conferences live on the internet.
The Federal Council consists of seven members, all with equal rights.

teile.einleitung: Neighbourly help means that people who live close to each other support one another. Often it is small things that make a big difference. This creates a good community in the building, the street or the village.
wichtigste: In **neighbourly help**, neighbours help each other.
You can **do the shopping** for neighbours who are ill or elderly.
When neighbours are on holiday, you can **water the flowers** or feed their pet if they ask you to.
In winter you help elderly neighbours with **shovelling snow**.
If a parcel for the neighbours was left with you, you take it round to them.
**Neighbours' Day** usually takes place at the end of May.

abschnitte.text: Someone who is ill or can no longer walk well often cannot manage the **shopping** alone. It helps a lot if a neighbour brings something back for them. In winter, snow and ice are dangerous for elderly people because they slip easily. Anyone who **shovels** the path in front of the house **clear** makes it safer. And if a parcel was left with you, you honestly take it to the neighbours.

When neighbours are on **holiday**, their plants still need water. You can water the flowers or empty the letterbox. A cat or another **pet** also needs food every day. What matters is: you only help if the neighbours have asked you to. Then you often get a key and exact instructions.

Someone who moves into a new building does not know anyone yet. A friendly **“Welcome”** helps them feel at home. Some people introduce themselves briefly or explain where the laundry room is. That is how you get to know each other. If you know your neighbours, it is also easier to ask for help later.

In many countries, including Switzerland, there is **Neighbours' Day**. It takes place in spring, usually at the end of May. Neighbours then meet in the courtyard, in the street or in the garden to eat and chat. Everyone brings something. This leads to new acquaintances and sometimes friendships.

gewusst: Neighbours' Day is celebrated in many European countries, often on the same day.
Good neighbourliness also helps with safety: people who know each other are more likely to notice when something is wrong.

teile.einleitung: With a constructive vote of no confidence, the German Bundestag can remove the Federal Chancellor. But at the same time it must elect a successor, so that the country is never without a government.
wichtigste: The constructive vote of no confidence is set out in Article 67 of the Basic Law.
The Bundestag must elect a new chancellor with a majority of its members.
There must be 48 hours between the motion and the vote.
Up to 2025 there were two such votes in the Bundestag, in 1972 and 1982.
The rule is a lesson learned from the Weimar Republic.
Spain also has the constructive vote of no confidence.

abschnitte.titel: The rule in the Basic Law
abschnitte.text: According to **Article 67 of the Basic Law**, the Bundestag can only express its lack of confidence in the Federal Chancellor by **electing a successor**. It then asks the Federal President to dismiss the previous chancellor. What is needed is the **chancellor majority**, that is a majority of all the legal members. Abstentions and absences therefore count like no votes. There must be **48 hours** between the motion and the vote.

In the **Weimar Republic** from 1919 to 1933, opposing parties could join forces to bring down a government. Afterwards they often failed to form a new majority. Governments were therefore very **unstable**. This was not to happen again. That is why the Basic Law requires a new majority to choose a new chancellor straight away.

In **1972** Rainer Barzel (CDU) tried to replace Federal Chancellor **Willy Brandt**. He missed the required majority by two votes. Later a member of parliament admitted to having received money for abstaining. In **1982** the second attempt succeeded: Helmut Kohl replaced Helmut Schmidt as Federal Chancellor. Up to 2025 there were only these two votes.

With the **destructive** or simple vote of no confidence, a majority against the government is enough. Whether a new majority then comes about remains open. **Spain** also has the constructive form, the “moción de censura”. In June 2018 the Spanish parliament used it to replace Mariano Rajoy with **Pedro Sánchez**. In **Switzerland** there is no vote of no confidence: the Federal Council is elected for four years and cannot be removed by parliament.

gewusst: Helmut Kohl is so far the only German Federal Chancellor who came into office through a constructive vote of no confidence.
The word “constructive” means “building up”: you do not just bring a government down, you build a new one at the same time.

teile.einleitung: When many people have to decide something together, they vote. The winner is then usually the majority, that is the side with more votes. This is how decisions are made in the class, in the municipality and in the whole of Switzerland.
wichtigste: In a vote, the side with more votes wins.
The majority is the larger group.
The smaller group is called the minority.
More than half of the votes is always a majority.
The result of a vote applies to everyone.
The minority deserves respect too.
In a democracy, the majority decides.

abschnitte.text: The word **majority** comes from the Latin for “greater”. It is the group that has **more votes** than the other. An example: 12 children want to play football, 8 children want to play dodgeball. 12 is more than 8. So football has the majority and is played. The group with fewer votes is called the **minority**.

Sometimes a proposal needs **more than half** of all the votes. In a class of 20 children, half is 10. So more than half means **11 votes** or more. This is called an **absolute majority**. If there are several proposals, often the one with the **most votes** simply wins. With 7 votes for painting, 9 for singing and 4 for crafts, singing wins. This is called a **relative majority**.

After a vote, the **result applies to everyone**. Even those who lost take part. This is sometimes not easy, but it is part of democracy. Next time you can vote again, and perhaps your own idea will win then. The majority must never **make fun of** the minority. The children who lost deserve **respect** too, and their opinion is just as important.

In a **democracy** people have a say. What the majority wants is done. In Switzerland the people vote several times a year. Some votes even need two majorities: the majority of voters, the **majority of the people**, and the majority of the cantons, the **majority of the cantons**. In this way both the many people in large cantons and the small cantons count.

gewusst: Changes to the Federal Constitution in Switzerland always need a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.
Sometimes votes are very close, and then only a few votes decide.

teile.einleitung: The National Council chamber is the largest council chamber in the Federal Palace in Bern. The National Council meets here, and both councils meet here when they elect the Federal Council together. A large mural recalls the beginnings of the Swiss Confederation.
wichtigste: The **National Council** meets in the National Council chamber.
The **United Federal Assembly** also meets here, for example to elect the Federal Council.
The large mural is called **“The Cradle of the Confederation”**.
It was painted by **Charles Giron** from Geneva.
The seats are arranged **in a fan shape** around the presidency.
Every year the **Youth Session** takes place here.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Palace** in Bern has two council chambers: one for the National Council and one for the Council of States. The **National Council chamber** is the larger. When both councils meet together, they need a lot of space. That is why the **United Federal Assembly** meets here. It elects, for example, the members of the **Federal Council**.

Behind the president's desk hangs a huge **mural**. It is called **“The Cradle of the Confederation”** and was created by the Geneva painter **Charles Giron**. It shows the landscape on **Lake Uri** with the **Rütli**, the village of Schwyz and the Mythen peaks. The title is a reminder that the Confederation came into being in this area.

The seats and desks form a **semicircle** facing the presidency. So everyone looks forward to the **lectern**. The members of the National Council sit arranged by **parliamentary group**; those who belong to the same group sit close together. At the United Federal Assembly the **members of the Council of States** sit at the back of the chamber. Above every two seats there is a wooden arch with the **coat of arms** of their canton.

The chamber does not only belong to those who have been elected. Since **1991** there has been the **Federal Youth Session**. Every year young people from all over Switzerland come to the Federal Palace. They discuss topics that are important to them and play at being parliament. Afterwards they pass their demands on to politicians.

gewusst: The mural in the National Council chamber shows the area around the Rütli, where according to tradition the alliance of the Confederates was made.
At joint sittings, members of the Council of States sit beneath the coat of arms of their own canton.

teile.einleitung: The national roads are the most important roads in Switzerland, above all the motorways. They connect the big cities and regions with each other. Since 2008 the Confederation has been solely responsible for them.
wichtigste: Signposts on Swiss motorways are **green**, on main roads **blue**.
On motorways the maximum speed is **120 km/h**.
To use the motorway you need a **vignette**; it costs **40 francs** a year (as of 2025).
Since **2008** the **Confederation** has been responsible for the national roads.
**FEDRO** (the Federal Roads Office) builds and maintains them.
The **A1** runs from Geneva via Bern and Zurich to St. Margrethen.

abschnitte.text: **National roads** are the roads of national importance. Most of them are **motorways** with separate carriageways for each direction. Switzerland's first stretch of motorway was opened near **Lucerne** in 1955. After that the network grew over decades. The **A1** from Geneva to St. Margrethen on Lake Constance is the longest motorway in Switzerland.

In Switzerland **signposts** on motorways are **green**. On main roads they are **blue**. So you can see at once which road you are on. On motorways the limit is **120 km/h**, on roads outside built-up areas 80 km/h. On expressways, which often look like small motorways, it is 100 km/h.

Anyone who drives a car on Swiss motorways needs a **motorway vignette**. It is available as a **sticker** for the windscreen or **electronically**. It costs **40 francs** and is valid for a whole calendar year (as of 2025). The vignette has existed since 1985. The money helps to finance the construction and maintenance of the national roads.

In the past it was mainly the **cantons** that built and ran the national roads. With the **New Fiscal Equalisation**, the network became entirely a **federal task** in 2008. Since then **FEDRO**, the Federal Roads Office, has taken care of construction, operation and maintenance. This makes responsibilities more clearly defined.

gewusst: The Gotthard road tunnel on the A2 opened in 1980 and is around 17 kilometres long.
Switzerland's first stretch of motorway, from 1955, was near Lucerne.

teile.einleitung: A postulate is a proposal in the Swiss parliament that instructs the Federal Council to examine something and report on it. Unlike a motion, it does not oblige the Federal Council to take action. Postulates are a popular tool for having a topic investigated more closely.
wichtigste: A postulate asks the Federal Council to examine something and write a report.
A motion obliges the Federal Council to act; a postulate only asks for an examination.
A postulate only has to be accepted by the council in which it was submitted.
It can be submitted by council members, parliamentary groups and committees.
The Federal Council's answer is called a postulate report.
The word comes from the Latin “postulare”, which means to demand.
Cantonal and municipal parliaments also have postulates.

abschnitte.text: A **postulate** is a parliamentary proposal. With it a council member asks the Federal Council to investigate a question thoroughly. The Federal Council is to examine whether a new law or a measure is necessary. At the end it writes a **report** on it.

A council member, a parliamentary group or a committee submits the postulate in writing. The Federal Council gives its opinion and recommends accepting or rejecting it. Then the council in which the postulate was submitted votes. Unlike with a motion, the second council does **not** have to agree.

The **motion** is a binding instruction; the Federal Council must carry something out. The postulate, on the other hand, only asks for an **examination**. That is why it is easier to get a postulate passed. Often a postulate is submitted first, and if the report shows a problem, a motion follows later.

The **postulate report** often contains figures, comparisons with other countries and proposals for solutions. The administration sometimes needs several years for such a report. There are postulates on very different topics, for example on the safety of cyclists, children's screen time or the energy supply. The reports are public and can be read on the internet.

There are also postulates in the **cantonal parliaments** and in municipal parliaments. There they are addressed to the cantonal government or the municipal council. The rules are similar to those at federal level but differ in the details. Besides the motion and the postulate there is also the **interpellation** and the simple question, with which you ask the government questions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A motion or a question from a member of parliament.
A text that examines and explains a topic in detail.
A binding instruction from parliament to the government.
A question to the government that must be answered.

gewusst: A great many postulates are submitted in the federal parliament every year, often over a hundred.
If a postulate has still not been dealt with after two years, the Federal Council must explain why in parliament.

teile.einleitung: A lampion is a colourful paper lantern with a light shining inside it. In Switzerland lanterns belong to 1 August, the national holiday, when children walk through the village in the evening carrying glowing lanterns.
wichtigste: A lampion is a lantern made of paper.
Inside, a candle or a small lamp shines.
A small battery lamp is safer than a candle.
On 1 August there are lantern processions in many places.
Many 1 August lanterns show the Swiss cross.
You carry the lantern on a stick.

abschnitte.text: A **lampion** is a colourful **paper lantern**. The paper is stretched over a frame, often in the shape of a ball or a cylinder. Inside, a light shines. In the **dark** the coloured paper glows especially beautifully. Paper lanterns have also been known in China and Japan for a long time.

In the past people put a **candle** in the lantern. But a candle can set the thin paper alight. That is why today people often use a **small battery lamp**. It has no flame and is therefore safer. You carry the lantern on a **stick**, so it stays well away from your body.

On **1 August** Switzerland celebrates its **national holiday**. In the evening, children in many villages and towns walk in a **lantern procession**. Many lanterns bear the **Swiss cross** or a **cantonal coat of arms**. Afterwards there is often a bonfire on a hill, a speech and music. Because the processions take place in the evening, you can see the lights well.

gewusst: 1 August commemorates the Federal Charter of 1291, which is regarded as the founding document of the Swiss Confederation.
Only since 1994 has 1 August been a public holiday throughout Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Magna Carta is a famous charter from England. In 1215 King John (John Lackland) had to use it to recognise the rights of his subjects. It is regarded as an early step towards the rule of law.
wichtigste: King John sealed Magna Carta in 1215.
“Magna Carta” means “Great Charter”.
It was sealed in the meadow of Runnymede on the Thames.
The barons forced the king to do so.
The charter is written in Latin.
No free man could be imprisoned without a lawful judgement.
Four original copies from 1215 survive.

abschnitte.text: **King John**, known as John Lackland, was King of England in the early 13th century. He demanded high taxes and lost expensive wars. The **barons**, the powerful nobles, were very angry about this. They rebelled against the king and wanted to limit his power. In **1215** they forced him to recognise their demands in a charter.
