The Latin name **“Magna Carta”** means **Great Charter**. “Magna” means great, “Carta” means charter or document. In German it is also called the Great Letter of Freedom. The charter was written in **Latin**, like most important documents in Europe at the time. It was sealed in the meadow of **Runnymede** on the **Thames**, west of London. That is where King John and his opponents met.

The originally continuous text was later divided into **63 clauses**. Many of them deal with dues and the rights of the barons. The most famous is one principle: no **free man** may be imprisoned or punished except by a **lawful judgement** or according to the law. This means: even the king is not above the law. This idea shapes the **rule of law** to this day.

At first Magna Carta did not last long. **Pope Innocent III** took King John's side. In August 1215 he declared the charter **null and void**, that is invalid. Later, however, it was **reissued** in a changed form. In this way its idea stayed alive and was confirmed again and again in England.

**Four original copies** of the 1215 Magna Carta still survive. Two are in the **British Library** in London, and one each in the cathedrals of **Lincoln** and **Salisbury**. Most of the clauses were repealed in the 19th and 20th centuries. In the United Kingdom only **three clauses** still apply today, including those on the freedoms of the Church and the rights of the City of London.

gewusst: Magna Carta is over 800 years old and is still quoted today as a symbol of freedom and justice.
King John was the younger brother of the famous King Richard the Lionheart.

teile.einleitung: With a vote of no confidence, a parliament can withdraw its confidence from a government and thus bring it down. This tool exists in countries with a parliamentary system. In Switzerland there is no vote of no confidence against the Federal Council.
wichtigste: A vote of no confidence is a vote in which parliament withdraws its confidence from the government.
It belongs to the **parliamentary system**, in which the government depends on parliament.
With a **confidence vote**, the head of government asks parliament whether it still supports him or her.
Germany has the **constructive vote of no confidence**: parliament must elect a successor at the same time.
The Swiss Federal Council is elected for a fixed four years and cannot be brought down.

abschnitte.text: In the **parliamentary system** the government is supported by parliament. If it loses the support of the majority, parliament can hold a **vote of no confidence**. If the majority votes against the government, it must resign. After that there is a new government or new elections. In this way parliament can keep an effective check on the government.

With a **confidence vote** the initiative comes from the government. The head of government has parliament vote on whether it still supports him or her. If he or she loses, this can lead to **new elections**. This is what happened in Germany: Federal Chancellor **Olaf Scholz** lost a confidence vote in December 2024. The Federal President dissolved the Bundestag, and an early election took place on 23 February 2025.

In Great Britain Prime Minister **James Callaghan** lost a vote of no confidence on 28 March 1979 by 311 votes to 310, that is by a difference of just one vote. In Germany, on 1 October 1982, the Bundestag voted out Federal Chancellor **Helmut Schmidt** and voted in Helmut Kohl of the CDU. To this day this is the only successful vote of no confidence in the Bundestag. In France the National Assembly brought down the government of **Michel Barnier** on 4 December 2024, for the first time since 1962.

Switzerland does not have a parliamentary system. The **Federal Assembly** elects the seven members of the Federal Council for a fixed term of four years. During this time it cannot remove the Federal Council with a vote of no confidence. The members remain in office until the next **general election of the Federal Council**. Only then can parliament decide not to re-elect someone.

gewusst: In 1979 James Callaghan lost by exactly one vote: 311 to 310.
In the history of the German Bundestag only a single vote of no confidence has succeeded, the one against Helmut Schmidt in 1982.

teile.einleitung: Every year the Corruption Perceptions Index compares how strongly corruption in politics and administration is perceived in different countries. It is published by the organisation Transparency International.
wichtigste: The index is published by Transparency International.
Transparency International was founded in Berlin in 1993.
Its founder was the former World Bank manager Peter Eigen.
The index has existed since 1995.
Since 2012 the scale has run from 0 (very corrupt) to 100 (very clean).
In the 2025 index Denmark was in first place.

abschnitte.text: **Corruption** means that someone misuses their power to gain advantages for themselves. One example is **bribery**: someone pays an official so that he or she grants a permit. Corruption is hard to measure directly because it usually happens in secret. That is why the index measures **perceived** corruption in the **public sector**.

The organisation **Transparency International** was founded in **Berlin** in **1993**. Its founder was the German **Peter Eigen**. As a director of the World Bank in Africa, he had experienced the consequences of corruption. Today the organisation has national chapters in over 100 countries, including **Switzerland**. It has published the index since **1995**, usually at the end of January or the beginning of February.

The index brings together assessments by **experts** and **businesses**. From these, each country receives a score. Since 2012 the scale has run from **0** for very corrupt to **100** for very clean. The higher the score, the less corruption is perceived. No country has yet reached 100 points. The 2025 index covers 182 countries and territories.

In the 2025 index, published in February 2026, **Denmark** was in first place, just ahead of Finland. **Switzerland** also regularly ranks among the ten best countries. At the bottom there are often countries with war and weak institutions. In the 2024 index **South Sudan** was in last place.

gewusst: The worldwide average in the 2025 index was only 42 out of 100 points.
The Nordic countries such as Denmark, Finland and Norway have been among the top group of the index for many years.

teile.einleitung: An opinion poll aims to find out what many people think without asking all of them. Before votes, polls show what the mood is. But they are only snapshots and not certain predictions.
wichtigste: The SRG trend polls before votes come from the gfs.bern institute.
A sample is a selection that is meant to reflect the whole population on a small scale.
Every poll has a margin of error.
With 1,000 people asked, it is around plus or minus 3 percentage points.
Socially desirable answers can distort polls.
A poll is a snapshot and not a prediction.
With popular initiatives, support often falls during the campaign.

abschnitte.text: You cannot ask all the voters. That is why a **sample** is asked. This is a selection of people that is meant to reflect the population as well as possible. For example, young and old people, women and men and all parts of the country should be properly represented in it. In Switzerland the **gfs.bern** institute carries out trend polls before federal votes on behalf of the **SRG**. It also produces the **projections** on voting Sunday.

Because only some of the people are asked, every result is somewhat uncertain. This is shown by the **margin of error**. With 1,000 people asked and a share of 50 per cent, it is about **plus or minus 3.1 percentage points**. If a poll shows 51 per cent yes, the true value is probably between 48 and 54 per cent. Because 50 per cent lies within this range, the outcome is **open**. If you want to **halve** the error, you have to ask **four times** as many people.

Poll results are given in **per cent**. You divide the number of answers by the number of all the people asked and multiply by a hundred. An example: of 1,200 people asked, 660 say yes. 660 divided by 1,200 gives 0.55. That is **55 per cent**. In this way polls with different numbers of people can be compared easily.

Some people prefer to give the answer that goes down well rather than their true opinion. These are called **socially desirable answers**. They can **distort** the result. Online polls in which anyone can take part are not **representative** either. There the participants select themselves. Mainly people who are particularly interested in the topic take part.

A poll only shows the mood at a particular moment. It is a **snapshot**. Many people can still change their minds before voting day. With **popular initiatives**, experts often observe that **support decreases**. At the beginning many people find the cause appealing. In the course of the campaign doubts often grow, and the yes share falls.

gewusst: Just around 1,000 well-chosen people are enough to estimate the mood across the whole country fairly accurately.
To halve the margin of error, you need four times as many people.

teile.einleitung: The police make sure that we can live safely. They help at accidents, direct traffic and look for people who have done something forbidden.
wichtigste: The police ensure safety and order.
Each canton has its own cantonal police.
Large towns often also have a city police force.
The police emergency number is 117.
In an emergency the police drive with blue lights and a siren.
Police officers wear a uniform.

abschnitte.text: The police protect people and keep **order**. They come when there is an accident and help the injured. They look for thieves and other people who break the law. They also direct **traffic** and check that everyone keeps to the rules. They often visit schools and practise safe behaviour on the road with the children.

In Switzerland the police are mainly a matter for the cantons. Each canton has its own **cantonal police**. Large towns often also have a **city police force**. There is also the Federal Office of Police, which helps, for example, with cases that involve several cantons or other countries. When the police are not out and about, they work at the **police station**. You can also report something there.

In an emergency the police switch on their **blue lights** and **siren**. That way everyone knows that they need to get through quickly. When a vehicle with blue lights comes, you make way immediately. This also applies to the fire brigade and ambulances. If you need help yourself, you call the emergency number **117**.

You can recognise police officers by their **uniform** with the word police on it. Some work with a **police dog**. Dogs have a very fine nose and find traces, missing people or hidden things. If you get lost in town, you may ask the police for help. They can also let your parents know.

gewusst: A dog's nose can tell apart many more smells than a human nose.
The European emergency number 112 also works in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: Local citizens (Ortsbürger) are people who hold the citizenship of a particular municipality. This municipality is their place of origin. It appears in every Swiss passport.
wichtigste: Every Swiss citizen has at least one place of origin.
The place of origin appears in the passport and on the identity card.
Local citizens hold the citizenship of this municipality.
You do not have to live in your place of origin.
Children usually get their place of origin from their parents.
In many cantons the local citizens form a citizens' community.

abschnitte.text: Take a look at a Swiss passport or identity card. It does not show the place of birth but the **place of origin**. It shows in which municipality the family holds **citizenship**. Every Swiss citizen has at least one place of origin. Some have several.

abschnitte.titel: Place of residence and place of origin
abschnitte.text: Many people do not live in their place of origin at all. Perhaps the family comes from a village in the Grisons but lives in Basel. That is completely normal. A child usually gets its place of origin **from its parents**. That is why families often have the same place of origin, even if they have lived elsewhere for a long time.

In many cantons the local citizens together form a **citizens' community** (Bürgergemeinde). In Aargau, for example, it is called the Ortsbürgergemeinde. It is not the same as the political municipality in which all the residents live. Many citizens' communities own **forest**, meadows or houses and look after them.

When someone from abroad becomes a Swiss citizen, this is called **naturalisation**. The person receives the citizenship of the **municipality**, the **canton** and the **Confederation**. In Switzerland these three always go together. So a naturalised person also gets a place of origin.

gewusst: Swiss citizenship has three levels: municipality, canton and Confederation.
In the canton of Bern the citizens' communities are called Burgergemeinden.

teile.einleitung: Congress is the parliament of the United States of America. It consists of two chambers, the Senate and the House of Representatives, and meets in the Capitol in Washington.
wichtigste: Congress consists of the Senate and the House of Representatives.
The Senate has 100 members, two from each state.
The House of Representatives has 435 voting members.
Senators are elected for six years, representatives for two years.
Congress meets in the Capitol in Washington.
With two thirds in both chambers it can override a veto by the President.

abschnitte.text: **Congress** consists of the **Senate** and the **House of Representatives**. Both chambers must approve a law. They meet in the **Capitol**, a building with a large dome on Capitol Hill in Washington. This is similar to Switzerland, where the National Council and the Council of States together form the Federal Assembly.

The Senate has **100 members**. Each of the 50 states sends **two senators**, no matter how big it is. This is reminiscent of the **Council of States**, where most cantons have two seats. Senators are elected for **six years**, and every two years about a third are newly chosen. The Senate must approve international **treaties** with a two-thirds majority.

Since 1913 the House of Representatives has in principle had **435 voting** members. The seats are distributed among the states according to **population**, as with the National Council. The whole House is re-elected **every two years**. It is led by the **Speaker of the House**, who is elected by the representatives. The Speaker is second in line to succeed the President, after the Vice President.

The President can stop a law with a **veto**. However, if **two thirds** in both chambers vote for it, the law comes into force anyway. The **Vice President** officially presides over the Senate. In the event of a tie, he or she casts the **deciding vote**. In this way parliament and government check each other; this is called the **separation of powers**.

gewusst: As Vice President from 2021 to 2025, Kamala Harris cast more deciding votes in the Senate than anyone before her.
Besides the 435 voting members, the House of Representatives also has delegates, for example from the capital Washington, who are not allowed to vote.

teile.einleitung: Populism is a political attitude that sets “the people” against a supposedly out-of-touch elite. It exists in left-wing and right-wing forms, and experts argue about how exactly to define it.
wichtigste: Cas Mudde calls populism a “thin ideology”.
At its core is the contrast between the pure people and the corrupt elite.
Jan-Werner Müller sees anti-pluralism as its most important feature.
In the 1890s the People's Party arose in the USA.
Populism can combine with left-wing or right-wing ideas.
Populists often appeal to a single will of the people.

abschnitte.text: The political scientist **Cas Mudde** describes populism as a **thin ideology**. Thin means: it has only a little content of its own and therefore combines with left-wing or right-wing ideas. At its core is the contrast between the “pure people” and the “corrupt elite”. Populists like to present themselves as **outsiders** against the political **establishment**. They count parties, the media and often the courts as part of this.

In “What Is Populism?” (2016), the political scientist **Jan-Werner Müller** emphasises **anti-pluralism**. According to him, populists claim that they alone represent the true people. Anyone who thinks differently is then quickly regarded as illegitimate. Many appeal to the idea of a single **general will**, the volonté générale. This idea was described by **Jean-Jacques Rousseau** in “The Social Contract” in 1762.

An early populist movement was the **People's Party** in the USA in the 1890s. It mainly represented indebted farmers against banks and railway companies. Today a distinction is made between **left-wing populism**, which is directed mainly against economic elites, and **right-wing populism**, which often also excludes immigrants. The political scientist **Chantal Mouffe**, together with ideas from Ernesto Laclau, argues for left-wing populism as a strategy.

Populists often call for more **direct democracy**, because popular votes are meant to express the will of the people directly. In Switzerland, on the other hand, popular votes have long been a firm part of the political system that almost all parties use. How populism should be judged is disputed. Critics see a danger to minorities and institutions; others see it as a sign of real problems that receive too little attention.

gewusst: The supporters of the People's Party in the USA were called “Populists”.
Populism exists on both the left and the right of the political spectrum.

teile.einleitung: The Landsgemeinde is the assembly of all the voters of the canton of Glarus. Once a year they meet in the open air in the cantonal capital Glarus and decide on laws, taxes and elections by raising their hands.
wichtigste: The Glarus Landsgemeinde takes place on the Zaunplatz in Glarus.
It is usually held on the first Sunday in May.
In the canton of Glarus you may vote from the age of 16.
In 2007 Glarus was the first canton with a voting age of 16.
You can only be elected to a cantonal office from the age of 18.
Before the Landsgemeinde every household receives the Memorial with all the items of business.
The government has five members and is elected at the ballot box.

abschnitte.text: The **Landsgemeinde** is a very old form of direct democracy. Instead of putting papers into a ballot box, the voters gather on the **Zaunplatz** in the middle of Glarus. They stand in a large circle, the so-called ring. Today there is a Landsgemeinde in only two cantons: Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden. Many visitors from all over Switzerland come to watch every year.

Anyone who wants to vote holds up their **voting card**. This shows that the person is allowed to vote. The Landammann presides over the assembly and estimates with the naked eye which side has more hands. If it is very close, he or she has the vote held a second time. Another special feature is that everyone may speak and put forward **motions**. So a proposal can be changed directly at the assembly.

So that everyone is well prepared, the canton sends out the **Memorial** beforehand. This booklet goes to every household with voters. It contains all the items to be voted on, with explanations. This allows the people of Glarus to form an opinion at home. At the Landsgemeinde itself, they then discuss and decide.

On **6 May 2007** the Landsgemeinde decided to lower the voting age for the canton to **16**. Glarus was thus the first canton in Switzerland to take this step. Since then young people have been able to have a say on cantonal and municipal questions. However, you can only be elected from the age of 18. This is called the **right to stand for election**. In federal votes the age of 18 still applies.

The Glarus government, the **Regierungsrat**, has **five members**. They are not elected at the Landsgemeinde but **at the ballot box**. The Landsgemeinde then decides which of them becomes **Landammann**. The Landammann chairs the government and presides over the Landsgemeinde. There is also the cantonal parliament, the Landrat, which prepares the items of business.

gewusst: In 2006 the Landsgemeinde decided to merge the canton's 25 municipalities at the time into just three large municipalities.
Because motions can be put forward at the Landsgemeinde, a proposal is sometimes passed in a completely different form from the one the government proposed.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland a concordat is a treaty between two or more cantons. The cantons use it to carry out shared tasks, for example in schools, prisons or grants for students.
wichtigste: A concordat is a treaty between cantons.
According to Article 48 of the Federal Constitution it must not run counter to the Confederation.
Each canton decides for itself whether to join.
The hooligan concordat is aimed at violence at sports events.
The cantons work together in three prison concordats.
The school concordat of 1970 coordinated the schools for the first time.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland the **cantons** have many tasks of their own. Some tasks are easier to solve together. For this, cantons conclude **concordats**, that is treaties with each other. According to **Article 48 of the Federal Constitution**, such treaties must not run counter to the law and interests of the Confederation. The rights of other cantons must also be respected.

Each canton decides according to its **own law** whether to join a concordat. Often the **cantonal parliament** approves it, sometimes the people do so in a **vote**. No canton can be forced to join. That is why not all cantons always take part in a concordat.

With the **school concordat** of 1970, the cantons agreed, for example, on the age at which children start school and the length of compulsory schooling. It was later developed further by **HarmoS**. The **grants concordat** sets minimum standards for education grants. The **Intercantonal University Agreement** states that the canton of residence pays a contribution when someone studies in another canton.

The so-called **hooligan concordat** is really called the Concordat on Measures against Violence at Sports Events. It makes possible, for example, **area bans**, that is bans on being near a stadium. For prisons there are three **prison concordats**: North-western and Central Switzerland, Eastern Switzerland, and Latin Switzerland. In them the cantons run institutions together.

gewusst: The word “concordat” also refers to treaties between a state and the Holy See, that is the Catholic Church.
A concordat can be very small: sometimes only two neighbouring cantons conclude a treaty, for example for a shared school.

teile.einleitung: In many cantons the Obergericht (High Court) is the highest court. It reviews judgements of the lower courts and ensures that the law is applied consistently throughout the canton.
wichtigste: In many cantons the High Court is the highest cantonal court for civil and criminal matters.
Above the High Court there is only the Federal Supreme Court.
The High Court is usually the second instance and reviews judgements of the first instance.
It does not have the same name everywhere: in St Gallen and Lucerne it is called the Cantonal Court, in Basel-Stadt the Court of Appeal.
A High Court is divided into chambers; often three judges decide together.
In the canton of Zurich the cantonal parliament elects the members of the High Court.

abschnitte.titel: The highest court in the canton
abschnitte.text: Each canton has its own courts. The High Court is right at the top. It decides on **civil matters**, that is disputes between private individuals, and on **criminal matters**, that is cases in which someone has broken a criminal law. Anyone who does not agree with the judgement of the High Court can, in many cases, still turn to the **Federal Supreme Court** in Lausanne.

A case usually begins at a court of **first instance**, in the canton of Zurich for example at the district court. If a party is not satisfied with the judgement, it can appeal. Then the High Court, as the **second instance**, examines whether the first judgement was correct. In this way a decision is looked at again by other experts. This protects against mistakes.

Switzerland is federal, which is why each canton organises its courts itself. In Zurich and Bern the highest court is called the **Obergericht** (High Court). In St Gallen and Lucerne it is called the **Kantonsgericht** (Cantonal Court). In the canton of Basel-Stadt it is called the **Appellationsgericht** (Court of Appeal). But the task is similar everywhere.

A High Court is divided into **chambers**, for example civil chambers and criminal chambers. Each chamber is responsible for certain cases. Many cases are decided by a chamber of **three** judges. That way not one person alone bears the responsibility. In the canton of Zurich the High Court judges are elected by the **Kantonsrat**, the cantonal parliament.

Besides reaching judgements, the High Court often has another task. In many cantons it **supervises** the lower courts. It makes sure that they work properly and promptly. But the judges remain **independent** in their judgements.

gewusst: Courts belong to the third power in the state, the judiciary. They are independent of government and parliament.
Because each canton organises its own courts, Switzerland has many different names for the highest cantonal court.

teile.einleitung: Every year the Federal Council publishes an official group photo. The President of the Confederation decides what the picture looks like and what message it shows.
wichtigste: The first official Federal Council photo dates from 1993.
Since then a new picture has appeared every year.
The President of the Confederation is usually at the centre.
The other members usually line up according to how long they have been in office.
If a member leaves, an adjusted photo usually appears.
After every Federal Council election there is also a group picture in the Federal Palace.

abschnitte.text: Since **1993** there has been an official **Federal Council photo** every year. It hangs in many offices and can also be seen on the internet. The design is chosen each year by the new **President of the Confederation**. That is why every photo looks different. It often has a title with a message.

In the photo the **president** usually stands at the centre or stands out in some other way. The vice-president often stands next to him or her. The other members line up according to **seniority**, that is how long they have been in office. If a member leaves during the year, an **adjusted photo** with the same design is usually published. After each Federal Council election the new body is also photographed in a room of the **Federal Palace** in Bern.

In 2022 President of the Confederation **Ignazio Cassis** chose the title “The Federal Council, united in its diversity”. In 2023 the picture by **Alain Berset** showed “Good cooperation with different points of view”. This fits the **principle of collegiality**: the Federal Council decides together and defends decisions together. In 2024, under **Viola Amherd**, the Federal Council stood in front of a Swiss mountain panorama. In 2025 the photo showed the Federal Council with **people from all over Switzerland**.

gewusst: Every Federal Council photo is different, because every year a different person holds the presidency and designs the picture.
The 2024 photo was titled “Swiss mountain panorama in the Federal Palace”.

teile.einleitung: Since 1946 Italy has been a republic with a parliamentary system. The government needs the confidence of parliament, and because it often lacked this, governments changed very frequently.
wichtigste: Since a referendum in 1946 Italy has been a republic.
The Chamber of Deputies and the Senate have equal rights; this is called perfect bicameralism.
The government needs the confidence of both chambers.
Since 1946 Italy has had almost 70 governments.
The “Mani pulite” investigations from 1992 ended the old party system.
Since the 2022 election parliament has had 400 deputies and 200 elected senators.
In 2022 Giorgia Meloni became Italy's first woman Prime Minister.

abschnitte.text: The head of state is the **President of the Republic**, who is elected by parliament for seven years. The government is led by the **Prime Minister** (President of the Council of Ministers). Parliament has two chambers: the **Chamber of Deputies** and the **Senate**, both in Rome. In **perfect bicameralism**, both chambers have the same rights. The government needs the confidence of both.

If the government loses its majority in just one chamber, it can fall. Quarrelling coalitions also often led to resignations. That is why Italy has had almost 70 governments since 1946; Giorgia Meloni's government is the 68th. On average a government lasted only just over a year. Sometimes **non-party experts** led the government, for example **Mario Draghi**, the former President of the European Central Bank, from 2021 to 2022.

From 1992 investigators in Milan uncovered a large system of bribes, known as **Tangentopoli** (“Bribesville”). The investigations were called **“Mani pulite”**, which means “clean hands”. Many politicians and businesspeople ended up in court. Large parties such as the **Democrazia Cristiana**, which had shaped the country for decades, then broke up. New parties and alliances emerged.

Prime Minister **Matteo Renzi** wanted to greatly reduce the size and power of the Senate in order to make governments more stable. In the referendum of December 2016 around 59 per cent voted no, after which Renzi resigned. In the **2020 referendum**, on the other hand, it was decided to make parliament smaller. The Chamber of Deputies shrank from 630 to 400 seats, the Senate from 315 to 200 elected senators. In October 2022 **Giorgia Meloni** of the Brothers of Italy (Fratelli d'Italia) became the first woman Prime Minister.

gewusst: On average, an Italian government since 1946 has stayed in office for only just over a year.
“Mani pulite” means “clean hands” in English.

teile.einleitung: Value added tax is a tax you pay when shopping. It is included in the price of almost all goods and services. For the Confederation it is one of the most important sources of income.
wichtigste: Switzerland has had value added tax since 1 January 1995.
It replaced the old turnover tax on goods, WUST for short.
In the end consumers bear the tax.
Within the country it is collected by the Federal Tax Administration, on imports by Customs.
Thanks to the input tax deduction, only the added value is taxed.
A special rate of 3.8 per cent applies to hotel stays (as of 2025).
Since 2024 the tax has been slightly higher to finance the AHV.

abschnitte.text: **Value added tax (VAT)** is included in the price of almost everything you buy. Businesses pay the tax to the Confederation. But they add it to the price. So in the end it is paid by **consumers**, that is everyone who buys something. On many till receipts you can see how much VAT is included in the price.

A loaf of bread is made in several stages: the farmer supplies grain, the mill makes flour, the bakery bakes the bread. At each stage some value is added, an **added value**. A business may deduct the VAT it has itself paid to suppliers from its own tax bill. This is called the **input tax deduction**. In this way, at each stage only the newly created added value is taxed.

Value added tax was introduced on **1 January 1995**. Switzerland introduced it later than most European countries. Before that the Confederation levied the **turnover tax on goods**, **WUST** for short. It taxed mainly goods but hardly any services. With the **AHV 21** reform, the people and the cantons accepted an increase in VAT in 2022. Since **2024** the additional money has gone to the **AHV** old-age insurance.

There is not just one tax rate. Since 2024 the **standard rate** has been 8.1 per cent. For everyday necessities such as food, books and medicines a **reduced rate** of 2.6 per cent applies. For **hotel stays** there is a **special rate** of 3.8 per cent (as of 2025). It is meant to support **tourism** in Switzerland.

Within the country the **Federal Tax Administration (FTA)** is responsible for VAT. It also checks businesses' tax returns. For goods **imported** into Switzerland, the **Federal Office for Customs and Border Security** collects the tax at the border. In this way imported goods are taxed in the same way as goods from within the country. Anyone with a turnover of less than **100,000 francs** a year does not have to account for VAT. Small businesses can, however, register voluntarily.

gewusst: Value added tax is one of the Confederation's largest sources of income.
Even if you shop online abroad, you often pay VAT when the goods are imported into Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: A petition is a written request to an authority. Anyone may submit a petition, including children. The right to do so is in the Federal Constitution.
wichtigste: The word comes from the Latin “petitio”, which means request or application.
The right of petition is in Article 33 of the Federal Constitution.
A petition does not need a minimum number of signatures.
You can address it to the municipality, the canton or the Confederation.
The authority must take note of it but does not have to carry it out.
A petition does not lead to a popular vote.

abschnitte.text: The word **petition** comes from the Latin **petitio**. It means **request** or **application**. With a petition you write to an authority about what you would like or what you would like to change. The right to do so is in **Article 33** of the Federal Constitution. It is one of the **fundamental rights**.

There is **no minimum number** of signatures for a petition. Even a single person can submit a petition. You also do **not have to be entitled to vote**. That is why children or people without a Swiss passport may also write a petition. There are no strict formal rules, which is why many petitions today are also collected **online**.

A class would like a **zebra crossing** in front of the school. It can write a petition to the **municipality** explaining why the crossing is important. Petitions can be addressed to many places: the **municipality**, the **canton** or the **Confederation**. Anyone who signs must not suffer any **disadvantages** as a result. The Federal Constitution protects this.

The authority must read a petition and **take note of it**. But it does not have to fulfil the wish. A petition also does **not lead to a popular vote**. That is the big difference from a **popular initiative** or a **referendum**. Nevertheless, petitions with many signatures can show that an issue matters to many people.

gewusst: A petition can be submitted not only by an individual but also by a club, a school class or another group.
Petitions to the federal parliament are examined by the responsible committees.

teile.einleitung: In a parliamentary system of government, the government depends on the confidence of parliament. If it loses its majority, it can be brought down. Examples are Germany and Great Britain.
wichtigste: The government needs the support of the parliamentary majority.
Government and parliamentary majority are closely linked; this is called the fusion of powers.
Checking the government is mainly the job of the opposition.
With a confidence vote, a head of government tests whether he or she still has a majority.
In Great Britain the largest opposition party forms a shadow cabinet.
Switzerland does not have a parliamentary system but a directorial system.

abschnitte.text: In the parliamentary system, parliament elects the government or the head of government. The government can only work as long as the **parliamentary majority** supports it. Members of the government are often also members of parliament. Instead of a strict separation of powers, people therefore speak of a **fusion of powers**. In the **presidential system** of the USA it is different: there the people elect the President separately from parliament.

abschnitte.titel: Confidence vote and vote of no confidence
abschnitte.text: In a **confidence vote** the head of government himself or herself puts to the vote whether parliament still trusts him or her. A **vote of no confidence**, on the other hand, comes from parliament. Germany has the **constructive vote of no confidence**: the Bundestag can only vote out the Federal Chancellor if it elects a new one at the same time. The German head of state, the **Federal President**, is elected by the **Federal Convention**. It is made up of all members of the Bundestag and the same number of delegates from the federal states.

Because the majority supports the government, critical scrutiny falls mainly to the **opposition**. In Great Britain the largest opposition party names a counterpart for every ministry. This **shadow cabinet** is meant to show that the opposition could take over the government at any time. Since the **Dissolution and Calling of Parliament Act** of 2022, the British Prime Minister can once again call **early elections**. The act repealed a rule from 2011 that provided for fixed election dates.

Switzerland has a **directorial system**. The Federal Assembly does elect the **Federal Council**, but cannot vote it out during its four-year term of office. The Federal Council is a **collegial body** of seven members without a head of government. The large parties sit together in the government. That is why there is no fixed opposition as in Great Britain.

gewusst: The British Parliament is regarded as one of the oldest in the world and as the model for many parliamentary systems.
The President of the Swiss Confederation is only the chair of the Federal Council for one year and not a head of government.

teile.einleitung: In a constitutional monarchy there is a king, a queen, a prince or an emperor as head of state. However, their power is limited by a constitution, and the country is usually governed by an elected government.
wichtigste: “Constitution” means the basic law of a state.
In a constitutional monarchy the monarch is bound by the constitution.
Examples are the United Kingdom, Spain and Japan.
Switzerland's neighbour Liechtenstein is a principality.
In a parliamentary monarchy the monarch has mainly ceremonial duties.
In an absolute monarchy, by contrast, the ruler has unlimited power.

abschnitte.text: The word **“constitution”** means the basic law of a state, its **charter**. In a constitutional monarchy even the **monarch** must keep to the constitution. The office is usually inherited within a family. The opposite is an **absolute monarchy**: there the ruler is not bound by any constitution. A well-known example of this is **Louis XIV** of France.

In many monarchies today the **elected government** makes the political decisions. This is then called a **parliamentary monarchy**. The monarch has mainly **ceremonial duties**: receiving guests, opening parliament and representing the country. In Great Britain the King reads out the **“King's Speech”** at the opening of Parliament. The text, however, is written by the government.

Since September 2022 the head of state of the **United Kingdom** has been **King Charles III**. He is also head of state of other countries such as Canada and Australia. **Spain**, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway and Sweden are also monarchies. In **Japan** an **emperor**, the Tenno, is head of state; he has only symbolic duties. Germany, Italy and Portugal, on the other hand, are republics.

Switzerland's neighbour **Liechtenstein** is a **principality**. The head of state is a prince. Its constitution combines the monarchy with **democratic rights** of the people, for example popular votes. The prince has more influence there than the monarchs in most other European countries. **Switzerland** itself is a republic without a monarch.

gewusst: Charles III became king when his mother Elizabeth II died in September 2022. She had been queen for around 70 years.
Liechtenstein uses the Swiss franc as its currency.

teile.einleitung: A majority election (in German “Majorzwahl”) is an electoral system in which the people with the most votes are elected. That is why it is also called a majoritarian election. In Switzerland, the Council of States is elected this way in most cantons.
wichtigste: In a majority election, whoever gets the most votes wins.
Another name for it is majoritarian election.
The Council of States is elected by majority vote in almost all cantons.
In the first round you usually need an absolute majority, that is more than half the votes.
In the second round a relative majority is enough, that is simply the most votes.
The cantons of Jura and Neuchâtel elect their members of the Council of States by proportional representation.
Most cantonal governments are also elected by majority vote.

abschnitte.text: In a **majority election** the focus is on people, not parties. Whoever gets the most votes is elected. The other candidates get nothing, even if they had many votes. The word comes from the Latin “maior”, which means greater.

In the first round you usually need an **absolute majority**. This means you must get more than half of the valid votes. If nobody manages this, there is a **second round**. There a relative majority is enough, so whoever simply has the most votes is elected.

The **Council of States** has 46 seats; each canton sends two people, and the six former half-cantons one each. The cantons decide for themselves how they elect their members of the Council of States. Almost all use majority voting. Only the cantons of Jura and Neuchâtel use proportional representation, and in Appenzell Innerrhoden the member of the Council of States is elected at the Landsgemeinde.

Most **cantonal governments** and many municipal councils are also elected by majority vote. Exceptions are, for example, the cantons of Ticino and Zug, which elect their government by proportional representation. The Federal Council is not elected by the people but by the United Federal Assembly. There, too, a person needs an absolute majority of the votes.

One advantage of majority voting is that well-known and popular personalities have a good chance. Those elected have the support of a broad majority. One disadvantage is that small parties hardly win any seats. The votes for the losers have no effect on the composition.

begriffe.erklaerung: One round of an election; sometimes two are needed.
More than half of the votes.
More votes than anyone else, even if it is less than half.
The small chamber of the federal parliament, which represents the cantons.

gewusst: Great Britain elects its House of Commons by majority vote; there, in each constituency, whoever has the most votes wins in the very first round.
In a majority election you can also write on the ballot paper the names of people who have not officially stood as candidates at all.

teile.einleitung: Parties need money for their work, for example for campaigns before elections and votes. How they get this money is called party financing. For some years now, transparency rules have applied to it at federal level.
wichtigste: Swiss parties are financed mainly privately, without direct state money.
Important sources of income are membership fees, donations and contributions from elected members.
Parties in the Federal Assembly must disclose their financing every year.
The rules are in the Federal Act on Political Rights.
The Transparency Initiative was withdrawn in favour of a counter-proposal.
Since 2011 donations to parties can be deducted from direct federal tax.

abschnitte.text: Switzerland has **no direct state financing of parties**. The parties live mainly on private money. Members pay a **membership fee** every year. On top of that there are **donations** and **contributions** from elected members, who give part of their allowance to the party. Only the **parliamentary groups** in parliament receive contributions from the Confederation for their work.

For a long time parties at federal level did not have to say where their money came from. A **Transparency Initiative** demanded that this change. In 2021 parliament passed an **indirect counter-proposal**. The initiators then withdrew their initiative conditionally, because many of their demands had been met. No referendum was called against the law. The rules are in the **Federal Act on Political Rights**.

The obligation applies to all parties represented in the **Federal Assembly**. They report their income and large donations **once a year**. The information is then published on the internet. There are also reporting obligations for larger campaigns before elections and votes. In this way voters can see who is behind a party or a campaign.

There have also been votes on transparency in the cantons. In **Basel-Landschaft** in 2013 and in **Aargau** in 2014, around 56 per cent said no to transparency initiatives each time. In March 2018, on the other hand, **Schwyz** and **Fribourg** accepted such initiatives. **Geneva** and **Ticino** already had disclosure rules earlier.

The state encourages donations to parties in another way. Since **2011** private individuals have been able to deduct membership fees and donations to political parties from **direct federal tax**. This applies up to a maximum amount. In this way political involvement is supported through the tax system.

gewusst: Whether parties must disclose their finances was disputed in Switzerland for a long time. Supporters stressed transparency, opponents the privacy of donors.
The cantons may set their own transparency rules for cantonal elections and votes.

teile.einleitung: The midterm elections are elections in the USA that take place in the middle of the President's four-year term of office. Above all, Congress is re-elected. They are often regarded as an interim report on the government.
wichtigste: In the midterms the whole House of Representatives is re-elected.
On top of that comes around a third of the Senate.
Voting takes place on the Tuesday after the first Monday in November.
The President's party usually loses seats.
In 2018 the Democrats won control of the House of Representatives.
After the 2022 midterms Congress was divided.
The 2026 midterms take place on 3 November.

abschnitte.titel: Elections in the middle of the term
abschnitte.text: The President of the USA is elected for **four years**. Two years after the presidential election, the **midterm elections** take place. “Midterm” means the middle of the term of office. It is not the President who is elected but above all **Congress**, the parliament of the USA. It consists of two chambers: the **House of Representatives** and the **Senate**.

Members of the House of Representatives are only elected for **two years**. That is why the **whole House of Representatives** is filled anew at the midterms. Senators are elected for six years. Every two years around **a third of the Senate** is re-elected, that is about 33 or 34 seats. In addition, many states elect their **governors**. In 2026, **36 governorships** are up for election.

A law of **1845** fixed election day: it is the **Tuesday after the first Monday in November**. It therefore always falls between 2 and 8 November. In 2026 the first Monday in November is 2 November. The midterms therefore take place on **3 November 2026**.

Historically, the **President's party** usually loses seats in the House of Representatives at the midterms. Many voters use the election to show their opinion of the government. In the **2018** midterms the **Democrats** gained 41 seats and afterwards controlled the House of Representatives. **Nancy Pelosi** became Speaker again, that is the leader of the chamber.

In the **2022** midterms the **Republicans** won a narrow majority in the House of Representatives. The **Democrats** kept the **Senate**. Congress was therefore **divided**. In such a situation the parties have to work together for new laws to be passed. Governing then often becomes harder for a President.

gewusst: Election day in the USA is a Tuesday because the law of 1845 laid it down that way.
In the House of Representatives every member has to stand for election again after just two years.

teile.einleitung: Lay judges help to reach verdicts in courts without having studied law. In Switzerland this is common above all in cantonal courts of first instance.
wichtigste: Lay judges have not completed any legal training.
They work mainly in lower courts such as the district courts.
The rules for this are made by the cantons, which is why they differ.
At the commercial and labour courts, expert judges from working life also take part in verdicts.
In the canton of Zurich the people elect the district judges.
Jury courts were abolished in 2011.

abschnitte.text: A **lay judge** has not completed a law degree. He or she brings **life experience** and knowledge from other professions into the court. In most cantons, lay judges take part in verdicts at criminal and civil courts of **first instance**, for example at the **district courts**. First instance means: this is where a case is judged for the first time. Because the cantons organise the courts themselves, the rules differ.

In the **canton of Zurich** the voters of a district elect their **district judges**. The fact that the people elect judges is a **Swiss peculiarity**. In **Aargau** any person **entitled to vote** can be elected as a justice of the peace, district judge or substitute judge. Legal training is not required for this.

At the **Zurich Commercial Court**, **commercial judges** from business sit alongside legally trained senior judges. They know companies and industries from their own experience. At the **labour court** there are expert judges from **employers'** and **employees'** circles. In this way practical knowledge from both sides goes into the verdict. Such a composition is called **parity-based**.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the jury courts
abschnitte.text: Some cantons used to have **jury courts**. There professional judges reached verdicts together with **jurors** from the general public. These courts were regarded as lengthy and expensive. They were abolished with the federal **Code of Criminal Procedure** of 2011. Lay judges are meant to bring an everyday view into the court and strengthen trust in the justice system. Critics doubt that this is still necessary today and would prefer only trained judges.

gewusst: The justice of the peace is often the first place to go in a dispute: he or she tries to get the parties to agree before it comes to a trial.
Since 2011 the same rules for criminal and civil proceedings have applied throughout Switzerland; before that each canton had its own.

teile.einleitung: Moutier is a French-speaking town in the Jura. It belonged to the canton of Bern for a long time and, after several votes, decided to move to the canton of Jura. Such a change of canton is a rare event in Switzerland.
wichtigste: With around 7,200 inhabitants, Moutier was the largest municipality of the **Bernese Jura**.
The first vote on the move, on 18 June 2017, was annulled because of **irregularities**.
When it was repeated on 28 March 2021, around **55 per cent** voted for Jura.
This vote took place under **federal supervision**.
The **Moutier Concordat** regulates the details and was accepted by both cantons in 2024.
The **Federal Assembly** had to approve the change of territory.

abschnitte.text: For a long time the whole of the Jura belonged to the canton of Bern. Many people in the French-speaking north wanted a canton of their own. So in 1979 the **canton of Jura** was created. The southern part, the **Bernese Jura**, stayed with Bern. This included **Moutier**, the largest municipality in the region. But in Moutier, too, many people wanted to join the Jura.

On **18 June 2017** Moutier voted on the move for the first time. After complaints, the district prefecture declared the vote invalid in 2018 because there had been **irregularities**. The Bernese administrative court confirmed this in 2019. On **28 March 2021** the vote was repeated, this time accompanied by **federal observers**. 2,114 voters, that is 54.9 per cent, wanted to join the Jura; 1,740 were against.

A change of canton needs many rules: what happens to the staff, the assets and the schools? This is regulated by the **Moutier Concordat**, a treaty between the cantons of Bern and Jura. On **22 September 2024** the voters of both cantons voted on it. In the canton of Bern 83.2 per cent said yes, in the canton of Jura 72.9 per cent. Both cantons had to agree.

According to the **Federal Constitution**, a change of territory between cantons needs the approval of the **Federal Assembly**. This is in Article 53, paragraph 3. In 2024 the Federal Council presented parliament with a **dispatch** on it, that is a report with a proposal. Only with parliament's yes could the move take place. So Moutier shows how municipalities, cantons and the Confederation work together in Switzerland.

gewusst: Repeating the Moutier vote under federal supervision was a unique event in Switzerland.
In the 2021 vote only 374 votes separated yes and no.

teile.einleitung: The New Fiscal Equalisation, NFA for short, regulates how money is distributed between the Confederation and the cantons. It ensures that financially weaker cantons can also carry out their tasks. At the same time it laid down who takes on which tasks.
wichtigste: NFA stands for the **reorganisation of fiscal equalisation and the division of tasks between the Confederation and the cantons**.
The people and the cantons accepted the NFA on **28 November 2004**.
It has applied since **1 January 2008**.
**Resource equalisation** supports cantons with little financial strength of their own.
**Burden equalisation** helps cantons with special costs.
A **resource index** of 100 corresponds to the Swiss average.

abschnitte.text: The cantons of Switzerland differ greatly in financial strength. That is why there is **fiscal equalisation**. With the **NFA** it was fundamentally reorganised. On **28 November 2004** the people and the cantons accepted the proposal with just under two thirds voting yes. Only **Schwyz, Nidwalden and Zug** rejected it. After the vote new laws were needed, which is why the NFA only came into force on **1 January 2008**.

**Resource equalisation** helps cantons with low economic and tax strength. This strength is measured with the **resource index**. A value of **100** corresponds to the Swiss average. Cantons above 100 are stronger, cantons below 100 weaker. The equalisation is paid for by the **Confederation** and the **resource-strong cantons**, with the Confederation bearing the larger share.

Some cantons have particularly high costs that are not their fault. Mountain cantons, for example, have to build roads on steep terrain and reach villages that lie far apart. For this there is **geographical-topographical burden equalisation**. **Socio-demographic burden equalisation** helps cantons with high social spending, for example in large cities. These contributions are paid by the Confederation.

The **paying cantons** include, for example, Zug, Zurich, Geneva, Schwyz, Nidwalden and Basel-Stadt. Cantons such as Uri, Jura and Valais **receive** money. The NFA also divided **tasks** more clearly. For example, the construction, operation and maintenance of the **national roads** became entirely a federal task. Other tasks went entirely to the cantons.

gewusst: In the 2004 vote, of all cantons, it was three financially strong ones that rejected the NFA: Schwyz, Nidwalden and Zug.
Since the NFA, the national roads have been purely a federal matter.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland the Federal Assembly re-elects the members of the Federal Council every four years. Almost always the existing members are re-elected. If someone is not re-elected, this is called a non-re-election. It is very rare and causes a great stir every time.
wichtigste: A member of the Federal Council **cannot be brought down by a vote of no confidence**.
Removal is only possible at the **general election** through non-re-election.
The first federal councillor not to be re-elected was **Ulrich Ochsenbein** in 1854.
In 1872 it happened to **Jean-Jacques Challet-Venel**.
In December 2003 **Christoph Blocher** was elected in place of Federal Councillor Ruth Metzler, who was not re-elected.
In 2007 Blocher himself was not re-elected; **Eveline Widmer-Schlumpf** was elected.

abschnitte.text: The members of the Federal Council are elected for a fixed **term of office of four years**. During this time the Federal Assembly cannot remove them. There is no **vote of no confidence**. But after each National Council election there is a **general election of the Federal Council**. Then the Federal Assembly can decide not to elect an existing member again and choose someone else.

**Ulrich Ochsenbein** from Bern was a member of the first Federal Council of 1848. He had lost support in parliament and in **1854** became the first not to be re-elected. In **1872** the Geneva Radical **Jean-Jacques Challet-Venel** lost his seat. He had opposed the total revision of the Federal Constitution. After that it was over 130 years until the next case.

In December **2003** the Federal Assembly elected the Zurich SVP politician **Christoph Blocher** in the third round. This gave the SVP a second seat, and the sitting Federal Councillor **Ruth Metzler** of the CVP was not re-elected. In December **2007** Blocher himself was not re-elected. In his place the Grisons cantonal councillor **Eveline Widmer-Schlumpf** was elected. She accepted the election the day after the vote and took over the **Federal Department of Justice and Police** (FDJP). In November 2010 she moved to the Finance Department.

The **SVP** did not regard the newly elected councillor as its representative and declared itself to be in **opposition**. It expelled the Grisons cantonal party because Widmer-Schlumpf belonged to it. This led in 2008 to the founding of the **Conservative Democratic Party (BDP)**. The SVP's role as opposition ended with the election of **Ueli Maurer** at the end of 2008. In 2021 the BDP merged with the CVP to form **the Centre** (Die Mitte).

gewusst: Between 1872 and 2003 not a single member of the Federal Council failed to be re-elected.
Eveline Widmer-Schlumpf was a federal councillor from 2008 to 2015.

teile.einleitung: The National Council elections have a long history in Switzerland. Since 1919 elections have been held by proportional representation, and since 1931 every four years. Each election is studied closely to understand how and why people vote.
wichtigste: The National Council is elected on the **second-to-last Sunday in October**, so in 2027 on **24 October**.
Since **1919** **proportional representation** has applied.
Until **1931** a term of office lasted three years; since then four.
Since the **1963** election the National Council has had a fixed **200 seats**.
From 2023 to 2027 the **52nd legislative period** is running.
The election study **Selects** examines every National Council election.

abschnitte.text: In the first decades of the federal state, the National Council was elected by **majority vote**. Often the strongest party won almost all the seats. A **popular initiative** introduced **proportional representation** in 1918. The first election under the new system took place in **1919**. Since then the parties have received seats according to their share of the vote.

Until **1931** the National Council was elected every three years. Since then a **legislative period** has lasted four years. In the past the number of seats depended on the population and kept rising. Since the **1963** election it has been fixed at **200**. The elections of October 2023 began the **52nd legislative period**, which ends with the 2027 elections.

The law states that the election takes place on the **second-to-last Sunday in October**. In October 2027 the Sundays fall on the 3rd, 10th, 17th, 24th and 31st. The second-to-last of these is **24 October 2027**. The number of lists and candidates has risen sharply in recent years. In 2019, 4,652 people stood on **511 lists**, which was a record at the time.

If a seat becomes vacant during the term of office, the next person on the same list usually moves up. If the list has no more substitutes, a **by-election** is needed. This is very rare. **Swiss citizens abroad** vote in their last municipality of residence in Switzerland or in their place of origin. After each election the **Selects** study asks many voters about their reasons. **Smartvote**, on the other hand, is a voting aid used before the election.

gewusst: Before 1963 the National Council grew with the population; today it stays at 200 seats.
The introduction of proportional representation in 1918 came about through a popular initiative.

teile.einleitung: The general strike (Landesstreik) of November 1918 was the largest general strike in the history of Switzerland. Around 250,000 workers downed tools to demand better living conditions and more political rights.
wichtigste: The general strike took place from 12 to 14 November 1918.
It began shortly after the end of the First World War.
The Olten Action Committee under Robert Grimm called the strike.
Around 250,000 people went on strike.
The first demand was a new election of the National Council by proportional representation.
In Grenchen three young workers died on the last day of the strike.

abschnitte.text: On **11 November 1918** the **First World War** ended with an armistice. Although Switzerland had not been involved in the war, many people suffered **hardship**. Food was scarce and expensive, and wages were often not enough. In addition, the **Spanish flu** was raging, and around 22,000 people in Switzerland died of it. The mood among workers was very tense.

The **Olten Action Committee**, made up of the Social Democratic Party and the trade unions, called for a strike. It was led by **Robert Grimm**. From 12 to 14 November 1918 around **250,000** people stopped work; that was a large part of the workforce. The Federal Council called up the **army** to keep order. After three days the committee called off the strike.

The strikers drew up a **nine-point programme**. First came the immediate **re-election of the National Council by proportional representation**. They also demanded the **48-hour week**, **votes for women** and old-age and disability insurance. Many demands were only met later: the National Council was first elected by proportional representation in 1919, the 48-hour week largely came in 1919 and 1920, and the AHV old-age insurance only in 1948.

On the last day of the strike, soldiers in **Grenchen** shot at strikers, and three young watch workers died. Around 1,500 soldiers who had been called up also died of the flu. After the strike Robert Grimm was sentenced to six months in prison. The general strike shaped the relationship between the middle classes and the workers for a long time. Today it is regarded as an important turning point in Swiss history.

gewusst: Votes for women, a demand from 1918, were only introduced at federal level in 1971.
Robert Grimm later became President of the National Council.

teile.einleitung: The National Council is one of the two chambers of the Swiss parliament. It represents the people and has 200 members. Together with the Council of States it makes the laws of the Confederation.
wichtigste: The National Council represents **the people** and is therefore also called the **chamber of the people**.
It has **200 members**, who are elected by the voters.
The last election was on **22 October 2023**; the next is in autumn 2027.
The National Council and the Council of States together form the **Federal Assembly**.
Parliament makes the **laws** and decides on the Confederation's money.
**Committees** prepare the items of business.

abschnitte.text: The **National Council** represents the people. The people entitled to vote in Switzerland elect its members every four years. The election takes place in each **canton**. Large cantons have more seats than small ones. The last election was on 22 October 2023; the next will take place in autumn 2027.

Switzerland has a parliament with two chambers: the **National Council** and the **Council of States**. Together they are called the **Federal Assembly**. Both councils are equally important. A law only applies if both agree. They meet in the **Federal Palace** in Bern, normally four times a year for a session.

Parliament makes and changes the **laws** of the Confederation. It also decides on the **budget**, that is how much money the Confederation spends. Before an item of business comes to the council, a **committee** discusses it. There a few members work on it in more detail. Then the whole council debates and votes.

Anyone who wants to speak in the National Council goes to the front, to the **lectern**. That way everyone can see and hear the person well. The members speak in their own national language. So that everyone understands everything, there is **simultaneous interpreting** into German, French and Italian. The interpreters work in small booths.

gewusst: In the National Council there is simultaneous interpreting: whoever speaks is immediately translated into the other languages.
A federal law always needs the approval of both councils.

teile.einleitung: Lobbying means that interest groups try to influence politics. Associations, companies and organisations want to convince members of parliament of their concerns. In the Federal Palace this often happens in the lobby hall (Wandelhalle).
wichtigste: In lobbying, interest groups want to win members of parliament over to their concerns.
Each member of parliament may give two people a permanent access pass to the Federal Palace.
Anyone with such a permanent pass is listed in a public register.
Members of parliament must disclose their interests.
Informally this is called the godparent system.
The association Lobbywatch collects and publishes members' interests.
The lobby hall runs along the south side of the National Council chamber.

abschnitte.text: In **lobbying**, associations, companies or other organisations try to convince politicians of their concerns. This often happens in **personal conversations**. Lobbyists provide, for example, information or arguments about a law. Supporters say that this way members of parliament learn what a law means for those affected. Critics fear that groups with a lot of money and good connections gain too much influence.

You cannot simply walk into the **Federal Palace**. According to the **Parliament Act**, each member of parliament can give **two people** a permanent **access pass**. Many lobbyists gain access this way. Because they need a member of parliament as a “godfather” or “godmother” for this, it is called the **godparent system** (Götti-System). Critics complain that access thus depends on personal connections.

To make visible who is exerting influence, there are **public registers**. One shows who has a permanent pass, what role the person has and which member of parliament the pass comes from. In another register the members of parliament must state their **interests**, for example seats on company boards or work for associations. The association **Lobbywatch** also researches such connections and puts them online.

Many conversations take place in the **lobby hall**. It curves around the **south side** of the National Council chamber. The English word “lobby” originally means an entrance hall, which is where the term lobbying comes from. The lobby hall also serves as a **banqueting hall**, reception room and meeting place. Light materials such as **stucco** and **stucco marble** give it a friendly atmosphere.

The lobby hall is richly decorated. The **radiators** are clad in marble from Saillon in Valais, with **lions' heads** on them as decoration. The **ceiling paintings** were painted by the Ticino painter **Antonio Barzaghi-Cattaneo**. They are arranged in three rows. In the middle they show **six virtues** of the state.

gewusst: The word lobbying comes from the English “lobby”, which means entrance hall or lobby hall.
Even the radiators in the lobby hall of the Federal Palace are decorated with lions' heads.

teile.einleitung: Political disenchantment (in German “Politikverdrossenheit”) means that people are disappointed with politics or turn away from it. The term is well known but also disputed, because many people are not unpolitical, just dissatisfied with politicians or parties.
wichtigste: “Politikverdrossenheit” was the German word of the year in 1992.
Falling turnout is often seen as a sign of it.
In the 2023 National Council elections turnout was 46.6 per cent.
If the discontent is directed mainly at parties, it is called disenchantment with parties.
Many young people are more likely to get involved in movements than in parties.
In the canton of Schaffhausen voting is compulsory, with a fine.

abschnitte.text: The **Society for the German Language** chose “Politikverdrossenheit” as its word of the year in 1992. The word describes a growing distance between citizens and politics. Someone who is disenchanted is disappointed, distrustful or no longer feels like taking part. Typical reasons are the feeling of not being heard or annoyance about broken promises.

A frequently mentioned sign is falling **turnout**. In Switzerland, in National Council elections since the 1970s, it has mostly been below half; in 2023, according to the Federal Statistical Office, it was 46.6 per cent. But low turnout can have many reasons, for example lack of time or even satisfaction. Switzerland also votes very often, which is why some people only go to the polls on topics that matter to them.

Researchers object that many people are definitely interested in politics. But they distrust the politicians or the parties. That is why people speak more precisely of **disenchantment with politicians**, **disenchantment with parties** or **disenchantment with institutions**. Young people, for example, more often take part in petitions, demonstrations or actions such as the **climate strikes**. Firm ties to a party, on the other hand, are decreasing.

If certain groups hardly ever vote for a long time, their concerns are missing in parliament. This is then called a **problem of representation**: those elected only represent part of the population. To strengthen participation there is, for example, political education at school, youth parliaments or simpler ways of voting such as postal voting. The canton of **Schaffhausen** is the only canton that still has **compulsory voting** with a small fine.

gewusst: Thanks to compulsory voting, Schaffhausen usually has the highest turnout in Switzerland.
Political disenchantment does not necessarily mean lack of interest; often there is disappointment behind it.

t2j0t9x.t: New Rail Link through the Alps

teile.einleitung: The NRLA (in German NEAT), the New Rail Link through the Alps, is one of the largest construction projects in Swiss history. With long tunnels deep beneath the Alps it connects north and south more quickly. The people voted yes to it in 1992.
wichtigste: NEAT stands for **New Rail Link through the Alps** (Neue Eisenbahn-Alpentransversale).
On **27 September 1992** the people voted yes with around **64 per cent**.
At the heart of the NRLA are the **base tunnels under the Gotthard and the Lötschberg**.
The **Gotthard Base Tunnel** has been in operation since **2016**.
The **Ceneri Base Tunnel** was opened in **2020** as the last big tunnel.
The NRLA is meant to shift more goods from road to rail.

abschnitte.text: A **referendum** had been called against parliament's **Alpine Transit Decree**. That is why the people voted on it on 27 September 1992. Exactly **63.6 per cent** said yes, around 1.3 million votes. Turnout was 45.9 per cent. The decree provided for a **base tunnel** each under the Gotthard and the Lötschberg, plus connections to Eastern and Western Switzerland.

A **base tunnel** does not go high up over a pass but deep down through the foot of the mountain. So the trains hardly have to climb any slopes. This allows long, heavy **goods trains** to travel faster and with less energy. Travellers also save a lot of time. The first completed NRLA tunnel was the **Lötschberg Base Tunnel**, which went into operation in 2007.

The **Gotthard Base Tunnel** was ceremonially opened on 1 June 2016, and scheduled services began in December 2016. At around 57 kilometres it is the **longest railway tunnel in the world**. In 2020 it was followed in Ticino by the **Ceneri Base Tunnel**. It completes the Gotthard axis in the south and shortens the journey between **Bellinzona and Lugano**. With this, the NRLA on the Gotthard was complete.

Every year a great many **lorries** travel through the Alps. They cause noise and exhaust fumes in the narrow valleys. The NRLA is meant to help shift goods traffic **from road to rail**. In 1994 the people also accepted the **Alpine Initiative**, which anchored the protection of the Alpine region from transit traffic in the constitution. So the NRLA is also a project for the **environment**.

gewusst: At around 57 kilometres, the Gotthard Base Tunnel is the longest railway tunnel in the world.
Almost two thirds of voters said yes to the NRLA in 1992.

teile.einleitung: On 22 October 2023 Switzerland elected a new parliament. All 200 members of the National Council and the members of the Council of States were elected, some of them in second rounds.
wichtigste: The National Council is elected on the second-to-last Sunday in October; in 2023 that was 22 October.
There were 618 lists with 5,909 candidates, a record.
Around 41 per cent of the candidates were women.
The SVP won the most votes, with 27.9 per cent.
In the Council of States the Centre remained the strongest party, followed by the FDP with 11 seats.
The Swiss Party of Labour lost its only National Council seat.

abschnitte.text: The **Federal Act on Political Rights** sets the National Council election for the **second-to-last Sunday in October**. In 2023 that was **22 October**. According to the Federal Statistical Office there were **618 lists** with **5,909 candidates**. This was another record. The share of women among the candidates was around **41 per cent**, and somewhat lower among those elected.

The **SVP** became by far the strongest party with 27.9 per cent and gained seats. The **SP** reached 18.3 per cent. The **Greens** lost several seats. The SVP, FDP, EDU, Lega and MCG together reached **95 seats**. The **absolute majority** in the National Council is 101 seats, so they were 6 short. The **Swiss Party of Labour** lost its seat in the canton of Neuchâtel to the SVP.

Three days after the election the **Federal Statistical Office** had to correct something. Because of an error in transmitting data, the **party strengths**, that is the shares of the vote, had been calculated incorrectly. The **distribution of seats** was not affected. This shows how important careful checks are in elections.

In cantons with only **one National Council seat**, the **majority system** applies: whoever has the most votes wins. In **Nidwalden** **Regina Durrer-Knobel** of the Centre took the seat previously held by the SVP. In the larger cantons, on the other hand, the National Council is elected by **proportional representation**, that is according to the proportion of votes.

In the Council of States the **Centre** remained the strongest party. The **FDP** lost one seat and ended up with **11 seats**. The **Greens** fell back from 5 to **3 seats**. In many cantons a **second round** was needed for the Council of States in November.

gewusst: Turnout in 2023 was just under half of those entitled to vote.
The newly elected Federal Assembly elected the Federal Council in December 2023.

teile.einleitung: An emergency call is a phone call you make to get help quickly in an emergency. In Switzerland there are different emergency numbers for the police, fire brigade, ambulance and other services. All of them are free and can be reached from any phone.
wichtigste: **117** is the police number, only for real emergencies.
**112** is the European emergency number and also works in Switzerland.
You can reach the **Rega** with its rescue helicopter on **1414**.
In case of **poisoning**, Tox Info Suisse helps on **145**.
On an emergency call you say **where you are** and what has happened.
An emergency call is **free**; calling for fun is forbidden.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland there are several **emergency numbers**. **117** connects you to the police, **118** to the fire brigade and **144** to the ambulance service. **112** is the European emergency number. It works all over Europe, and in Switzerland it connects you to the police. All these numbers are **free** and work from any phone.

The **Rega** is the Swiss Air-Rescue service. It helps with **rescue helicopters**, for example in accidents in the mountains. You can reach it on the number **1414**. If someone has swallowed something **poisonous**, such as cleaning products or medicines, you dial **145**. There experts from **Tox Info Suisse** give advice.

abschnitte.titel: How to make an emergency call
abschnitte.text: First take a deep breath and speak **calmly and clearly**. Say **who** you are, **where** you are and **what** has happened. The location is particularly important, because the helpers need to know where to come. The helpers often ask more questions. That is why you only hang up when **the helpers tell you to**.

You only dial an emergency number when **someone is in danger**. That can be an accident, a fire, a burglary or when someone is being threatened. Anyone who calls for no reason or for fun **blocks the line** for real emergencies. A false alarm can be punished. If you have dialled by mistake, stay on the line and say that it was a mistake.

gewusst: The emergency number 112 works in all EU countries and in Switzerland too.
With its helicopters the Rega also flies to areas that cannot be reached by car.

teile.einleitung: Freedom of opinion means that everyone may say what they think. But for a conversation to go well, rules are also needed: listening, letting others finish and staying friendly.
wichtigste: Different opinions are normal.
With an “I” sentence such as “I think ...” you give your opinion in a friendly way.
A good listener lets others finish speaking and looks at them.
If you have not understood something, you ask.
You criticise an idea, not the person.
A speakers' list or a talking stick makes sure everyone gets a turn.
The Convention on the Rights of the Child gives children the right to be heard.

abschnitte.text: People often have **different opinions**. That is completely **normal**. One person loves football, another prefers drawing. In a democracy people talk about different opinions and look for a way forward together. In Switzerland the **Federal Constitution** protects freedom of opinion. Everyone may say what they think, even if others think differently.
