The **UN Convention on the Rights of the Child** says that children may **give their opinion** on things that affect them. Adults should listen to them and take their opinion seriously. **Switzerland** has accepted this convention. That is why children may have a say, for example at school or in the family, when it is about them.

abschnitte.titel: Giving your opinion in a friendly way
abschnitte.text: If you begin with **“I think ...”**, you are talking about yourself. That way you do not attack anyone. This is called an **“I” sentence**. It is also good to **give reasons** for your opinion. With a reason, it becomes clear why you think something. Then the others can think about it better. You may criticise an opinion, but never **insult the person**.

A good conversation includes **listening**. A good listener lets the other person **finish speaking**. You look at the person who is talking. This is polite and shows that you are paying attention. If you have not understood something, you may **ask** in a friendly way. This leads to fewer misunderstandings, and everyone feels taken seriously.

In a large group, many people often want to talk at the same time. A **speakers' list** helps. It contains the names of the children who have put their hands up, and they take turns in order. Some classes use a **talking stick**. Only the person holding the stick may speak. The others listen until the stick is passed on.

gewusst: Children's right to be heard is in Article 12 of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child.
Parliament also has a speakers' list so that everyone can speak in turn.

teile.einleitung: The right of petition allows all people to approach the authorities with a request, a suggestion or a complaint. A petition is usually submitted with many signatures. In Switzerland almost anyone may sign a petition, including children.
wichtigste: A petition is a request or demand that is submitted with signatures.
The right of petition is in Article 33 of the Federal Constitution.
Almost anyone may sign a petition, including children and people without a Swiss passport.
No minimum number of signatures is needed.
The authorities must take note of the petition.
A reply on the content is not compulsory, but the petition is often examined.
Unlike a popular initiative, a petition does not lead to a vote.

abschnitte.text: A **petition** is a written request or demand to an authority. You can, for example, ask for a zebra crossing to be built near the school. To give the petition more weight, you collect **signatures** from people who support the cause. The word comes from the Latin “petere”, which means to ask or demand.

The right of petition is in **Article 33 of the Federal Constitution**. It has applied since the founding of the federal state in 1848. Nobody may be disadvantaged because they have submitted or signed a petition. The cantonal constitutions also contain a right of petition.

Unlike voting, the right of petition has no minimum age. **Children** and young people may also sign and submit petitions. Foreign nationals may take part too. That is why a petition is one of the few ways for children to approach politics directly.

Petitions to the federal parliament are submitted to the Federal Assembly and examined by a **committee**. The authorities must take note of a petition, but they do not have to reply on its content. Often the matter is still discussed, and sometimes a council member then submits a proposal. You can also send petitions to the municipality and the canton.

A good petition has a clear request and a short explanation. The signature list contains the name, address and signature of the supporters. Today many petitions are also collected online. At the **Youth Session** in Bern, young people pass petitions every year, which are then handed to parliament.

begriffe.erklaerung: Your own name, written by hand, as a sign of agreement.
A state body such as the municipal council, government or parliament.
A demand by the people with 100,000 signatures that leads to a vote.
An event at which young people discuss politics in the Federal Palace.

gewusst: A petition can be signed by just one person and still be valid.
The right of petition is much older than democracy; even in the Middle Ages people sent petitions to kings and princes.

teile.einleitung: The Laufen Valley (Laufental) is a German-speaking region on the River Birs. For a long time it belonged to the canton of Bern; since 1994 it has belonged to the canton of Basel-Landschaft. Getting there took almost twenty years and needed many votes.
wichtigste: The Laufen Valley is German-speaking, the canton of Jura is French-speaking.
The founding of the canton of Jura turned the Laufen Valley into a Bernese exclave.
In 1980 the Laufen Valley chose Basel-Landschaft as a possible partner canton.
In 1983 it first voted to stay with Bern, but the vote had to be repeated.
In 1989, 51.7 per cent said yes to moving to Basel-Landschaft.
In 1993 the people and the cantons of the whole of Switzerland agreed.
The district of Laufen has 13 municipalities.

abschnitte.text: Like the Jura, the Laufen Valley belonged to the canton of Bern for a long time. In the 1970s the people in the Jura voted on their future in several **plebiscites**. This led to the new **canton of Jura** in 1979. The German-speaking Laufen Valley did not want to join the French-speaking Jura. But because the new canton lay between the Laufen Valley and the rest of Bern, the valley became an **exclave**. This is an area that is cut off from the rest of its canton. The plebiscites gave the Laufen Valley the right to decide on a change.

In January 1980 the people of the Laufen Valley could choose between three cantons. **Basel-Landschaft** received 52 per cent, **Solothurn** 32 and **Basel-Stadt** 16 per cent. In March 1980 there followed a **run-off** between the two strongest. Basel-Landschaft won against Solothurn. This settled which canton would be negotiated with.

On **11 September 1983** the Laufen Valley voted. Just under 57 per cent wanted to stay with the canton of Bern. But in 1984 the **Bernese finance affair** came to light. The canton of Bern had secretly supported the pro-Bern campaign with money from secret funds. This is not allowed, because votes must be fair. The **Federal Supreme Court** therefore ordered the vote to be repeated.

On **12 November 1989** the Laufen Valley voted again. This time **51.7 per cent** said yes to the **Laufen Valley Treaty** and thus to joining Basel-Landschaft. Because this changed the borders of cantons, the whole of Switzerland also had to agree. On **26 September 1993** the **people and the cantons** said yes with around 75 per cent. Since 1 January 1994 the Laufen Valley has belonged to Basel-Landschaft.

Today the Laufen Valley forms the **district of Laufen**. It is one of five districts of the canton of Basel-Landschaft and has **13 municipalities**. They include, for example, Laufen, Zwingen, Grellingen and Röschenz. The **Birs** flows through the valley. The history of the Laufen Valley shows how border questions, too, are solved democratically in Switzerland.

gewusst: Before the final move, the Laufen Valley voted several times, and in the end even the whole of Switzerland had a say.
Because Bern put money into the campaign without permission in 1983, the result of the vote was declared invalid.

teile.einleitung: The left-right scheme is a simple way of ordering parties and political opinions. You imagine a line: on the left are parties that want more equality through the state, on the right those that emphasise more freedom for the economy and the individual.
wichtigste: The terms left and right come from France.
They arose in 1789 from the seating arrangement in the French National Assembly.
Left-wing parties usually call for more redistribution by the state.
Parties to the right of centre usually want lower taxes and less state.
Among the Federal Council parties, the SP is furthest to the left and the SVP furthest to the right.
The SVP, FDP and the Centre are often called the bourgeois parties.
A second axis distinguishes between liberal and conservative.

abschnitte.text: The division into left and right comes from **France**. In **1789**, at the time of the French Revolution, the **National Assembly** was meeting. Seen from the president, the supporters of great changes sat on the **left** side. The supporters of the king and the old order sat on the **right**. Over time this **seating arrangement** gave rise to political terms that are still used all over the world today.

**Left-wing** parties want to reduce the differences between rich and poor. They support a strong **welfare state** and want more **redistribution**. This means: the state takes in money through taxes and spends it, for example, on social benefits, education or health. In Switzerland the **SP** and the **Greens** in particular count as left-wing parties.

Parties **to the right of centre** want the state to hold back. They often call for **lower taxes** and fewer regulations, so that the economy can act as freely as possible. Many also emphasise personal responsibility and tradition. The **SVP** represents national-conservative positions and is furthest to the right among the Federal Council parties. **The SVP, FDP and the Centre** are together often referred to as the **bourgeois parties**, in contrast to the SP and the Greens.

Between left and right lies the **centre**. Centre parties take more left-wing positions on some topics and more right-wing ones on others. One example is the **Green Liberals (GLP)**. On environmental questions they are close to the Greens, on economic questions close to the FDP. That is why they are usually placed in the centre.

A single line is often not enough to describe parties precisely. A party can, for example, be economically right-wing but socially open. That is why people often draw a **second axis** between **liberal** and **conservative**. Liberal here means open to new things and to many ways of life; conservative means rather holding on to what has proved itself. This creates a field with four corners into which you can place parties and also your own opinions.

gewusst: The terms left and right are over 230 years old and go back to a simple seating arrangement.
Online voting aids show voters where they themselves stand in the political field.

teile.einleitung: The Federal Constitution is Switzerland's most important law. In 1999 the people and the cantons accepted a new, completely revised Federal Constitution. It came into force on 1 January 2000 and replaced the constitution of 1874.
wichtigste: The people and the cantons accepted the new Federal Constitution in **1999**, with around **59 per cent** voting yes.
It has applied since **1 January 2000**.
The Federal Council called its draft an **update** of the existing law.
The constitution is divided into **six titles**.
Art. 19 guarantees all children **free primary education**.
Every change needs the approval of **the people and the cantons**.

abschnitte.text: Work on a new constitution took **over 30 years**. As early as 1965, proposals in parliament called for a **total revision**. But for a long time no progress was made. Only in 1998 did the councils adopt the text. On 18 April 1999 the people and the cantons voted: the proposal was accepted with **59.2 per cent** voting yes, and a narrow majority of the cantons also agreed.

The Federal Council described its draft as an **update**. This means: the existing constitutional law was to be reorganised and written in **modern language**. Big changes in content were not the aim. Many rules that had previously only been found in court judgements or unwritten principles were now written down explicitly. The constitution is divided into **six titles**, for example on fundamental rights, on the Confederation and the cantons, and on the federal authorities.

The constitution contains a long list of **fundamental rights**. **Art. 19** guarantees adequate and **free primary education**, which is why state schools charge no school fees. **Art. 13** protects **privacy** and gives every person the right to protection against the misuse of their data. **Art. 120** requires that the **dignity of living beings** be respected in genetic engineering. This means animals, plants and other organisms.

The Federal Constitution can be changed at any time. But every change is subject to the **mandatory referendum**. This means the people must always vote on it. It needs the **majority of the people**, that is the majority of voters, and the **majority of the cantons**. Since 2000 the constitution has already been added to many times, for example by accepted **popular initiatives**.

gewusst: Before 1999 Switzerland had only two federal constitutions: that of 1848 and that of 1874.
The Federal Constitution begins with the words “In the name of Almighty God!”.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland every person who lives here must be insured against illness. This compulsory health insurance is also called basic insurance and is regulated in the Health Insurance Act.
wichtigste: Basic insurance is regulated in the Federal Health Insurance Act (KVG), which came into force in 1996.
In basic insurance, every health insurer must accept all persons resident in Switzerland.
The lowest deductible (franchise) for adults is 300 francs, the highest 2,500 francs.
Above the deductible you usually pay a 10 per cent share of costs, for adults at most 700 francs a year.
The premium does not depend on income.
The Federal Office of Public Health (FOPH) approves the premiums every year.

abschnitte.text: The **Health Insurance Act**, **KVG** for short, came into force in 1996. Since then all people resident in Switzerland have had to have basic insurance. You may choose your health insurer freely. Every insurer has an **obligation to accept**: it must accept everyone, no matter how old or how healthy someone is. Basic insurance pays for the same services with every insurer.

You pay part of the costs yourself. The **deductible** (franchise) is the amount you first pay yourself every year. For adults it is at least 300 francs and at most 2,500 francs. Anyone who chooses a high deductible pays a lower premium but bears more risk. Above the deductible you usually pay a **10 per cent share of costs**. This is limited to 700 francs a year for adults and 350 francs for children.

Every month you pay the health insurer a **premium**. It is a **per-person premium**: it does not depend on income. But it differs according to region of residence, age group, deductible and insurer. The **Federal Office of Public Health** (FOPH) checks and approves the premiums every year. People who earn little can receive a **premium reduction** from the canton.

Basic insurance pays, for example, for visits to the doctor, many medicines and a stay in the general ward of a hospital. Anyone who wants more, for example a **single room** in hospital, needs **supplementary insurance**. This is voluntary. Unlike with basic insurance, an insurer may turn people down here.

gewusst: There is no minimum deductible for children, so they can have a deductible of zero francs.
The Swiss people voted on the KVG before it came into force in 1996.

teile.einleitung: Compulsory military service requires Swiss men to serve in the army. The Swiss Army is a militia army: most soldiers are citizens with a civilian job. Service lasts from the orientation day until discharge from the army.
wichtigste: Before recruitment you attend the orientation day.
Basic training is called recruit school.
This is usually followed by refresher courses every year.
Single-term servers do all their service in one go.
The days of service completed are recorded in the service record book.
The Income Compensation Scheme replaces part of your wages during service.
In 2013 the people clearly rejected the abolition of compulsory military service.

abschnitte.text: The Swiss Army follows the **militia principle**. Most soldiers are citizens with a **civilian job**. They do service from time to time alongside their normal lives. Only a small proportion of army members work for the army full-time. With the **Further Development of the Army (WEA)**, the target strength was set at **100,000 army members**. In the past the army was much bigger.

abschnitte.titel: From orientation day to recruit school
abschnitte.text: The path into the army begins with the **orientation day**. There young men find out how **recruitment**, **military service**, **civilian service** and **civil protection** work. It usually takes place in their canton of residence. After recruitment comes **recruit school**, RS for short. It is the basic training for all new soldiers. There they learn the most important military skills.

After recruit school, soldiers usually do a **refresher course** every year, **WK** for short. There they brush up their skills. For soldiers a refresher course usually lasts **three weeks**. But there are also **single-term servers** (Durchdiener). They do all their days of service in a **single block**. After that they have completed their training service and go into the reserve.

abschnitte.titel: Service record book and income compensation
abschnitte.text: The **service record book** contains, among other things, the **days of service** completed, the **assignment** and the **rank**. It is important proof that compulsory service has been fulfilled. During service the **Income Compensation Scheme (EO)** pays compensation for lost wages. People doing civilian service and civil protection also receive it. So those doing service do not have to give up all their income.

Compulsory military service is discussed again and again in Switzerland. On **22 September 2013** the people voted on an initiative to **abolish compulsory military service**. Around **three quarters** of voters rejected it. The supporters wanted a voluntary army; the opponents regarded the militia army as having proved itself. Compulsory military service for Swiss men therefore remained.

gewusst: The Swiss Army has a target strength of 100,000 members, even though most of them have a perfectly normal job in everyday life.
Today the Income Compensation Scheme also pays compensation outside military service.

teile.einleitung: Personalised proportional representation (in German “personalisierte Verhältniswahl”) is the electoral system for the German Bundestag. It combines electing people in constituencies with distributing seats according to the parties' share of the vote.
wichtigste: With the first vote you elect a person in the constituency.
With the second vote you elect a party's list.
Germany is divided into 299 constituencies.
Since 2009 the seats have been distributed using the Sainte-Laguë method.
After the 2023 reform the Bundestag regularly has 630 seats.
Since 2023 constituency seats must be covered by second votes.

abschnitte.text: In the Bundestag election you have **two votes**. With the **first vote** you elect a constituency candidate in your **constituency**. This element makes proportional representation “personalised”. With the **second vote** you elect a party's list. It decides how many seats a party gets in total. Germany is divided into **299 constituencies**.

Since the 2009 election the seats have been distributed using the **Sainte-Laguë method**. This is a method of calculation with standard rounding. Before that the **Hare-Niemeyer** method was used. In addition, a **five per cent threshold** applies: small parties must reach enough votes to get seats.

In the past a party could win more constituencies than it was entitled to seats according to second votes. These extra seats were called **overhang seats**. From 2013 to 2023 the other parties received **compensatory seats** in return. This brought the result back into line with the second votes. But it made the Bundestag very large: in the end it had **736** members.

The **electoral reform** of 2023 fixed the size of the Bundestag at **630 seats**. The principle of **second-vote coverage** applies: a party receives at most as many seats as it is entitled to according to second votes. Constituency winners with the weakest results can therefore miss out. The reform was politically controversial.

Anyone who gives their first and second votes to different parties is **splitting their vote**. For example, you vote for the constituency candidate of a large party and give your second vote to a possible coalition partner. The German system has also served as a model for other countries. After a referendum, **New Zealand** first voted under the “Mixed Member Proportional” system in 1996.

gewusst: The Swiss National Council is also elected by proportional representation in most cantons, but without first and second votes.
In Switzerland you can cross out candidates on a list, list them twice or add them from other lists.

teile.einleitung: Every four years the voters of Switzerland elect the 200 members of the National Council. Each canton holds its own election. The last election was in 2023, the next is in 2027.
wichtigste: In the National Council election **each canton is a constituency**.
Each person may cast **only one ballot paper**.
You have **as many votes as the canton has seats**.
In cantons with several seats, **proportional representation** applies.
In 2023 **almost 6,000 people** stood as candidates, more than ever before.
Turnout in 2023 was around **47 per cent**.
The next National Council elections are in **2027** (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: In the National Council election **each canton is a constituency**. It elects its own members of the National Council. Large cantons have many seats, small cantons few. So anyone who lives in a canton with many seats may write more names on the ballot paper. In cantons with only one seat you write only one name.

Each voter may hand in exactly **one ballot paper**. You can take a party's pre-printed **list**. But you may cross out names on it or add names from other lists; this is called **panachage**. You can also write a name twice; this is called **cumulating**. In total you may write as many names as the canton has seats.

In cantons with several seats, **proportional representation** applies. The lists receive as many seats as corresponds to their share of the votes. In this way smaller parties are also represented in the National Council. Within a list, the people who received the most votes are elected. In cantons with only one seat, whoever has the most votes is elected.

The last election took place in October 2023. There were **almost 6,000 candidates**, more than ever before. But only 200 could be elected. **Turnout** was around 47 per cent, that is just under half of the voters. **77 women** were elected, which is around 39 per cent of the seats. On the same Sunday almost all cantons also elected their **members of the Council of States**. Only Appenzell Innerrhoden elects at the **Landsgemeinde**.

gewusst: When cumulating, you may write a name on the ballot paper at most twice.
In 2023 there were on average almost 30 candidates for each seat in the National Council.

teile.einleitung: The Landsgemeinde of Appenzell Innerrhoden is an open-air assembly at which the voters vote and elect. It takes place every year in the village of Appenzell and is one of the oldest forms of democracy.
wichtigste: The Landsgemeinde takes place in the cantonal capital Appenzell.
It is normally held on the last Sunday in April.
Only Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden still have a Landsgemeinde.
Appenzell Ausserrhoden abolished its Landsgemeinde in 1997.
Women in Innerrhoden have only been able to vote since 1991.
The Landsgemeinde also elects the government and the court.

abschnitte.text: The Innerrhoden **Landsgemeinde** is normally held on the **last Sunday in April**. If this day falls on **Easter**, it is held a week later, on the first Sunday in May. The meeting place is the **Landsgemeinde square** in the cantonal capital **Appenzell**. The voters stand together there in the **ring**.

In the morning the government and many people attend a **church service**. Afterwards a ceremonial **procession** moves from the **town hall** to the Landsgemeinde square. The government walks in it too. Many men traditionally carry a sword or a side arm, which used to count as proof of the right to vote. For many people of Innerrhoden the Landsgemeinde is a day of celebration.

At the Landsgemeinde voting is done **openly**: anyone who agrees raises their hand. This is called a **show of hands**. The voters decide on laws and elect the government, which in Innerrhoden is called the **Standeskommission**. The **court** is also elected at the Landsgemeinde. Everything happens in the open air.

Appenzell Innerrhoden was the **last canton** to introduce votes for women at cantonal level. The men had rejected it several times at the Landsgemeinde. In November 1990 the **Federal Supreme Court** decided that women in Innerrhoden must also be allowed to vote. In **April 1991** women stood in the ring for the first time.

In the past several cantons had a Landsgemeinde. Today it only exists in **Glarus** and **Appenzell Innerrhoden**. **Appenzell Ausserrhoden** voted at the ballot box in **1997** to abolish it. Since then votes there are only held at the ballot box. Supporters value the tradition and the sense of community at the Landsgemeinde; critics complain that the vote is not secret.

gewusst: At federal level women in Switzerland have been able to vote since 1971; in Innerrhoden at cantonal level only 20 years later.
Appenzell Innerrhoden is one of the smallest cantons in Switzerland, which is why almost all the voters fit into the Landsgemeinde square.

teile.einleitung: The Lega dei Ticinesi is a political party in the canton of Ticino. It was founded in 1991 as a protest party and today is represented in the Ticino government and in the National Council.
wichtigste: The Lega dei Ticinesi was founded in January 1991.
Its founders were the businessman Giuliano Bignasca and the journalist Flavio Maspoli.
The party publishes the free Sunday newspaper “Il Mattino della domenica”.
Since 2011 it has provided two of the five members of the Ticino Council of State.
In the Federal Palace its representatives belong to the SVP parliamentary group.
Important topics are cross-border commuters and criticism of the EU.

abschnitte.text: The **Lega dei Ticinesi** was founded in January 1991. Behind it were the businessman **Giuliano Bignasca** and the journalist **Flavio Maspoli**. They wanted to protest against the established parties and against the authorities in “Bern”. In its very first year the Lega won a seat in the **National Council**. Giuliano Bignasca was president of the party for a long time; he died in 2013.

The Lega publishes the **“Mattino della domenica”**. This is a free newspaper that appears on Sundays. It is regarded as the mouthpiece of the party. The newspaper is known for its **provocative style** with sharp headlines. Supporters value the direct language; critics often find it hurtful.

The Lega has been represented in the Ticino **Council of State**, the cantonal government, since 1995. Since 2011 it has provided **two of the five** members. A well-known Lega politician was **Marco Borradori**. He was a member of the Council of State for a long time and mayor of **Lugano** from 2013 to 2021. He was regarded as the moderate face of the party and died in office in 2021.

Since the 2023 elections the Lega has held one of Ticino's eight seats in the National Council. It is held by **Lorenzo Quadri**, who has sat in the National Council since 2011. With so few seats the Lega cannot form its own **parliamentary group**. Its representatives therefore join the **SVP group**. In 2015 the Ticino councillor of state **Norman Gobbi** of the Lega was on the SVP's official ticket of three candidates for the Federal Council. Guy Parmelin was elected at the time.

One main topic of the Lega is **cross-border commuters**. These are people from Italy who work in Ticino and commute across the border every day. The Lega criticises that they compete with Ticino workers. The party also rejects **joining the EU** and criticises the federal authorities. Other parties counter that the Ticino economy depends on cross-border commuters.

gewusst: The Lega made it into the National Council in the very year it was founded.
The name “Lega dei Ticinesi” means “League of Ticinese” in English.

teile.einleitung: A woman member of parliament (Parlamentarierin) is a woman who sits in a parliament. In the Swiss federal parliament these are the women members of the National Council and of the Council of States.
wichtigste: A woman in the National Council is called a Nationalrätin, a woman in the Council of States a Ständerätin.
Since 1971 women have been able to be elected to the federal parliament.
Lise Girardin from Geneva became the first woman member of the Council of States in 1971.
Elisabeth Blunschy from Schwyz became the first woman President of the National Council in 1977.
Most members of parliament also have a job besides parliament.
That is why it is called a militia parliament.

abschnitte.titel: Members of the National Council and the Council of States
abschnitte.text: The Swiss parliament is called the **Federal Assembly**. It has two chambers: the **National Council** with 200 members and the **Council of States** with 46 members. A woman in the National Council is a **Nationalrätin**. A woman in the Council of States is a **Ständerätin**. Members of the Council of States represent their canton in Bern.

For a long time only men were allowed to vote and be elected in Switzerland. Only in **1971** did women receive the right to vote and stand for election at federal level. In the same year the first women were elected to parliament. **Lise Girardin** from Geneva became the first woman member of the Council of States. Since then the share of women in parliament has kept rising.

In **1977** **Elisabeth Blunschy** from the canton of Schwyz became President of the National Council. She was the first woman in this office. The President of the National Council chairs the sittings of the council and for one year is regarded as the “highest Swiss woman”. In 1984 Elisabeth Kopp was elected as the first woman to the Federal Council.

For many council members politics is not a full-time job. Besides it they work, for example, as a **farmer**, a **lawyer** or a **teacher**. That is why it is called a **militia parliament**. The advantage: members of parliament bring experience from everyday life with them. However, many need a great deal of time for politics.

gewusst: The presidency of the National Council changes every year, so a woman President of the National Council can only hold the office for one year.
In the 2019 election the share of women in the National Council rose to over 40 per cent.

teile.einleitung: Polarisation means that political groups move away from each other and the centre becomes weaker. In Switzerland political scientists have observed this development since the 1990s.
wichtigste: Since the 1990s the parties at the poles have become stronger and the centre has lost ground.
Above all the SVP on the right and the SP and Greens on the left gained.
The EEA vote of 1992 is regarded as an important trigger for the rise of the SVP.
The parliamentary groups in the National Council have moved apart on the left-right axis.
Affective polarisation describes feelings towards other parties.
In 2023 the SVP and SP together won around 46 per cent of the vote.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from **pole**, that is an end point. In polarisation the parties at the poles gain, and the **centre** becomes weaker. In Switzerland, since the 1990s, above all the **SVP** on the right and the **SP** and **Greens** on the left have gained. The **FDP** and **CVP**, on the other hand, clearly lost shares of the vote. In the 2023 elections the SVP won 27.9 per cent and the SP 18.3 per cent, together around **46 per cent**.

An important trigger was the **EEA vote** of 1992. Under **Christoph Blocher**, the SVP fought almost alone among the Federal Council parties against joining the European Economic Area. The vote went its way. After that the European question became its main topic. The political scientist **Hanspeter Kriesi** saw **globalisation** as a new dividing line between **opening up** and **staying apart**.

Researchers analyse how council members vote in the **National Council**. These analyses show: the **parliamentary groups** have moved away from each other on the **left-right axis**. The centre has become narrower. When the poles are further apart, it becomes harder to find **compromises**. But compromises are important, especially in Switzerland with its concordance.

Polarisation does not only concern opinions but also **feelings**. In **affective polarisation**, liking for your own group grows, as does dislike of supporters of other parties. People then do not only disagree on factual questions but distrust each other. Researchers study how strongly this is the case in different countries.

Political science has developed measures. The **effective number of parties** according to **Laakso and Taagepera** weights parties by their size and thus measures fragmentation. Switzerland has a high value compared with the rest of Europe. The **Pedersen index** shows **electoral volatility**, that is how much the shares of the vote shift from one election to the next. To calculate it, you add up all the gains and losses and halve the total.

gewusst: Despite polarisation, the large parties from left to right sit together in the Federal Council in Switzerland.
The Pedersen index is named after the Danish political scientist Mogens Pedersen.

teile.einleitung: The party presidency is at the head of a party. The president represents the party in public and leads it together with other bodies.
wichtigste: The party presidency is usually elected by the assembly of delegates.
In a co-presidency, several people share the leadership.
Since 2025 the FDP has been led by Susanne Vincenz-Stauffacher and Benjamin Mühlemann.
Philipp Bregy has been president of the Centre since 2025.
Lisa Mazzone has led the Greens since 2024, Jürg Grossen the GLP since 2017 (as of 2025).
The general secretariat organises a party's day-to-day work.

abschnitte.text: The **party president** is the best-known face of a party. He or she gives interviews, appears in debates and chairs meetings. In the large Swiss parties, the **assembly of delegates** usually elects the president. It is made up of representatives of the cantonal parties. The president is supported by the **general secretariat**, the party's head office.

Some parties are led by a **co-presidency**. Then usually two people lead the party with equal rights and share the work. In 2025 the **FDP** elected **Susanne Vincenz-Stauffacher** from St Gallen and **Benjamin Mühlemann** from Glarus as co-presidents. The SP also has a co-presidency (as of 2025).

As of 2025 the situation is as follows: in the **Centre**, the Valais National Council member **Philipp Bregy** has been president since 2025. The **Greens** have been led since 2024 by **Lisa Mazzone** from Geneva, who succeeded Balthasar Glättli. The **GLP** has been led by **Jürg Grossen** from Bern since 2017. The president of the **EVP** since June 2021 has been **Lilian Studer** from Aargau. Because such offices change, this list only applies to a particular point in time.

A president can change a party a great deal. **Gerhard Pfister** was president of the CVP from 2016. Under him the party dropped the “C” (for Christian) from its name and has since been called **“Die Mitte”** (the Centre). It wanted to appeal to more people this way. The new presidency then has to carry such decisions forward.

gewusst: Many party presidents also sit in the National Council or the Council of States at the same time.
In Switzerland party presidencies are usually part-time offices alongside a seat in parliament.

teile.einleitung: A consultative vote is a non-binding poll of the people on a particular question. The authorities want to find out what the population thinks, but they do not have to stick to the result. This makes it very different from the normal popular votes in Switzerland.
wichtigste: A consultative vote is a non-binding poll of the people.
The result is not legally binding.
Consultative means advisory.
The normal popular votes in Switzerland, by contrast, are binding.
At federal level Switzerland does not provide for consultative votes.
Politically, the result of such a poll often carries great weight all the same.

abschnitte.text: The word **consultative** comes from the Latin consultare and means advisory or asking for advice. In a consultative vote the people vote on a question, just as in a real vote. But the result is only a **recommendation** to the government or parliament. In the end the authorities may also decide differently.

In Switzerland popular votes are normally **binding**. If the people accept an initiative, it becomes part of the constitution, and if they reject a law, it does not come into force. With a consultative vote this is not the case. That is why there are none at federal level in Switzerland; there the people always decide in a binding way.

Some cantons and municipalities nevertheless have non-binding **public consultations**. A municipality can, for example, ask the population whether they could imagine a merger with the neighbouring village. The result helps the authorities to plan the next steps. Each canton decides for itself whether such polls are allowed.

In many countries public polls are rare and often only advisory. In Austria a non-binding **public poll** on compulsory military service took place in January 2013, and the majority voted to keep it. The 2016 vote on Great Britain leaving the EU was also legally only advisory. The government nevertheless carried out the result, **Brexit**, because it wanted to respect the will of the majority.

One advantage is that the authorities learn the opinion of the population before they decide. Critics say such polls could disappoint people if the authorities do not carry out the result in the end. In addition, it is often unclear how much a narrow result should count. That is why consultative votes are controversial in Switzerland and rather the **exception**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Advisory, meant only as a recommendation.
Must be complied with.
A vote used to find out the opinion of the population.
The joining of two or more municipalities into one.

gewusst: Brexit was carried out on the basis of a vote that was legally only advisory.
In Switzerland the people always have the last word in votes at federal level; a mere poll does not exist there.

teile.einleitung: The National Council is the large chamber of the Swiss federal parliament. It has 200 members and represents the people. Every four years it is re-elected by the voters.
wichtigste: The National Council has 200 members.
It is re-elected every four years, most recently in October 2023.
The seats are distributed among the cantons according to population.
Each canton has at least one seat.
Anyone who wants to be elected to the National Council must be at least 18 years old.
Elections are mostly by proportional representation, that is according to party strength.
Together with the Council of States, the National Council forms the Federal Assembly.

abschnitte.text: The **National Council** is the larger of the two chambers of the **Federal Assembly**. It represents the Swiss people, while the Council of States represents the cantons. It meets in the National Council chamber in the Federal Palace in Bern. Every law must be passed by the National Council and the Council of States.

The 200 seats are distributed among the cantons according to **population**. The canton of Zurich has the most, with 36 seats. Six small cantons, namely Uri, Obwalden, Nidwalden, Glarus and the two Appenzells, have only one seat each. When the population changes, the distribution is adjusted before each election.

Elections are held every four years in October, most recently in 2023 and next in 2027. Swiss citizens aged **18** and over may vote and be elected. In most cantons elections are by **proportional representation**, so the seats are distributed according to the parties' share of the vote. In cantons with only one seat, the majority system is used.

abschnitte.titel: Who sits in the National Council?
abschnitte.text: Members of many parties sit in the National Council; in the 2023 election the SVP became the strongest party. The members join together in **parliamentary groups**. After the 2023 election the share of women was almost 40 per cent. Most members are militia politicians and have a job besides their office.

The National Council elects a new president every year. This person is regarded in that year as the “highest Swiss woman” or “highest Swiss man”. The National Council has existed since the founding of the federal state in 1848. Since 1919 it has been elected by proportional representation, and since 1971 women have also been able to vote and be elected.

begriffe.erklaerung: One part of a parliament; Switzerland has two chambers.
The Swiss parliament, made up of the National Council and the Council of States.
A group of council members from the same or similar parties.
An electoral system in which seats are distributed according to party strength.

gewusst: The number of 200 seats has applied since 1963; before that the National Council grew with the population.
In the 1971 election the first ten women were elected to the National Council.

teile.einleitung: Consociational democracy (in German “Konkordanzdemokratie”) is a form of democracy in which as many of the important forces as possible govern together. In Switzerland this means: the largest parties sit together in the Federal Council, instead of a majority governing and the others going into opposition. The word concordance comes from Latin and means agreement.
wichtigste: In a consociational democracy the largest parties govern together.
That is why Switzerland has no strong opposition as other countries do.
Solutions are found through negotiations and compromises.
From 1959 to 2003 the so-called magic formula applied in the Federal Council.
The opposite is competitive democracy with a government and an opposition.
Popular rights such as the referendum have strongly encouraged concordance.

abschnitte.text: In a **consociational democracy** as many parties and groups as possible should share in power. Instead of the majority deciding alone, people look for solutions that many can live with. This is also called a **compromise**. In Switzerland this can be seen above all in the composition of the Federal Council.

In countries such as Germany or Great Britain there is a **competitive democracy**. There the party or coalition with the majority forms the government. The other parties are in **opposition** and criticise the government. After elections the government can change completely, which hardly ever happens in Switzerland.

After the federal state was founded in 1848, at first only the Liberals (Freisinnige) provided all the federal councillors. In 1891 Josef Zemp became the first Catholic Conservative to be elected, and in 1943 Ernst Nobs the first Social Democrat. In 1959 the **magic formula** came into being: two seats for the FDP, two for the CVP, two for the SP and one for the SVP. This distribution remained unchanged until 2003.

In 2003 the SVP, as the strongest party, received a second seat, and the CVP lost one in return. Today the SVP, SP and FDP each have two seats and the Centre (Die Mitte) has one. The parties try to reflect their strength in elections roughly in the Federal Council. However, there are repeated arguments about what a fair distribution is.

An important reason is **popular rights**. With a referendum, groups that were not allowed to have a say can bring down a law at the ballot box. That is why it pays to involve all important forces early on, for example in the **consultation procedure**, in which parties and associations give their opinion on new laws. The variety of languages, religions and regions has also helped Switzerland to rely on balance.

Concordance ensures **stability**, because politics does not change greatly after every election. Many people feel represented because their party is part of the government. Critics say that decisions therefore take a long time and responsibilities are less clear. In addition, there is no clear opposition to keep a check on the government; this role is often taken on by the people and the media.

begriffe.erklaerung: Agreement; here: many parties governing together.
Parties that are not in the government and criticise it.
The fixed distribution of Federal Council seats from 1959 to 2003.
A solution in which all sides give way a little.
Asking parties, cantons and associations for their views on a new law.

gewusst: The magic formula stayed the same for 44 years, from 1959 to 2003.
In Switzerland there is no change of government after elections as in many other countries.
In many cantons and municipalities, too, several parties sit together in the government.

teile.einleitung: A majority means that more than half have decided the same way. In a democracy this is how it is settled which proposal is accepted or who is elected. But there are different kinds of majority, and in Switzerland sometimes two are even needed at the same time.
wichtigste: Majority means that more than half have decided the same way.
With a simple majority, one side has more votes than the other.
An absolute majority requires more than half of all valid votes.
Some decisions need a qualified majority, for example two thirds.
Changes to the constitution in Switzerland need a majority of the people and a majority of the cantons.
There are 23 cantonal votes because six cantons only have half a vote.
In a democracy the rights of the minority must also be protected.

abschnitte.text: A **majority** is the larger part of a group. If, in a class of 24 children, 13 vote for a trip to the zoo, that is a majority. The other 11 children form the **minority**. In a democracy, what the majority has decided usually applies.

With a **simple majority**, the proposal with more yes than no votes wins. With an absolute majority you need more than half of all valid votes, that is more than all the others put together. With a **qualified majority** even more is needed, for example two thirds. Such strict rules often apply to particularly important decisions, for example changes to the rules of a club.

abschnitte.titel: Majority of the people and of the cantons
abschnitte.text: In a federal vote on a change to the constitution, two majorities are needed. The **majority of the people** means that more than half of those voting in the whole of Switzerland say yes. The **majority of the cantons** means that yes is also said in the majority of the cantons. For simple referendums on laws, on the other hand, the majority of the people is enough.

Switzerland has 26 cantons but only 23 **cantonal votes**. The six former half-cantons Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden each have half a vote. For a majority of the cantons you need at least twelve cantonal votes. In a tie of 11.5 to 11.5, the proposal is rejected.

The majority may not decide everything. The **fundamental rights** in the Federal Constitution protect all people, even if they are in the minority. Switzerland also makes sure that language groups and small cantons can have a say. That is why, for example, there is the Council of States, in which every canton has the same number of seats, no matter how big it is.

begriffe.erklaerung: The smaller part of a group in a vote.
The majority of all voters in the whole of Switzerland.
The majority of the cantons in a vote.
A particularly large majority, for example two thirds.

gewusst: It has happened that a proposal had a majority of the people but failed to win a majority of the cantons, for example the Responsible Business Initiative in 2020.
Blank ballot papers are not counted in federal votes when the result is calculated.

teile.einleitung: Politicians are people who hold political offices and help to govern the country, the canton or the municipality. They make laws, take decisions and represent the interests of the population. In Switzerland most of them are elected by the people.
wichtigste: Politicians hold political offices and help to govern.
There are politicians at the level of the municipality, the canton and the Confederation.
Most are elected by the people, the Federal Council by parliament.
Many Swiss politicians work in the militia system alongside a job.
Most belong to a political party.
Members of parliament must disclose their interests.
At federal level, anyone who is a Swiss citizen and at least 18 years old may vote and be elected.

abschnitte.text: **Politicians** shape how people live together in a state. They decide, for example, how much money is spent on schools, roads or environmental protection. To do this they discuss with others, look for compromises and vote. The word politics comes from the Greek “polis”, which means city or community.

In Switzerland there is politics at three levels: municipality, canton and Confederation. In the municipality there is, for example, the mayor and the **municipal council**. In the canton there is the cantonal parliament and the cantonal government. At federal level there are the members of the National Council and the Council of States and the seven members of the **Federal Council**.

abschnitte.titel: How do you become a politician?
abschnitte.text: Most politicians are **elected**. They often start in a party or youth party and first stand for election in their municipality. Over time they can be elected to a cantonal or federal office. The members of the Federal Council are elected by the United Federal Assembly.

Politicians must keep to the laws and the **constitution**. Members of the federal parliament must state publicly in which companies, associations or organisations they work; these are called **interests**. For statements in the council they enjoy special protection, immunity. At the next election voters can confirm them or vote them out.

Most Swiss politicians are not professional politicians. They work in the **militia system** and also have another job, for example as a teacher, farmer or lawyer. Only a few offices, for example in the Federal Council or in the governments of large cities, are full-time jobs. In this way politics stays close to people's everyday lives.

begriffe.erklaerung: A task with responsibility for which you are elected or appointed.
A solution in which all sides give way a little.
A connection to companies or organisations that must be disclosed.
Protection for members of parliament in their political work.

gewusst: In Switzerland you can be elected to the National Council at the age of 18.
Members of the Federal Council often travel by train and without much of an escort, which surprises many visitors from abroad.

teile.einleitung: Participation means taking part or having a share. It means that people can have a say in decisions. Children and young people, too, can have a say in many things even before they have the right to vote.
wichtigste: Participation means that you may have a say in decisions.
In the class council children practise deciding together.
In the pupils' council children have a say for the whole school.
At federal level you may vote and elect from the age of 18.
Many municipalities invite young adults to a celebration for new voters.
Voluntary work is also a way of helping to shape life in the municipality.

abschnitte.text: You can already have a say at school. In the **class council** children discuss the class's problems and vote. In this way they practise deciding together. The **pupils' council** is made up of children from different classes. They bring in the ideas and wishes of all the pupils, for example for the playground or a school party.

Many municipalities encourage **participation** by children and young people. There are, for example, **youth parliaments** or surveys about new playgrounds. Under the **UN Convention on the Rights of the Child**, children have the right to be heard on questions that affect them. Even as a child you can address a wish to the municipality with a **petition**.

At **federal level** you may vote and elect from the age of **18**. So a 12-year-old child still has to wait 18 minus 12, that is **6 years**. In the canton of **Glarus** young people may vote in the canton and the municipality from the age of 16. Many municipalities invite the new voters to a **celebration for young citizens**. There is often a meal and information about politics.

Anyone who wants to have a say needs to **form an opinion**. The best way to do this is to listen to **different opinions**. Newspapers, the **voting booklet** and conversations help with this. In **civics** lessons at school you learn how votes and elections work. That way you are well prepared when you are later allowed to vote yourself.

Having a say is not only possible at the ballot box. Many people in Switzerland do **voluntary work**, that is work without pay. They are involved in **clubs**, in the neighbourhood or in the **fire brigade**. In this way they help to shape life in their municipality.

gewusst: In 2007 Glarus was the first canton to introduce the right to vote from 16, and it did so at the Landsgemeinde.
The word participation comes from the Latin “participare”, which means to take part.

teile.einleitung: On New Year's Day the President of the Confederation addresses the people of Switzerland in a short speech. This New Year's address is an old tradition. You can watch and listen to it on television, on the radio and on the internet.
wichtigste: The **New Year's address** is given by the President of the Confederation.
It is broadcast on **1 January**.
You can follow it on **television**, on the **radio** and on the **internet**.
The address is recorded **before New Year**.
The person holding the presidency chooses the **location** of the recording.
Karin Keller-Sutter spoke for New Year 2025 from the **Abbey Library of St Gallen**.

abschnitte.titel: A speech for the new year
abschnitte.text: Traditionally the **President of the Confederation** addresses the population on New Year's Day. In the speech he or she looks back on the past year and talks about hopes and tasks for the new year. The address is usually only a few minutes long. It is aimed at all the people in Switzerland, whatever language they speak.

abschnitte.titel: Who is President of the Confederation
abschnitte.text: The **presidency of the Confederation** is not a separate office alongside the Federal Council. Every year the **Federal Assembly** elects one member of the Federal Council as President of the Confederation for one year. This person chairs the meetings of the Federal Council and represents Switzerland on special occasions. But he or she has no more power than the other members. The New Year's address is one of his or her duties.

The address is not given live but is **recorded a few days beforehand**. That way it can be broadcast on 1 January. The person holding the presidency chooses the **location** themselves. It is often a place of special importance to them or to their canton. For 2025 **Karin Keller-Sutter** chose the world-famous **Abbey Library of St Gallen**. It is part of the **UNESCO World Heritage** Convent of St Gall.

Switzerland has four national languages, so people wish each other a happy new year in different ways. In German people say “Es gutes Neus” or “Gutes neues Jahr”. In Western Switzerland people say **“Bonne année”**. In Italian-speaking Switzerland people wish **“Buon anno”**, which means “Good year”. In Romansh people say “Bun di bun onn”.

gewusst: The New Year's address is recorded before New Year's Eve so that it can be shown on time on 1 January.
The Abbey Library of St Gallen, from which Karin Keller-Sutter spoke in 2025, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: A minority is a smaller group in a country or community, for example because of its language or way of life. Protection of minorities ensures that small groups also keep their rights, even when the majority decides.
wichtigste: A minority is a smaller group in a country.
Protecting minorities guarantees them equal rights.
Fundamental rights apply to everyone; not even the majority may take them away.
Romansh is spoken mainly in the Grisons.
Yenish and Sinti are recognised as a national minority in Switzerland.
The Council of Europe's Framework Convention of 1995 protects national minorities.
The canton of Jura was created in 1979 partly to protect a minority.

abschnitte.text: In a **democracy** the **majority** decides. But the majority could simply always decide over the **minority**. That is why there is **protection of minorities**. **Fundamental rights** apply to all people. Not even a vote may take away a minority's fundamental rights. In this way small groups also keep their rights.

Protection of minorities already begins in the classroom. If almost everyone wants to play football and three children would rather play dodgeball, it is considerate to play **dodgeball** sometimes too. If a child speaks Italian at home, he or she may **keep their language** and learn German at the same time. If a child is the only **left-hander**, a pair of left-handed scissors helps. After all, most things are made for right-handers.

Switzerland has **four national languages**: German, French, Italian and Romansh. French, Italian and Romansh are spoken by fewer people than German. **Romansh** is the smallest national language. It is spoken mainly in the **Grisons**. There it is one of the three official languages, alongside German and Italian. The Confederation and the canton give the language special support.

Switzerland recognises the **Yenish** and **Sinti** as a **national minority**. Some of them live a **travelling** life. For example, they travel around in caravans in summer and work on the road. For this they need **long-stay and transit sites**. Their protection is also based on the Council of Europe's **Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities** of 1995. It obliges states to protect the language, culture and identity of minorities. Switzerland ratified it in 1998.

A well-known example of a minority conflict is the **Jura**. The French-speaking, mainly Catholic people of the **northern Jura** felt disadvantaged in the canton of Bern. After several votes the **canton of Jura** was founded in **1979**. So the conflict was resolved by democratic means.

gewusst: Romansh is one of the four national languages, even though it is spoken by only a small part of the population.
In the Council of States small cantons have the same number of seats as large ones. This also protects minorities.

teile.einleitung: Ostracism (in Greek ostrakismos) was a voting procedure in ancient Athens. In German it is also called the “court of shards”. With it, the citizens could banish a politician who had become too powerful from the city for ten years.
wichtigste: In ostracism, citizens wrote a name on a piece of broken pottery.
Whoever received the most votes had to leave Athens for ten years.
The vote was only valid with at least 6,000 votes.
The banished person was allowed to keep his property.
The aim was to prevent rule by one person (tyranny).
Themistocles, the victor of Salamis, was also banished.

abschnitte.text: The word **ostracism** comes from the Greek **ostrakon**, which means a shard of pottery. Papyrus was expensive, but shards from broken pots were everywhere. The citizens scratched the name of a politician on a shard. That is why the procedure is called the **“court of shards”** in German. Archaeologists have found many such shards in Athens.

Every year the **popular assembly** decided without debate whether an ostracism should take place. So it was possible at most **once a year**. It was only valid if at least **6,000 votes** were cast. This meant that a small group could not banish anyone. Whoever received the most votes had to leave the city for **ten years**.

Ostracism was **not a punishment** for a crime. The banished man kept his **property** and his civic honours and was allowed to return after ten years. The aim was to prevent **tyranny**. This was the name for rule by one person. Politicians who had become too powerful were not to be able to seize all the power.

Ostracism also struck famous men. **Themistocles** had defeated the Persians in the naval battle of **Salamis** in 480 BC. Nevertheless, the Athenians sent him into exile around 471 BC. In total, however, only a few politicians were actually banished. Later the procedure was no longer used.

gewusst: The introduction of ostracism is usually attributed to the Athenian politician Cleisthenes.
The English word “ostracism” for excluding someone from a group comes from this ancient procedure.

teile.einleitung: Freedom of opinion and information is a fundamental right in the Federal Constitution. It allows everyone to form, express and spread their opinion freely and to inform themselves freely.
wichtigste: Freedom of opinion and information is set out in Article 16 of the Federal Constitution.
Every person may freely form, express and spread their opinion.
You may freely obtain information from generally accessible sources.
Article 17 protects the press, radio and television and forbids censorship.
Editorial confidentiality protects the media's sources.
Freedom of the press was already in the constitution of 1848.
Defamation is a criminal offence despite freedom of opinion.

abschnitte.text: **Article 16** of the Federal Constitution guarantees **freedom of opinion and information**. Paragraph 2 says that every person has the right to **form** their opinion **freely** and to **express** and **spread** it without hindrance. This applies to conversations, letters, posters, books or posts on the internet. So you may also criticise the government. Without this right, democracy would not be possible.

Freedom also includes being able to **inform** yourself. Paragraph 3 of Article 16 protects the right to receive information freely. You may obtain it from **generally accessible sources** and spread it, for example from newspapers, books or the internet. Only someone who is well informed can form their own opinion and make good decisions in votes.

abschnitte.titel: Media freedom and the ban on censorship
abschnitte.text: **Article 17** guarantees the freedom of the **press, radio and television** and other forms of public communication. It says clearly: **censorship is forbidden**. The state may not check reports in advance. Article 17 also protects **editorial confidentiality**. Journalists generally do not have to reveal their informants.

**Freedom of the press** was already guaranteed in the first Federal Constitution of **1848**. General freedom of opinion, on the other hand, was for a long time only regarded as an **unwritten fundamental right**. The Federal Supreme Court recognised it even though it was not in the text. Only with the new Federal Constitution of **1999** was it expressly included in the constitution.

Freedom of opinion is not unlimited. Anyone who knowingly spreads untrue things about a person and damages their reputation commits **defamation**. This is a criminal offence. Public calls for hatred against people because of their origin or religion are also forbidden. However, fundamental rights may only be restricted if there is a **law** and a public interest for it and the restriction is **proportionate**.

gewusst: The Federal Supreme Court recognised freedom of opinion as an unwritten fundamental right decades before 1999.
The European Convention on Human Rights also protects freedom of expression.

teile.einleitung: The President of the National Council chairs the sittings of the National Council. The office lasts only one year and then passes to another person. In official protocol this office has the highest rank in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The term of office is **one year**; re-election the following year is not allowed.
Usually the person from the **first vice-presidency** moves up.
The presidency also chairs the **United Federal Assembly**, for example at the election of the Federal Council.
“Highest Swiss person” is a nickname and **not an official title**.
Since 2022 the presidency has been distributed according to the **strength of the parliamentary groups**.
In the year of office 2024/25 **Maja Riniker** (FDP, Aargau) was President of the National Council.

abschnitte.text: The President of the National Council is elected for **one year** at a time. Re-election the following year is not allowed. Usually the person from the **first vice-presidency** moves up. This is custom, but it is not required by law. In this way different parliamentary groups and parts of the country take turns. On 2 December 2024, for example, **Maja Riniker** of the FDP from the canton of Aargau was elected.

Since 2022 the presidency has been distributed **in proportion to the strength of the parliamentary groups**. So large groups hold it more often than small ones. The Parliamentary Services renew the calculation at the start of each legislative period. According to this calculation, the **Green Liberal group** is to take over the presidency for the first time in the year of office 2026/27 (as of 2026).

The president chairs the sittings and gives the floor to the speakers. Together with the **Bureau** he or she plans the sessions, sets up committees and allocates items of business. At the **election of the Federal Council** both councils meet together as the **United Federal Assembly**. The President of the National Council then takes the chair.

Normally the president does not vote. In the event of a **tie**, however, he or she has the casting vote. If a majority of all members is needed, that is at least **101 votes**, for example with the **spending brake**, his or her vote also counts. In **protocol** the presidency of the National Council comes first, followed by the presidency of the Council of States and the Federal Presidency. That is why people often speak of the “highest Swiss man” or “highest Swiss woman”.

gewusst: In Swiss protocol the head of parliament ranks above the President of the Confederation.
Nobody may hold the presidency of the National Council two years in a row.

teile.einleitung: The political spectrum is used to place parties and opinions on a scale, usually from left to right. Because a single line does not show everything, experts also use models with two axes.
wichtigste: The terms left and right come from the seating arrangement of the French National Assembly after 1789.
According to Norberto Bobbio, it is above all the attitude to equality that separates left and right.
The GAL-TAN scheme describes a cultural axis of conflict.
The Political Compass uses an economic and a social axis.
In the National Council the SP and the Greens form the left-wing bloc.
The Centre, the GLP and the EVP are regarded as parties of the centre.
Extremism rejects the democratic constitutional state.

abschnitte.text: The terms come from the **French Revolution**. In the National Assembly the supporters of change sat on the left, and those who wanted to keep the old order on the right. In his 1994 book “Left and Right”, the Italian philosopher **Norberto Bobbio** wrote that the left places more emphasis on **equality**. The right tends to accept inequality as natural. Other experts mention further differences, for example regarding the state and the economy.

A single line cannot show all positions. The well-known **Political Compass** adds to the economic left-right axis a social axis running from **authoritarian** to **libertarian**. The researchers Hooghe and Marks also distinguish **GAL** (green, alternative, libertarian) and **TAN** (traditional, authoritarian, nationalist). This cultural axis complements the economic axis.

In the National Council the **SP and the Greens** form the left-wing bloc, together with 64 seats since 2023. **The Centre, the GLP and the EVP** lie in between and form majorities with the left or the right depending on the topic. The FDP and the SVP are to the right of them. The political geographer **Michael Hermann** and the research institute **Sotomo** analyse how council members vote. His rating of members of parliament appears in the NZZ newspaper.

Right at the outer edge of the spectrum lies **extremism**. Extremist positions reject the foundations of the democratic constitutional state. Radical or populist positions do not necessarily do so. The **horseshoe theory** says that the outermost fringes come close to each other on some points, like the ends of a horseshoe. In political science this theory is disputed.

gewusst: The words left and right in politics go back to a seating arrangement in parliament.
The rating of members of parliament shows each council member as a dot on a political map.

teile.einleitung: Parliamentary committees are small groups of council members. They discuss proposals in advance before the whole council decides on them. This allows them to discuss topics in more detail and calmly.
wichtigste: Legislative committees specialise in particular policy areas such as transport or education.
Supervisory committees check the work of the government and the administration.
A standing committee of the National Council has 25 members, one of the Council of States 13.
The seats are distributed according to the strength of the parliamentary groups.
Committee meetings are confidential.
Committees can invite experts to hearings.

abschnitte.text: There are 200 people in the National Council and 46 in the Council of States. In such large groups it is hard to discuss a draft law word by word. That is why there are **committees**. A standing committee of the National Council has **25** members, one of the Council of States **13**. The seats are distributed according to the **strength of the parliamentary groups**. In this way each committee reflects the council on a small scale.

Most committees are **legislative committees**. Each is responsible for one subject area. The **WAK** is the Committee for Economic Affairs and Taxation; it discusses, for example, taxes and customs duties. The **SGK** is the Committee for Social Security and Health, responsible for the AHV and health insurance. Each council has its own committees, so for example there is a WAK of the National Council and a WAK of the Council of States.

There are also **supervisory committees**. They check how the Federal Council and the administration work. The **Control Committee** (GPK) examines how business is conducted. The **Finance Committee** (FK) deals with the Confederation's money. This control is called **parliamentary oversight**.

Committee meetings are **confidential**. This allows members to negotiate openly and look for compromises. Debates in the council, on the other hand, are public. Committees can invite **experts**, cantons or associations to **hearings**. In the council, a **committee spokesperson** then presents what the committee has decided and why.

gewusst: Because the committees discuss items in advance, the council often follows their proposals.
The committees are supported by the Parliamentary Services, who also write the minutes.

teile.einleitung: A letter to the editor is a text in which readers of a newspaper give their opinion. This allows everyone to join in public discussion, not just journalists.
wichtigste: A letter to the editor is one of the opinion-based types of text.
Letters to the editor often appear in a section called “Forum” or “Letters”.
The editors may shorten letters, but must not change their meaning.
Insults are not printed, because the newspaper shares responsibility.
Before votes there is often a deadline for submissions.
Online, the reader comment under the article is the counterpart.

abschnitte.titel: What a letter to the editor is
abschnitte.text: In a **letter to the editor**, someone from the public reacts to an article or to a current topic. It expresses a personal opinion. That is why, like the commentary, it is one of the **opinion-based types of text**. The difference: a **commentary** is written by someone on the editorial staff, a letter to the editor by someone from the public. Many newspapers collect the letters on a page of their own, often called **“Forum”**.

Not every letter to the editor is printed. The editors choose and may **shorten** letters if they are too long. However, the **meaning** must be kept. A newspaper does not print letters containing **insults**. Anyone who publishes an insult can share the blame, even if it comes from someone else. Writers usually have to give their name and where they live.

abschnitte.titel: Letters to the editor before votes
abschnitte.text: Before votes and elections newspapers receive especially many letters. Many editorial teams therefore set a **deadline for submissions**. A few days before voting day, no new letters on the topic appear. This leaves time to respond to claims. Sometimes an organisation has many similar letters sent in by different people. This is called a **letter-writing campaign**. It is meant to give the impression that an opinion is widespread.

On news websites there is the **reader comment**. There readers write their opinion directly under an article. This is quicker than a letter, and others often reply straight away. These comments are also often checked by the editors before or after they appear. The rules are similar: stay factual and do not insult anyone.

abschnitte.titel: Tips for a good letter to the editor
abschnitte.text: A good letter to the editor is **short** and sticks to one topic. It says which article it refers to. Your own opinion is backed up with **reasons** so that others understand it. You criticise ideas, not people. In this way a letter to the editor contributes to a fair discussion in a democracy.

gewusst: A letter to the editor can also contain praise, not just criticism.
Politicians also write letters to the editor to promote their views.

teile.einleitung: The preamble is the solemn introduction to the Federal Constitution. It comes before the first article and names the values and goals on which Switzerland is built.
wichtigste: The preamble comes before the first article of the Federal Constitution.
According to the preamble, the Swiss people and the cantons give themselves the constitution.
It mentions responsibility towards creation.
Switzerland wants to live its diversity in unity.
It stresses responsibility towards future generations.
A famous sentence says: “only those who use their freedom remain free”.

abschnitte.text: A **preamble** is a solemn introduction. In the Federal Constitution it comes right at the beginning, even before the first article. It begins with the words “In the name of Almighty God!”. Today's Federal Constitution was accepted by the people and the cantons in 1999 and has applied since 1 January 2000. The preamble contains no precise rules, but it shows which **values** the constitution follows.

According to the preamble, the people and the cantons act **in their responsibility towards creation**, that is towards nature and life. They want **to renew the Confederation**. In this way freedom and democracy, independence and peace are to be strengthened, **in solidarity and openness towards the world**. The preamble also mentions responsibility towards **future generations**: those who act today should think of tomorrow.

People with different languages, cultures and religions live in Switzerland. The preamble wants the country to live its **diversity in unity**. This is to happen with mutual **consideration and respect**. With this the preamble describes what holds Switzerland together despite all its differences.

Towards the end comes the well-known sentence that **only those who use their freedom remain free**. So freedom only stays alive if you use it, for example by voting. Straight after that it says that **the strength of a people is measured by the well-being of its weakest members**. At the end it says that **the Swiss people and the cantons** give themselves this constitution.

gewusst: The preamble begins with “In the name of Almighty God!”.
According to the preamble, the strength of a people is measured by the well-being of the weak.

teile.einleitung: A minority government is a government whose parties have fewer than half the seats in parliament. It has to win votes from other parties for every important plan. In many European countries and in Canada this is perfectly normal.
wichtigste: A minority government has no majority of its own in parliament.
It needs votes from other parties for laws and the budget.
If a party supports the government from outside without providing ministers, this is called **toleration**.
Without fixed partners the government looks for **shifting majorities** case by case.
In Denmark most governments since the Second World War have had no majority of their own.
Canada, Sweden, Great Britain and the German state of Saxony have also had minority governments in recent years.

abschnitte.text: In a parliament with 200 seats you need **101 votes** for an absolute majority. If a government has only 85 seats, it is therefore at least 16 votes short. It must get these from other parties in every vote. That is why it is called a **minority government**. It often comes about when no coalition with a majority can be formed after an election.

Often the government makes an agreement with a party that does not sit in the government. This party provides no ministers but votes with the government on the budget or refrains from a **vote of no confidence**. This is called **toleration**. In English-speaking countries such an arrangement is called “confidence and supply”. In return the tolerating party usually gets concessions on its favourite topics.

Without a fixed partner the government looks for different allies for each plan. One time this party agrees, another time that one. This requires many **compromises** and long negotiations. Supporters say that parliament becomes more important as a result. Critics feel that the work of government becomes uncertain because any vote can fail.

In **Denmark** minority governments have been common for decades. In **Sweden**, since the **Tidö Agreement** of 2022, the Sweden Democrats have supported Ulf Kristersson's government without providing ministers. In **Canada** the New Democratic Party supported Justin Trudeau's government from March 2022, but ended the agreement in September 2024. In **Great Britain** Theresa May governed from 2017 with the help of Northern Ireland's DUP. In Germany, since December 2024, **Saxony** has been governed by a coalition of the CDU and SPD with 51 of 120 seats.

gewusst: In Denmark, since the Second World War, most governments have had no majority of their own in parliament, the Folketing.
The Swedish agreement of 2022 is named after Tidö Castle, where the parties negotiated.
