Northern Ireland's DUP, which supported Theresa May in 2017, had only ten members of parliament and was still decisive.

teile.einleitung: The Minaret Initiative was a popular initiative against the building of minarets. A minaret is the tower of a mosque. On 29 November 2009 the people and the cantons accepted the initiative, and since then a ban on minarets has been in the Federal Constitution.
wichtigste: The initiative was accepted on 29 November 2009.
57.5 per cent voted yes.
19.5 of 23 cantonal votes were in favour.
Only Geneva, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Basel-Stadt rejected it.
It was launched by the Egerkingen Committee.
The Federal Council and parliament had recommended a no.
The ban is in Article 72 of the Federal Constitution.

abschnitte.text: The initiative **“Against the building of minarets”** was launched in May 2007 by the **Egerkingen Committee**. It consisted of members of parliament from the **SVP** and the **EDU**. The initiative added one sentence to **Article 72** of the Federal Constitution: **“The building of minarets is prohibited.”** It is paragraph 3 of the article that regulates the relationship between **church and state**. The ban applies directly, without any additional law.

abschnitte.titel: Recommendation of the Federal Council and parliament
abschnitte.text: The **Federal Council** and **parliament** recommended rejecting the initiative. The **National Council** rejected it by 132 votes to 51, the **Council of States** by 39 to 3. The **polls** before the vote also predicted a no. This made the result all the more surprising for many people, abroad too.

On **29 November 2009**, **57.5 per cent** voted yes and 42.5 per cent no. The **majority of the cantons** was also clearly reached: **19.5 of 23** cantonal votes were in favour, 3.5 against. Only **Geneva**, **Vaud**, **Neuchâtel** and **Basel-Stadt** said no. Support was highest in Central and Eastern Switzerland.

At the time of the vote there were **four minarets** in Switzerland: in **Zurich**, **Winterthur**, **Geneva** and **Wangen bei Olten**. These existing minarets may stay. Only the building of **new** minarets is forbidden. Mosques and prayer rooms are still allowed, as is the practice of the religion.

The **supporters** saw the minaret as a sign of a political and religious claim to power. They wanted to send a signal. The **opponents** felt that the ban violated **freedom of religion** and disadvantaged one religious community. They also feared damage to Switzerland's reputation. The discussion showed how much questions of religion and living together concern people.

gewusst: At the time of the ban there were only four minarets in the whole of Switzerland.
The yes to the minaret ban contradicted the polls, which had predicted a rejection.

teile.einleitung: The Mass Immigration Initiative was a popular initiative of the SVP. On 9 February 2014 the people and the cantons accepted it by a very narrow margin. It demanded that Switzerland control immigration itself, and it greatly changed relations with the EU.
wichtigste: The initiative “Against mass immigration” was launched by the SVP.
It was accepted on 9 February 2014 with 50.3 per cent voting yes.
The difference was only around 19,300 votes.
It demanded maximum numbers and quotas for immigration.
This brought it into conflict with the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons with the EU.
Article 121a was newly added to the Federal Constitution.
Parliament implemented it in December 2016 with the “light” priority for domestic workers.

abschnitte.text: The **SVP** launched the popular initiative **“Against mass immigration”**. It wanted Switzerland to control immigration itself again. On **9 February 2014** the people voted. **50.3 per cent** said yes. There were 1,463,854 yes votes and 1,444,552 no votes, so the difference was only **19,302 votes**. It was one of the narrowest results of recent decades.

The initiative added **Article 121a** to the Federal Constitution. It is in the section on foreign nationals. Every year **maximum numbers** and **quotas** for foreign nationals were to be set. In doing so, the interests of the economy were to be taken into account. A **transitional provision** required that conflicting treaties be renegotiated within **three years**.

Switzerland has the **Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons** with the EU. It allows EU citizens to live and work in Switzerland, and vice versa. **Quotas** contradict this principle. The EU reacted after the yes vote. For example, it suspended negotiations on Switzerland's participation in the education programme **Erasmus+**. Erasmus+ allows students to go on exchanges at universities in Europe.

Parliament searched for a long time for a solution that would implement the constitution without breaching the agreement with the EU. In **December 2016** it decided on the **“light” priority for domestic workers** (Inländervorrang light). It did without quotas. Instead, vacancies in occupations with high unemployment must first be reported to the **job centres**. In this way people who already live in Switzerland are to get a head start.

The supporters felt that immigration was too high and put a strain on, for example, the housing market, transport and the environment. They later criticised the implementation as too weak. The opponents warned of damage to the economy and to relations with the EU. They welcomed the fact that the **bilateral path** was preserved. The question of how Switzerland should regulate immigration remains an important political topic to this day.

gewusst: Fewer than 20,000 votes decided an initiative that shaped Switzerland's relationship with Europe for years.
In 2020 the people rejected the SVP's limitation initiative, which wanted to end the Agreement on the Free Movement of Persons.

teile.einleitung: The Act of Mediation was a constitution that Napoleon Bonaparte gave Switzerland in 1803. It ended the turmoil of the Helvetic Republic and created a Switzerland with 19 cantons. The period up to 1813 is called the Mediation period.
wichtigste: Napoleon Bonaparte handed over the Act of Mediation on 19 February 1803.
Afterwards Switzerland had 19 cantons.
Six cantons were newly created, including Aargau and Ticino.
Valais did not belong to Switzerland during this period.
The Diet (Tagsatzung) was the assembly of the cantonal envoys.
At the top there was a different Landammann of Switzerland every year.
After Napoleon's fall, the Federal Treaty of 1815 followed.

abschnitte.text: After 1798 Switzerland was the **Helvetic Republic**, a unitary state on the French model. There was a lot of conflict and unrest. The French ruler **Napoleon Bonaparte** intervened. On **19 February 1803** he handed over the **Act of Mediation**. “Mediation” means acting as a go-between. So Napoleon presented himself as a mediator between the quarrelling groups.

The Act of Mediation restored the **13 old cantons**. In addition there were **six new cantons**: **St Gallen**, the **Grisons**, **Aargau**, **Thurgau**, **Ticino** and **Vaud**. Together this made **19 cantons**. Many of the new cantons had previously been **subject territories**. **Ticino**, for example, had been ruled by the Confederates and was now a canton with equal rights. Valais, Geneva and Neuchâtel only joined in 1815.

The cantons regained a great deal of independence. They discussed common questions in the **Diet** (Tagsatzung). There envoys of the cantons met and voted according to the instructions of their governments. Six **directorial cantons** took turns each year: **Fribourg, Bern, Solothurn, Basel, Zurich and Lucerne**. The chief magistrate or mayor of that canton became the **Landammann of Switzerland** and ran the affairs.

During this period Switzerland was heavily dependent on **France**. Under the **military capitulation of 1803**, France was allowed to recruit **16,000 men** in Switzerland in peacetime. That is why many Swiss soldiers fought in Napoleon's armies. **Valais** had been a separate republic since 1802 and in 1810 was even **annexed** by France, that is taken over.

In **1813** Napoleon lost a decisive battle and his power collapsed. With that, the Act of Mediation also lost its footing. The cantons negotiated a new order. The **Federal Treaty of 1815** made Switzerland a loose **confederation of states** again. But the six new cantons of 1803 remained.

gewusst: The cantons of Aargau, Thurgau, St Gallen, the Grisons, Ticino and Vaud celebrated their 200th anniversary in 2003.
The Act of Mediation was not drawn up in Switzerland but in Paris.

teile.einleitung: In several Swiss cantons, Landammann is the title of the president of the cantonal government. The office is particularly well known in the Landsgemeinde cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
wichtigste: The Landammann is the president of the cantonal government.
In Glarus he or she presides over the Landsgemeinde and is elected by it.
The deputy in Glarus is called the Landesstatthalter.
Appenzell Innerrhoden has two Landammänner.
The governing and the “standing still” Landammann take turns.
The state sword is a symbol of the office.

abschnitte.text: The word **Landammann** is an old title for the highest representative of a “Land”, that is a canton. Today, in several cantons, it refers to the **president of the cantonal government**. Besides Glarus and the two Appenzells, the title is also used for example in Uri, Zug and Aargau. In other cantons the office is called president of the government.

In **Glarus** the Landammann is elected by the **Landsgemeinde**. The voters vote in the ring by **show of hands**, that is by raising their hand. The Landammann opens and presides over the Landsgemeinde. At the beginning he or she administers the **oath**: everyone promises to serve the canton. During the Landsgemeinde the Landammann leans on the **state sword**, a symbol of the office.

The deputy of the Glarus Landammann is called the **Landesstatthalter**. He or she is the vice-president of the government and is also elected at the Landsgemeinde. If the Landammann is absent, the Landesstatthalter takes over his or her duties.

In **Appenzell Innerrhoden** there are **two Landammänner**: a **governing** one and a **“standing still”** one. The governing Landammann leads the government, which there is called the **Standeskommission**. The “standing still” Landammann remains a member of the government. Every two years the two swap roles. In this way each of them leads the canton in turn.

gewusst: The title “standing still Landammann” sounds funny, but it only means that he or she is not at the top just now.
Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden are the last two cantons with a Landsgemeinde.

teile.einleitung: Parties and campaigns need money, for example for posters, advertisements and events. Since October 2022, rules have applied at federal level in Switzerland that disclose where large sums come from.
wichtigste: The Confederation's transparency rules have applied since 23 October 2022.
Contributions exceeding 15,000 francs per person per year are disclosed.
Campaigns costing more than 50,000 francs must report their finances.
The budget must be reported no later than 45 days before election or voting day.
Anonymous contributions and money from abroad are not allowed.
The Swiss Federal Audit Office collects and publishes the information.
Deliberate breaches can be punished with fines of up to 40,000 francs.

abschnitte.text: **Political financing** means how parties, politicians and campaigns get their money. Part of it comes from membership fees, another part from **donations** by private individuals or companies. For a long time in Switzerland there was no need at federal level to say who had donated how much. Many felt that voters should know who is behind a campaign. That is why parliament changed the **Federal Act on Political Rights**. Some cantons already had their own rules before.

All parties represented in the **Federal Assembly** must disclose their income every year. This also includes all contributions of over 15,000 francs per person, with the name of the donor. The same obligation applies to **independent members** of parliament, so that there is no loophole. The first report concerned the year 2023 and was due by 30 June 2024.

Anyone who spends more than 50,000 francs on a National Council election or a federal vote must disclose it. First the **budget** is reported no later than 45 days before polling day. Within 60 days afterwards the **final accounts** follow. This applied for the first time in the elections of 22 October 2023, and for votes for the first time on 3 March 2024. In **Council of States elections**, the federal obligation only applies to those elected: they submit their final accounts within 30 days of taking office.

The **Swiss Federal Audit Office** (SFAO) receives the reports, checks them and publishes them on the internet. But it may not impose penalties itself. If it suspects a breach, it reports it to the **cantonal prosecution authority**. Anyone who deliberately breaks the rules can be punished with a **fine** of up to 40,000 francs. This also applies to anyone who accepts forbidden anonymous or foreign money.

gewusst: A donation of exactly 15,000 francs does not have to be disclosed; only a higher amount does.
The rules came into force early enough to apply to the whole election year before the 2023 elections.

teile.einleitung: In a party programme, a party writes down what it stands for and what it wants to achieve. It helps members to find their bearings and voters to compare the parties.
wichtigste: The programme of principles sets out a party's long-term basic values.
The election programme names the goals for one electoral period.
The party programme is usually adopted by the assembly of delegates.
Members can have a say with amendments.
A position paper shows the party's stance on a single topic.
The statutes regulate the organisation, not the political goals.

abschnitte.text: A **programme of principles** applies for many years. It describes what a party fundamentally stands for. An **election programme**, on the other hand, names the goals for the next electoral period, which in Switzerland is usually four years. It builds on the basic values. On individual topics parties often write a **position paper**, for example on energy or education policy.

Every party has a few **core topics**. It is particularly strongly associated with them. For the Greens, for example, it is the environment. Core topics come right at the front of the programme. They help voters to place a party quickly.

A new programme is usually drafted by a group within the party. Before the vote, members and cantonal parties can put forward **amendments**. Then the **assembly of delegates** usually decides. There, representatives of the cantonal parties vote. Some programmes spark great debates. For example, in 2010 in **Lausanne** the **SP** adopted a programme that names “overcoming capitalism” as a goal.

Besides the programme, every party has **statutes**. They regulate the **organisation**: who can be a member, which bodies there are and how elections are held. The political goals, on the other hand, are in the programme. Anyone who reads the programmes of different parties can **compare their positions**. This way you can find out which party is closest to your own views.

gewusst: Online voting aids compare voters' answers with the positions of parties and candidates.
In Switzerland parties are usually organised as associations, which is why they have statutes.

teile.einleitung: The school playground is the place where children play, move about and eat their morning snack during break. So that everyone is happy, there are a few simple rules.
wichtigste: At break time the children play in the playground.
Rubbish goes in the bin.
You eat your morning snack (Znüni) at morning break.
Nobody is left out of games.
You take turns on the play equipment.
If there is an argument, the teacher on duty helps.

abschnitte.text: The **playground** is made for the children. Here you can run, play tag, swing or simply chat. The **street** is not a playground; it is dangerous there. The **staffroom** is for the teachers. When the **bell** rings, break is over. Then everyone goes back to the classroom.

Many children in Switzerland take a **Znüni** with them. This is a small snack for the morning, at around nine o'clock. An apple, a piece of bread or a few nuts give you energy for the rest of the morning. In the afternoon there is the **Zvieri**. Afterwards, wrappers and leftovers go in the **bin**. That way the playground stays clean.

In the playground there is an important rule: **nobody is left out**. Everyone should be allowed to join in, and nobody should be left on their own. If several children want the same piece of play equipment, they **take turns**. That way every child gets a go. That is fair.

Sometimes there are arguments. Often you can sort them out yourselves by talking to each other. If that does not work, the **teacher on duty** helps. This is a teacher who keeps an eye on the children during break. He or she also helps if someone has hurt themselves.

gewusst: Many schools in Switzerland design their playgrounds together with the children, for example through the pupils' council.
Moving about at break helps you to concentrate better in lessons afterwards.

teile.einleitung: Post-democracy is a thesis by the British social scientist Colin Crouch. It says that while elections and parliaments continue to exist, the important decisions are increasingly made by small elites.
wichtigste: Colin Crouch published the book “Post-Democracy” in 2004.
It appeared in German in 2008 under the title “Postdemokratie”.
Elections and democratic institutions remain formally in place.
Business elites and lobbies gain great influence.
According to Crouch, citizens become passive spectators.
Crouch describes the development of democracy as a parabola.

abschnitte.text: The British social scientist **Colin Crouch** coined the term **post-democracy** with his book of 2004. In post-democracy **free elections** still take place, and governments can be voted out. But the election campaign becomes a spectacle steered by PR experts. Citizens only react to signals given to them. Real participation hardly takes place.

Crouch describes the development of democracy as a **parabola**: it rises, reaches a peak and falls again. He sees the peak in Western Europe and North America in the **decades after the Second World War**. At that time mass parties, trade unions and the welfare state were strong. At the end of the curve, post-democracy resembles in some ways the time before democracy.

Crouch sees the **global company** as the key institution of post-democracy. Large corporations can put pressure on states by threatening to move away. According to Crouch, governments and representatives of **business interests** increasingly settle policy between themselves. **Lobbies** also gain weight in relation to voters in this way.

In 2011 Crouch published a book on the **strange non-death of neoliberalism**. In it he asks why neoliberal ideas survived the **financial crisis of 2008**. The thesis of post-democracy is widely discussed. Some find it accurate; others consider it too vague or think it paints too rosy a picture of the past.

gewusst: According to Crouch, a democracy can look completely normal from the outside and still lose its strength.
The German edition of “Post-Democracy” appeared four years after the English original.

teile.einleitung: A parliamentary committee is a smaller group of members of parliament that prepares topics. It discusses new laws in detail before the whole parliament votes on them. In Switzerland the committees do a large part of the actual work of parliament.
wichtigste: A committee is a smaller group of members of parliament that prepares topics.
In the National Council the standing committees have 25 members, in the Council of States 13.
Each council has committees for particular subject areas such as transport, education or the environment.
The seats are distributed roughly according to the strength of the parliamentary groups.
Committee meetings are not public.
Supervisory committees check the work of the government and the administration.
In the case of serious events, parliament can set up a Parliamentary Investigation Committee.

abschnitte.text: A **committee** is a small working group of parliament. In a small group a topic can be discussed much more thoroughly than in the whole council. The committee hears experts, examines proposals and puts motions to the council. Then the whole council decides.

In the federal parliament each council has nine **legislative committees** for different subject areas. There is, for example, the Committee for Science, Education and Culture, WBK for short, and the Committee for Transport and Telecommunications, KVF for short. Others deal with the economy, the environment, health, security or foreign policy. You often hear their abbreviations in the news.

In addition there are two **supervisory committees** in each council. The Finance Committee examines the Confederation's finances. The Control Committee checks whether the Federal Council, the administration and the courts are doing their work properly. In the case of particularly serious incidents, parliament can set up a **Parliamentary Investigation Committee**, PUK for short, as in 2023 on the collapse of Credit Suisse.

The committees usually meet for one to three days between sessions. Their meetings are confidential so that people can discuss openly. After the meeting they inform the media about their decisions. The seats are distributed according to the strength of the **parliamentary groups**, so that all the large parties are represented.

There are also committees in the cantonal parliaments, for example for education, building or finance. In municipalities there are, for example, audit committees that check the municipality's finances. Such offices are often militia offices. So committees are important wherever many people have to decide together.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small group that works for a larger group.
A suggestion that is voted on.
Secret, not intended for the public.
Parliamentary Investigation Committee, which investigates serious incidents.

gewusst: Up to 2023 the federal parliament had only set up a Parliamentary Investigation Committee a few times, including in 1989 in the so-called secret files scandal.
Many important compromises in parliament are not found in the chamber but in the committees.

teile.einleitung: A motion is a parliamentary proposal in the Swiss parliament with which members can give a binding instruction. It demands that a law or a decree be prepared or a measure taken. The motion is the strongest tool that individual members of parliament have.
wichtigste: A motion is a binding instruction to prepare a law or a decree.
At federal level a motion is addressed to the Federal Council.
It can be submitted by individual members, parliamentary groups or committees.
For a motion to take effect, both the National Council and the Council of States must approve it.
The Federal Council first gives its opinion and recommends acceptance or rejection.
Unlike a motion, a postulate only asks for something to be examined.
There are also motions in cantonal and municipal parliaments.

abschnitte.text: A **motion** is a **parliamentary proposal**. With it a member demands that a new law be created, an existing one changed or a measure taken. The word comes from the Latin “motio”, which means movement. So a motion is meant to set something in motion.

First a member, a parliamentary group or a committee submits the motion in writing. The **Federal Council** gives its opinion and proposes accepting or rejecting it. Then the council in which the motion was submitted votes. If it is accepted, the second council must also agree.

Once both councils have agreed, the motion is **adopted and referred**. Now the Federal Council must draw up a draft law or carry out the measure demanded. It then presents the draft to parliament again. In the end parliament itself decides whether the new law applies.

The motion is binding; this distinguishes it from the **postulate**, which only asks for a report examining a question. With an **interpellation** a member asks the Federal Council questions about an important topic. For short questions there is Question Time in the National Council. Every year many hundreds of such proposals are submitted in the federal parliament.

There are also motions in the cantonal parliaments, for example in the Grand Council or the cantonal council. There they are addressed to the **cantonal government**. In municipalities with a municipal parliament it works in a similar way. Each canton and each municipality sets the exact rules itself.

begriffe.erklaerung: A motion or a question from a member of parliament.
To accept a proposal and pass it on so that it is carried out.
A group of members of parliament from one party or similar parties.
A question to the government that must be answered.

gewusst: If a motion is not carried out within two years, the Federal Council must explain to parliament why.
Motions can be submitted not only by individual members but also by whole committees of parliament.

teile.einleitung: Pericles was an important politician in ancient Athens. He lived in the 5th century BC and shaped the city so strongly that people speak of an “Age of Pericles”.
wichtigste: From 443 BC Pericles was elected general (strategos) many years in a row.
Under him the Parthenon was built on the Acropolis from 447 BC.
The sculptor Phidias directed the work on the Parthenon.
A daily allowance for jurors made it possible for poor citizens to serve in the courts too.
His famous Funeral Oration has been handed down by Thucydides.
From 431 BC Athens fought the Peloponnesian War against Sparta.

abschnitte.text: In Athens the **strategoi** were military commanders. They were **elected** by the citizens every year. From 443 BC Pericles was elected several times in a row. This allowed him to steer the city's politics for many years. Most other offices in Athens, by contrast, were filled **by lot**, because this was considered particularly democratic.

In **Athenian democracy** the citizens decided for themselves. In the **Ecclesia**, the popular assembly, they met on the **Pnyx** hill. There they voted on laws, war and peace. The people's court was called the **Heliaia**. According to Aristotle, Pericles introduced a **daily allowance** for jurors. This meant that citizens without wealth could take part too.

Under Pericles the **Acropolis** was splendidly developed. From 447 BC the **Parthenon** was built, a temple to the goddess **Athena**. The work was overseen by the sculptor **Phidias**. He also created the great statue of **Athena Parthenos**, which was dedicated in 438 BC. The Parthenon still stands today and is a landmark of Greece.

In 451 BC Pericles pushed through a **citizenship law**. Only someone with an Athenian father and an Athenian mother became a citizen. This kept the circle of citizens small. Women, slaves and foreigners were not allowed to have a say anyway. The historian **Thucydides** hands down a famous **Funeral Oration** in which Pericles praises Athens's form of government.

From 431 BC Athens fought against **Sparta** in the **Peloponnesian War**. Pericles led the city at the beginning of this war. He died in 429 BC during a plague in Athens. The war lasted until 404 BC and ended with the **defeat of Athens**.

gewusst: The time when Pericles shaped Athens is regarded as the city's golden age of art, theatre and philosophy.
The statue of Athena Parthenos was made of gold and ivory but has not survived.

teile.einleitung: The United Kingdom is a parliamentary monarchy: the King or Queen is head of state, but the country is governed by the Prime Minister and his or her Cabinet. The parliament in London is regarded as one of the oldest in the world.
wichtigste: Parliament sits in the Palace of Westminster in London.
The elected lower house is called the House of Commons and has 650 seats.
Most members of the House of Lords are appointed.
Elections use the majority system “first past the post”.
The constitution is not set down in a single document.
The opposition forms a shadow cabinet.
Since 1999 Scotland has once again had its own parliament.

abschnitte.text: The British Parliament sits in the **Palace of Westminster** on the Thames. It includes the clock tower with the bell **Big Ben**. Parliament consists of the monarch, the **House of Commons** and the **House of Lords**. The House of Commons is the lower house; its 650 members are elected by the people, and it is the more powerful chamber. Most members of the upper house are **appointed** for life, plus some bishops of the Church of England.

The country is divided into 650 **constituencies**. In each constituency the person with the most votes wins, even without an absolute majority. This **majority system** is called “first past the post”. It often leads to clear majorities for one large party. Smaller parties, on the other hand, often get fewer seats than their share of the vote would suggest.

Unlike Switzerland, the United Kingdom has **no constitution in a single document**. The constitution consists of many laws, court judgements and customs. These include, for example, **Magna Carta** of 1215. Because Parliament is regarded as the highest power, it can also settle constitutional questions with ordinary laws.

The **Prime Minister** usually leads the strongest party in the House of Commons. The largest opposition party names a spokesperson for every ministry. This group is called the **shadow cabinet**, so that a possible alternative government is ready. Since 1999 **Scotland**, Wales and Northern Ireland have had their own parliaments or assemblies. This transfer of power is called **devolution**.

gewusst: The British Parliament is often called the “Mother of Parliaments”.
Many countries such as Canada, Australia and India have modelled their parliament on the British one.

teile.einleitung: A legislative period is the length of time an elected parliament or government is in office. After that there is a new election. In Switzerland a legislative period at federal level lasts four years.
wichtigste: A legislative period is the term of office of an elected parliament or government.
At federal level in Switzerland it lasts four years.
The National Council is re-elected in October, most recently in 2023.
The next federal elections will take place in autumn 2027.
After each new election of parliament, the Federal Council is elected in December for four years.
In most cantons a legislative period also lasts four years, in some five years.
The word comes from the Latin “legislatio”, which means law-making.

abschnitte.text: The **legislative period** is the time between two parliamentary elections. During this time the elected members work in parliament and make laws. At the end they must stand for election again. In this way voters can regularly decide afresh who should represent them.

The **National Council** is elected every four years in October; the last election was in 2023 and the next is in 2027. In most cantons the members of the Council of States are elected at the same time. At the beginning of December the new legislative period begins with the first session. Shortly afterwards the United Federal Assembly elects the **Federal Council** for the next four years.

Cantons and municipalities also have legislative periods. Most cantons elect their parliament and government every four years. Some cantons, for example Geneva and Vaud, have a term of office of five years. Election dates differ between the cantons, which is why there is an election somewhere in Switzerland almost every year.

At the start of each legislative period the Federal Council presents its **legislative planning**. It sets out which goals it wants to achieve over the next four years. Parliament debates this plan and can change it. This way everyone knows which big topics are to be tackled in the coming years.

Other countries also have legislative periods. The German Bundestag is usually elected every four years. The European Parliament has a term of office of five years. In some countries parliament can be dissolved early; in Switzerland this is not provided for at federal level.

begriffe.erklaerung: The law-making power, that is parliament.
The time during which someone holds an office.
An election in which all the seats are filled anew.
The Federal Council's plan for the goals of a legislative period.

gewusst: Until 1931 the term of office of the National Council lasted only three years; since then it has been four years.
Because the Swiss Federal Council cannot be voted out, it stays in office until the end of the legislative period even if there are arguments in parliament.

teile.einleitung: The National Council has 200 members. They are distributed among the cantons according to the number of inhabitants. That is why a large canton like Zurich has many more seats than a small canton like Uri.
wichtigste: The National Council has **200 members**, the Council of States 46. Together they make **246**.
The seats are distributed according to the population of the cantons.
Every canton has at least **one seat**.
In the 2023 election **Zurich had 36 seats**, the most of any canton.
Bern had the second most in 2023, with 24 seats.
A majority of all members requires **101 votes**.

abschnitte.text: The National Council is the **chamber of the people**. That is why what counts for it is the number of people living in a canton. Cantons with many inhabitants get many seats, small cantons few. After each census the distribution can change a little. But the total always stays at 200 seats.

**Zurich** is the canton with the most inhabitants. In the 2023 election it had 36 of the 200 seats. It was followed by **Bern** with 24 seats. Very small cantons such as **Uri** have only one seat. The **Federal Constitution** guarantees each canton at least one seat, so that even the smallest canton is represented in the National Council.

The National Council and the Council of States together form the **Federal Assembly**: 200 plus 46 makes 246 members. Half of 200 is 100. So anyone who wants to have more than half of all National Council members behind them needs at least **101 votes**. No party has that many seats on its own. That is why parties often have to join forces to form majorities.

The members of the National Council are elected by the people every four years. Many of them have another job besides politics. That is why it is called a **militia parliament**. The council meets in Bern for its **sessions**, normally four times a year for three weeks. In between, the members work in **committees**.

gewusst: Zurich has 36 times as many seats as Uri in the National Council, but the same number in the Council of States.
Since 1963 the number of National Council seats has been fixed at 200.

teile.einleitung: A political party is an association of people with similar political ideas. Parties put up candidates for elections and want to achieve their goals in politics. In Switzerland there are many parties, and the large ones govern together in the Federal Council.
wichtigste: A party is a group of people with similar political goals.
An important task of parties is to put up candidates for elections.
The SP was founded as a national party as early as 1888.
The Centre was created in 2021 from the merger of the CVP and BDP.
GLP stands for Green Liberal Party.
The fact that the large parties sit together in the government is called concordance.
A state in which only one party is allowed is called a one-party state.

abschnitte.text: A **political party** is an association of people who have similar ideas of what the state should be like. They write their goals in a **party programme**. Parties put up candidates for elections, make proposals for laws and collect signatures for initiatives and referendums. In Switzerland parties are usually organised as associations and are financed partly by membership fees and donations.

Four parties are represented in the Federal Council today. The **SVP** (Swiss People's Party) was founded in 1971 and has been the party with the most voters since 1999. The **SP** (Social Democratic Party) was founded in 1888, the **FDP** (Free Democratic Party) in 1894. The Centre was created in 2021 from the CVP and the BDP.

The **Greens**, founded in 1983, and the Green Liberal Party, GLP for short, are also strongly represented in parliament. The GLP was founded in 2004 in the canton of Zurich and became a national party in 2007. There are also smaller parties such as the EVP or the EDU. Many parties have a youth party for young members.

In Switzerland the large parties govern together; this is called **concordance**. From 1959 to 2003 the so-called **magic formula** applied: two seats for the FDP, two for the CVP, two for the SP and one for the SVP. Today the SVP, SP and FDP each have two seats and the Centre one. That is why the parties often have to make compromises.

In a **democracy** there are several parties between which people can choose freely. In some countries there are two very large parties that take turns in government, for example in the USA. In a **one-party state**, on the other hand, only a single party is allowed, and there are no free elections there. Since 2022 Swiss parties have had to disclose larger donations, so that people can see who finances them.

begriffe.erklaerung: A text in which a party describes its goals.
The cooperation of the large parties in the government.
The fixed distribution of Federal Council seats from 1959 to 2003.
A state in which only one party is allowed.

gewusst: Until 2003 the distribution of Federal Council seats under the magic formula remained unchanged for 44 years.
Since 2022 parties in Switzerland have had to disclose donations of more than 15,000 francs per year and person.

teile.einleitung: Every car in Switzerland carries a number plate, also called a registration plate or licence plate. The two letters on it reveal in which canton the vehicle is registered.
wichtigste: The two letters show the canton, followed by a number.
Zurich has ZH, the Grisons GR, Nidwalden NW.
TI for Ticino comes from the Italian name Ticino.
VS for Valais comes from the Latin name Vallesia.
At the back you can see the Swiss coat of arms and the cantonal coat of arms.
Normal plates are white with black lettering.

abschnitte.text: A Swiss **number plate** starts with **two letters**. They show in which **canton** the car is registered. They are followed by a **number**. You get the plate from the cantonal **road traffic office**. This means every vehicle can be traced to its keeper.

Many abbreviations are easy to guess: **ZH** stands for Zurich, **GR** for the Grisons (Graubünden), **NW** for Nidwalden, that is Nid and Walden. Some come from another language. **TI** comes from the Italian name **Ticino**, because Italian is spoken in Ticino. **FR** comes from the French **Fribourg**; in Fribourg people speak French and German. **VS** stands for Valais (Wallis), in Latin **Vallesia** and in French Valais.

abschnitte.titel: Coats of arms on the plate
abschnitte.text: On the **rear plate** you can see two coats of arms next to the number: the **Swiss coat of arms** and the **cantonal coat of arms**. So you can also recognise the canton from the picture. The front plate only carries the letters and the number. Abroad, a **CH** sticker also shows that the car comes from Switzerland.

Normal car plates are **white with black lettering**. This makes them easy to read. Other vehicles have other colours: mopeds carry small **yellow** plates. Agricultural vehicles such as tractors have **green** plates. Working machines carry **blue** plates.

gewusst: CH stands for “Confoederatio Helvetica”, the Latin name of Switzerland.
In Switzerland the number plate belongs to the keeper and not to the car: with a new car you can keep the old number.

teile.einleitung: The Landsgemeinde is an open-air assembly at which the voters of a canton vote and elect together. Instead of putting a paper into a ballot box, everyone raises their hand. Today the Landsgemeinde only exists in the cantons of Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
wichtigste: The Landsgemeinde is the oldest form of direct democracy in Switzerland.
Today it only exists in Glarus and Appenzell Innerrhoden.
Voting is done by raising hands in a large square.
The Landsgemeinde in Appenzell takes place on the last Sunday in April.
The Glarus Landsgemeinde meets on the first Sunday in May.
Other cantons such as Nidwalden, Obwalden and Appenzell Ausserrhoden abolished it in the 1990s.
In 2007 Glarus was the first canton to introduce a voting age of 16, and it did so at the Landsgemeinde.

abschnitte.text: The **Landsgemeinde** is the assembly of all the voters of a canton. It takes place once a year in a large square, the **ring**. There people vote on new laws, taxes and spending. In addition, the government and judges are elected.

Voting is done by raising hands; this is called a **show of hands**. The Landammann, that is the head of the cantonal government, estimates from a stage which side has more hands. If the result is close, the vote is repeated until it is clear. Anyone may also step forward and make a speech in front of everyone.

Landsgemeinden already existed in the Middle Ages in several places in Central and Eastern Switzerland. In Glarus the Landsgemeinde has been documented since the 14th century. Uri, Schwyz, Zug, Obwalden, Nidwalden and Appenzell Ausserrhoden also used to have a Landsgemeinde. One by one these cantons replaced it with voting at the ballot box, most recently Obwalden in 1998.

For a long time only men were allowed to take part in the Landsgemeinde. In Appenzell Innerrhoden the men used to carry a **sabre** or sword as proof of identity. Only in 1990 did the Federal Supreme Court decide that women in Appenzell Innerrhoden could also have a say at cantonal level. Since 1991 women and men have stood together in the ring there.

The Landsgemeinde in **Appenzell** takes place on the Landsgemeinde square in the middle of the village. The people of Glarus gather on the Zaunplatz in Glarus. In 2006 the Glarus Landsgemeinde decided to greatly reduce the number of municipalities; since 2011 there have been only three. Both Landsgemeinden attract many visitors from Switzerland and abroad every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: The square where the voters stand at the Landsgemeinde.
The president of the cantonal government in some cantons.
A vote in which you raise your hand and the larger side wins.
People who are allowed to vote and elect.

gewusst: At the Glarus Landsgemeinde even 16-year-olds may vote; in 2007 this did not exist in any other canton.
At the Landsgemeinde there is no secret ballot, because everyone can see how you raise your hand.

tx3n2z3.t: Supreme Court of the United States

teile.einleitung: The highest court of the United States is called the Supreme Court. It decides whether laws are in line with the constitution.
wichtigste: Since 1869 the Supreme Court has had nine members: one Chief Justice and eight Associate Justices.
The number nine is not in the constitution but in a law.
The judges are in principle appointed for life.
Since the Marbury v. Madison judgement of 1803 the court may declare laws unconstitutional.
In 1954, with Brown v. Board of Education, it declared racial segregation in schools unconstitutional.
John Roberts has been Chief Justice since 2005 (as of 2025).

abschnitte.titel: The highest court of the USA
abschnitte.text: The **Supreme Court** is based in Washington, D.C. It is the last instance for questions of federal law and the constitution. Since 1869 it has had **nine** members. It is presided over by the **Chief Justice**; the other eight are called Associate Justices. The number of members is laid down in a law, not in the constitution.

New judges are nominated by the **President** and confirmed by the **Senate**. According to the constitution they stay in office as long as they behave well. In practice this means: **for life**. They only leave through death, resignation or impeachment. In this way they are meant to be able to judge independently of elections and politics.

In 1803 the court decided the case of **Marbury v. Madison**. In it, Chief Justice John Marshall declared a federal law unconstitutional. This was the birth of **judicial review**. Since then the Supreme Court can strike down laws if they breach the constitution. In Switzerland, by contrast, the Federal Supreme Court may not strike down federal laws.

A very important judgement came in 1954: **Brown v. Board of Education**. The court decided unanimously that separate schools for Black and white children can never be equal. With this it overturned, for schools, the rule of “separate but equal” from 1896. Many Supreme Court judgements spark great debates because they change life throughout the country.

Since 2005 **John Roberts** has led the court (as of 2025). He was appointed by George W. Bush and is the 17th Chief Justice. In 1981 President Ronald Reagan appointed **Sandra Day O'Connor**. She was the first woman on the Supreme Court and remained in office until 2006.

gewusst: Since the founding of the USA there have been only 17 Chief Justices (as of 2025).
The number of judges on the Supreme Court was changed several times in the 19th century before it was fixed at nine in 1869.

teile.einleitung: In Switzerland men are required to do military service. Women can take part voluntarily. The service begins with recruit school, in which young people receive the army's basic training.
wichtigste: Swiss men are liable for service; for Swiss women service is voluntary.
Before service there is the orientation day and recruitment.
Recruit school usually lasts 18 weeks (as of 2026).
Someone in recruit school is called a recruit.
During service you receive income compensation instead of wages.
Anyone who does not do service pays an exemption tax.
Soldiers keep their personal equipment at home.

abschnitte.text: The Federal Constitution states that every **Swiss man** must do military service. This is called **compulsory service**. **Swiss women** may do military service **voluntarily**. Anyone who cannot do military service for reasons of conscience may do **civilian service**. It lasts longer than military service. Anyone who is not fit for military service often goes into **civil protection**.

First there is the **orientation day**. It takes place in the 18th year of life, that is when you are about 17 years old. There young people find out what options there are. Then comes **recruitment**. There you are **examined** and **tested**. At the end you know whether you will do service and in which unit.

Basic training is called **recruit school**, RS for short. Normal recruit school lasts **18 weeks**. For special units it can last longer. In recruit school the young people are called **recruits**; afterwards they are soldiers. During the week they usually sleep in **barracks**. At weekends they are often allowed to go home.

Anyone doing service cannot work and earns no wages. That is why you receive **income compensation**, abbreviated **EO**. It replaces part of your income. Anyone who is liable for service but does not do it pays the **military service exemption tax**. It amounts to **3 per cent** of income. In this way everyone contributes, either with service or with money.

The Swiss Army is a **militia army**. Most soldiers have a perfectly normal job and only do service from time to time. One special feature: soldiers take their **personal equipment** home with them, for example the **uniform**. That way they are ready for the next period of service. After recruit school, further periods of service follow in the next few years, the refresher courses.

gewusst: Anyone doing military service also receives a small amount of soldier's pay in addition to income compensation.
Civilian service lasts one and a half times as long as military service.

teile.einleitung: The Responsible Business Initiative (in German “Konzernverantwortungsinitiative”) wanted Swiss companies to respect human rights and environmental standards abroad too and to be liable for damage. On 29 November 2020 a narrow majority of the people did vote yes, but the initiative failed because it did not win a majority of the cantons.
wichtigste: The vote took place on 29 November 2020.
50.7 per cent of voters said yes.
The initiative failed because the majority of the cantons said no.
Only 8.5 cantonal votes were in favour, 14.5 against.
Behind the initiative were aid organisations, human rights groups and environmental organisations.
An indirect counter-proposal with reporting duties came into force.

abschnitte.text: Companies based in Switzerland were to respect **human rights** and **environmental standards** **abroad** too. In the event of violations they would have been **liable** for damage, including for companies they control. The initiative was launched by an alliance of over a hundred organisations, including many **aid organisations**. In October 2016 they handed in a good 120,000 signatures.

abschnitte.titel: Majority of the people, but not of the cantons
abschnitte.text: A popular initiative needs a **majority of the people** and a **majority of the cantons**, that is the majority of voters and the majority of the cantons. On 29 November 2020, **50.7 per cent** voted yes. The cantons, however, rejected it: only **8.5 cantonal votes** were in favour, **14.5** against. A majority of the cantons would have needed at least 12. Turnout was around 47 per cent.

It is very rare for a popular initiative to fail because of the cantons despite a majority of the people. Before that, it had only happened to the **tenant and consumer protection initiative** of 1955. The Responsible Business Initiative was therefore only the second. The result shows how the majority of the cantons strengthens the small cantons.

The campaign was one of the most elaborate of recent years. A well-known face was the former Ticino member of the Council of States **Dick Marty** of the FDP, co-president of the initiative committee. The supporters wanted to hold companies to account. The opponents, including business associations and the Federal Council, warned of disadvantages for Swiss companies and of difficult court cases.

Parliament had passed an **indirect counter-proposal**. It came into force after the no to the initiative. Since then, large companies have had to report on **human rights** and the **environment**. In some areas, for example child labour, additional due diligence duties apply. However, the companies do not have to be liable in the way the initiative had demanded.

gewusst: In the cantonal votes, the cantons of Obwalden, Nidwalden, Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft, Appenzell Ausserrhoden and Appenzell Innerrhoden each count as half, which is why there are results like 8.5 to 14.5.
There are 23 cantonal votes in total, so a majority of the cantons needs at least 12.

teile.einleitung: Freedom of the media means that newspapers, radio, television and online media may report freely. The state may not dictate their content to them. Independent media are important for democracy.
wichtigste: The media are regarded as the fourth power in the state.
The Federal Constitution guarantees radio and television independence in designing their programmes.
Anyone affected by false statements of fact can demand a right of reply.
OFCOM supervises radio and television without dictating programmes.
Complaints against broadcasts are decided by the UBI.
Advertising and journalism must be clearly separated.
The media package was rejected by the people in February 2022.

abschnitte.text: In the state there are three powers: parliament, the government and the courts. Independent media are often called the **fourth power** (or fourth estate). They inform the public, put events into context and uncover **abuses**. In this way they keep a check on government, parliament and the courts. To be able to do this, they must be allowed to report freely. That is why the Federal Constitution protects **freedom of the media**.

**Article 93** of the Federal Constitution states that radio and television are **independent** and design their programmes themselves. The state may not dictate their content. Nevertheless there is supervision. The **Federal Office of Communications (OFCOM)** checks, for example, whether broadcasters comply with their **licences**. It may not interfere with the content of programmes.

Anyone who thinks a broadcast is unfair can first turn to an **ombudsman's office**. It mediates. After that the **Independent Complaints Authority for Radio and Television (UBI)** decides. It examines, for example, whether a broadcast has breached the **requirement of fair and accurate reporting**. Its decisions can be appealed to the Federal Supreme Court. Anyone directly affected by a presentation of facts in a medium can also demand a **right of reply**. In it, their own view of the facts is published in the same medium.

Media should clearly separate **advertising** and **editorial content**. Whoever pays must not decide what the journalists write. Hidden advertising that looks like a normal article is called **surreptitious advertising**. It deceives the public and endangers the independence of the media. That is why advertising is usually labelled with words such as “advertisement” or “sponsored”.

For democracy it is important that there are many different media. When a few companies own many media, this is called **media concentration**. Then the variety of voices decreases, which can weaken the forming of opinions. The Confederation wanted to give the media more support. But on **13 February 2022** voters rejected the **media package** with around 55 per cent voting no. Supporters wanted to safeguard diversity this way; opponents feared dependence on the state.

gewusst: The right of reply is regulated in the Swiss Civil Code.
Censorship is expressly forbidden in the Swiss Federal Constitution.

teile.einleitung: Human rights are rights that every person has simply because they are a human being. They apply to everyone, no matter what skin colour, religion, language or origin someone has. On 10 December 1948 the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which is still regarded as the most important document on the subject.
wichtigste: Human rights apply to all people all over the world.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1948.
It has 30 articles.
Article 1 says: all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
10 December is International Human Rights Day.
In 1974 Switzerland ratified the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR).
The UN Human Rights Council is based in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: **Human rights** are fundamental rights that must not be taken away from anyone. They include the right to life, to liberty and to security. The ban on torture and slavery, freedom of opinion and the right to education are also among them. No state may violate these rights arbitrarily.

After the horrors of the Second World War, the states of the world wanted to prevent such crimes in future. On 10 December 1948 the UN General Assembly in Paris adopted the **Universal Declaration of Human Rights**. The American Eleanor Roosevelt played an important role in drafting it. The Declaration has 30 articles and has been translated into more than 500 languages.

In 1950 the members of the Council of Europe signed the **European Convention on Human Rights**, ECHR for short. Anyone who believes their rights have been violated can turn to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. Switzerland joined the Council of Europe in 1963 and ratified the ECHR in 1974. Since then people from Switzerland have also brought cases in Strasbourg.

The UN Human Rights Council, founded in 2006, is based in **Geneva**. The office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights is also there. Many human rights are laid down in the Swiss Federal Constitution as **fundamental rights**, such as human dignity, equality before the law and freedom of religion. Switzerland also stands up for human rights in its foreign policy.

In 1989 the UN also adopted the **Convention on the Rights of the Child**; Switzerland joined it in 1997. Children have, for example, the right to protection, to education, to play and to be heard. Sadly, human rights are still violated in many countries. Organisations such as Amnesty International monitor the situation and draw attention to abuses.

begriffe.erklaerung: The United Nations, an organisation of almost all the states in the world.
To officially recognise an international treaty as binding.
The European Convention on Human Rights, a treaty of the states of the Council of Europe.
The worth that every human being has and that must be respected.

gewusst: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is regarded as one of the most translated documents in the world.
Eleanor Roosevelt called the Universal Declaration of Human Rights a “Magna Carta for all mankind”.

teile.einleitung: The general election in India in 1951/52 was the first election in independent India. It lasted around four months and was at the time the largest democratic election in the world.
wichtigste: Voting took place in many stages from 25 October 1951 to 21 February 1952.
Around 173 million people were entitled to vote.
All adults aged 21 and over could vote, women and men equally.
Symbols helped people who could not read.
The Indian National Congress won 364 of 489 elected seats.
Jawaharlal Nehru remained Prime Minister.

abschnitte.text: India became independent in 1947. The **constitution** of the republic came into force on **26 January 1950**. Today this day is a holiday, Republic Day. The constitution made the first free election possible. The **Lok Sabha** was elected; the name means “House of the People”. The second chamber, the Rajya Sabha, is not directly elected by the people.

The country was huge, and there were hundreds of thousands of **polling stations**. That is why voting took place in many stages, from **25 October 1951** to **21 February 1952**. The organisation was led by **Sukumar Sen**, who became the first Election Commissioner in 1950. Around **173 million** people were on the electoral rolls.

From the very beginning India gave all adults aged **21** and over equal voting rights. It made no difference whether someone was a woman or a man, rich or poor. Many people could not read at the time. That is why each candidate had their own **ballot box** with their name and a **symbol**. This way people could vote correctly even without being able to read.

The clear winner was the **Indian National Congress**. It had led the independence movement and won **364 of 489** elected seats. **Jawaharlal Nehru** had already been Prime Minister since 1947. After his party's election victory he remained in office.

gewusst: Symbols for parties and candidates are still used in elections in India today.
Today India is regarded as the democracy with the largest population in the world.

teile.einleitung: A list combination is formed when two or more parties link their electoral lists. In this way they cooperate in the distribution of seats. In Switzerland list combinations play a big role above all in the National Council elections.
wichtigste: In a list combination, two or more parties link their lists.
The votes of the linked lists are added together in the first distribution of seats.
This means fewer votes are lost that would otherwise not be enough for a seat.
List combinations exist in proportional elections, for example for the National Council.
Usually parties that think alike politically link up.
Within a party there are also sub-list combinations, for example between the main party and its youth party.
List combinations must be registered before the election.

abschnitte.text: In a **list combination** parties join forces for an election. But they still stand with their own lists and their own candidates. The link only has an effect when the seats are calculated. The ballot paper shows which lists a list is linked with.

When the seats are distributed, the votes of all the linked lists are first added together. The group is treated like a single large list. Afterwards the seats won are distributed within the group among the individual parties. For the National Council the **Hagenbach-Bischoff** method is used for the distribution.

Imagine two small parties each have a few thousand votes, but neither alone reaches enough for a seat. If they link their lists, their votes together may be enough for a **remaining seat**. This seat then goes to the party in the group with more votes. Without the link, the votes of both parties would have had no effect.

Within a list combination there can also be **sub-list combinations**. Often a party links its main list with the list of its youth party or a list from a particular region. First the seat is distributed within the group, then within the sub-list. In this way the votes stay as far as possible within the same political family.

List combinations are controversial. Supporters say that fewer votes are lost and small parties have a chance. Critics feel that voters often do not know whom their vote helps in the end. That is why the media report in detail before every election on which parties have linked up.

begriffe.erklaerung: The calculation of how many seats each party receives.
A seat that is still left over after the first distribution.
The party of the young members of a large party.
A method of calculation for distributing seats, named after a physicist from Basel.

gewusst: A list combination can mean that a party gets a seat even though it has fewer votes than another party without a link.
In the canton of Zurich and several other cantons, list combinations are no longer needed in cantonal elections because of the “double Pukelsheim” method.

teile.einleitung: The No Billag Initiative wanted to abolish radio and television licence fees in Switzerland. On 4 March 2018 the people voted on it and rejected it very clearly. The vote sparked one of the most intense media debates of recent years.
wichtigste: The vote on the **No Billag Initiative** took place on **4 March 2018**.
The initiative demanded the **abolition of radio and television licence fees**.
Around **71.6 per cent** of voters rejected it.
**Not a single canton** accepted it.
Turnout was around **54 per cent**.
In 2019 the household levy fell from 451 to **365 francs** a year.

abschnitte.text: The official title was **“Yes to abolishing radio and television licence fees”**. The Confederation would no longer have been allowed to levy reception fees or to **subsidise** radio and television stations. For the **SRG** this would have meant losing most of its income. Many private local radio stations and regional television channels also received money from the fees.

Until the end of 2018 **Billag AG** collected the radio and television licence fees on behalf of the Confederation. In everyday speech its name therefore stood for the fees themselves. Many people simply said they were “paying Billag”. Since 2019 another company has collected the levy. But the name of the initiative is still known today.

Around **2.1 million** voters said no, and only about 834,000 yes. That is around **71.6 per cent** no. Not a single canton accepted the initiative. The highest yes share was in **Schwyz** and **Schaffhausen**, with just over 37 per cent. **Romandy** rejected it particularly clearly: **Neuchâtel** said no with around 78 per cent, just ahead of Jura. At around 54 per cent, turnout was above average.

The fee was not abolished but reorganised. Since **2019** households have paid a **levy that does not depend on devices**. So it no longer matters whether you own a radio or a television. At the same time the amount fell from **451 to 365 francs** per household per year. The level of the levy is still being debated in politics.

gewusst: 365 francs a year is exactly one franc a day.
In the No Billag vote, all 26 cantons rejected the initiative.
